lawyer:
Mr. T.H. Khan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant (In C.A. No.270 of 2003) 

Mr. Mahbubey Alam, Attorney General, instructed by Mr. B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellants (In C.A. No.271 of 2003) 

Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Nurul Islam Bhuiyan, Advocate-on-Record ----- For Respondent No.1 (In C.A. No.270 of 2003) For Respondent Nos.2-6 (In C.A. No.270 of 2003) and For the Respondents, (In C.A. No.271 of 2003) : Not Represented.
parties:
Md. Jahangir Alam (Md) and another (In C.A. No.270 of 2003)
Government of Bangladesh and others ..... Appellant (In C.A. No.271 of 2003)
Vs.
Md. Shamsur Rahman Sarder and others ....... Respondents (In both the appeals)
full_judgment:
S.K. Sinha, J: These appeals by leave is directed from the judgment and order dated 24th August, 2002 of a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 408 of 2002 making the rule absolute and declaring the memo dated 15th January, 2002 of the writ respondent No. 2, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

<u>2. The dispute relates to a piece of land appertaining to S.A. Khatian No.955 of S.A. Khatian No.542 measuring an area of 16 decimals, situates at Bara Magbazar, Dhaka. The parties are at loggerheads over the ownership of the said land and legal proceedings cropped up since 1961. One Shamsul Huda claiming title of the said plot along with another plot through one Biswanath instituted Title Suit No.170 of 1961 for declaration of title and cancellation of deed No. 8142 dated 2nd September, 1961 against Shamsuzzoha Begum in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Bakergonj, Barisal and got an ex-parte decree. According to the writ petitioner said Shamsuzzoha Begum sold the said property to Anis Fatema Begum, the predecessor of interest of the appellant Md. Jahangir Alam suppressing the decree passed in Title Suit No. 170 of 1961. One Abdul Wahed Sarder, also instituted Title Suit No. 371 of 1991 against aforesaid Anis Fatema and others in the First Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title and for further declaration that the deed of Anis Fatema is void, illegal and inoperative. The said suit was also decreed ex-parte on dated 23rd November, 1998. According to the writ petitioner in pursuance of the judgment of the civil court he has been peacefully possessing the disputed land and filed several petition to the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka for mutation of the said land and while his petitions are awaiting decision, he was served with a notice by the writ respondent No. 2 of dispossession for implementation of judgment in Writ Petition No. 165 of 1998, and he was directed to hand over possession to the Kanoongo which compelled him to institute writ Petition No. 408 of 2002 in the High Court Division seeking the above relief.</u>

3. Appellant in Civil Appeal No. 270 of 2003 contested the writ petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition claiming that the writ petitioner Md. Shamsur Rahman has had no right, title and interest in the disputed property, that the ex-parte decree obtained Abdul Wahed Sarder in Title Suit No.170 of 1961 is void and collusive, that he purchased the disputed property from Anis Fatema by registered deed dated 3rd April, 1987 and there upon filed Writ Petition No.165 of 1998 seeking a direction upon the Government to release the property from the list of abandoned property and to deliver possession to him, that the High Court Division upon hearing the parties by judgment and order dated 28th July, 1998 directed the Government including the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka to give delivery of possession to him within 2 months from the date of receipt of the judgment and that the decree obtained by Abdul Wahed Sarder in Title Suit No. 371 of 1991 is collusive and not binding upon him, inasmuch as, Begum Anis Fatema was not alive when the suit was filed and that he has acquired right, title and interest in the property long before the institution in the said suit. The writ respondent No. 2, in the premises, it is claimed, rightly and legally issued the notice upon the writ petitioner with a view to implement the judgment passed in Writ Petition No.165 of 1998.

<u>4. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties by judgment and order dated 24th August, 2002 made the rule absolute observing as under: "In the instant case before us the decision of the civil Court was given in that civil suit (Title Suit No.371 of 1991) which the predecessor-in-interest of the present petitioner (sic)(respondent) was defendant No.1 and the relevant Ministry and the concerned officers were also defendant Nos. 2-4. As the question whether the property is abandoned property or not has already been decided in that civil suit, the decision is binding upon the Government. The present petitioner was not made respondent in Writ Petition No.165 of 1998 and it was not brought to the notice of this Court in that writ petition that there is a decision of the Civil Court about the nature of the property which was subject matter of that writ petition. In view of the above position, we are of the view that the petitioner cannot be evicted form the property in question."</u>

5. Mr. T.H. Khan, learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant contended that the High Court Division on a misconception of law based its decision relying upon the judgment passed in Title Suit No.371 of 1991 in failing to consider that Anis Fatema had no semblance of title when the suit was filed, who was also not alive when the said decree was passed. Mr. Khan further contended that the writ respondent No. 2 issued the impugned notice dated 15th January, 2002 in order to give effect to the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 165 of 1998, in which judgment, the High Court Division, relying upon the Ministry of Land's letter under memo dated 24th August, 1996 approving the decision of the Land Appeal Board releasing the disputed property in favour of Begum Anis Fatema, directed the Deputy Commissioner to effect delivery of possession. It is apparent, as contended, from the said letter that the disputed property is not abandoned property and that the decree passed in Title Suit No.371 of 1991 is not binding upon the appellant.

<u>6. The High Court Division made the rule absolute relying upon the judgment of the civil Court passed in Title Suit No. 371 of 1991. This shows that the sheet anchor of the judgment of the High Court Division is the decree passed in Title Suit No. 371 of 1991 which is apparently not binding upon the appellant since he was not a party in the suit. The reasons assigned by the High Court Division is absolutely devoid of substance, inasmuch as, the day on which the said suit was instituted Anis Fatema had no right, title and interest in the property. In paragraph 11 of his affidavit-in-opposition the appellant asserted that Anis Fatema had transferred the disputed property in his favour by registered deed dated 2nd April, 1987. In this connection Mr. Khan has taken us to the judgment of the said suit and submits that long before the delivery of the said judgment, Anis Fatema's title has been extinguished. On the strength of this deed he had instituted Writ Petition No. 165 of 1998 in the High Court Division and the High Court Division made the rule absolute. Despite those positive statements regarding the acquisition of title by the appellant, the High Court Division observed that the decree is binding upon the appellant as well.</u>

7. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel appearing for the writ petitioner, while supporting the impugned judgment contended that since Anis Fatema's title was extinguished in pursuance of the judgment passed in Title Suit No.371 of 1991, the High Court Division is perfectly justified in observing that the judgment is also binding upon her successor. We find no basis in the contention of the learned Counsel.

<u>8. When a judgment is given in evidence, the party against whom it is given in evidence may, in the proceeding in which it is given in evidence, show that the judgment was obtained by fraud or collusion, and a separate suit to have the said judgment set aside is not necessary. In view of the wide terms used in section 44 of the Evidence Act, it cannot be said that it is not open to a Court other than the Court from which the decree was passed, in cases fraud or collusion, to deal with the matter and decide whether the decree was obtained by fraud or collusion.</u>

9. The High Court Division though noticed that before the suit was instituted, whatever right, title and interest Anis Fatema had that had been extinguished after execution of deed in 1987 in favour of the appellant, on a misconception of law observed that the said decree is binding upon the appellant. The High Court Division had committed another fundamental error in holding that as the government did not appear the said suit, the decree is also binding upon it in failing to notice that after the decision of the Land Appeal Board dated 29th October, 1991, Annexure-6, which was approved by the Government declaring that the property is not abandoned property, the government had no interest in the disputed property. The High Court Division fell in an error in failing to consider that this judgment would in no way affect the appellant's title in the disputed property.

10. According to Mr. Bhuiyan, the transfer of the disputed land in favour of the appellant Jahangir Alam is barred by section 6 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985. If the transfer is barred by provisions of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985, then the suit is also barred by the same provision. It has been provided in section 6 amongst others that no suit or any other legal proceedings shall lie before any Court for declaration that a building is not an abandoned property etc. Mr. Bhuiyan, however, contended that section 6 will not stand in the way in maintaining the suit as framed since there is no existence of building on the disputed property and that the property in question is not included in any of the lists mentioned section 5 of the Ordinance. In elaborating his submission learned counsel tries to make out a case that in section 6, the expression "building" has been used but there is no existence of "building" in the disputed property. This submission is self contradictory, inasmuch as, if the transfer is hit by section 6 of the Ordinance, there is no reason to hold otherwise that the suit is maintainable.

<u>11. What is more, in paragraph 6 of the writ petition the writ petitioner stated, "Even after getting this 0.16 acre of land the petitioner Md. Samsur Rahman Sardar constructed some valuable shops and assets upon the land by huge expenditure of money and man power. "The expression 'building' has been defined in section 2(a) of the Ordinance, which means "any residential or other building or structure of any kind in an urban area and includes the land adjunct thereto and the court yard, tank, place of worship and private burial or cremation ground appertaining to such building". From the above definition there is no gainsaying that building includes any structure in the urban area and any land adjunct thereto. There is no dispute that there are structures on the disputed land as has been admitted by the writ petitioner in the writ petition. In view of this admitted position, there is no merit in the contention of Mr. Bhuiyan. Over and above, admittedly the property has not been enlisted in the abandoned property list in accordance with section 5 of the Ordinance.</u>

<u>12. It is not clear to us how the writ petitioner is claiming right in the disputed property. In the writ petition he did not clarify as to how he acquired title in the disputed property. He stated in paragraphs 6 and 7 that he got possession of the disputed land through Court in pursuance of the judgment passed "in Civil Suit No.371 of 1991". This is totally based upon distorted fact. Abdul Wahed Sarder instituted the above suit who got ex-parte decree. The writ petitioner is neither claiming title on the basis of purchase from Abdul Wahed Sarder nor as a successor of Abdul Wahed Sarder. Admittedly he is not the son of Abdul Wahed Sarder. In such view of the matter, we find that the High Court Division upon superficial consideration of the materials on record made the rule absolute. Therefore, the reasons basing upon which the High Court Division declared the impugned notice illegal are not available to the writ petitioner. In view of the above, the High Court Division committed fundamental error in making the rule absolute.</u>

<u>13. Over and above, the observation that the judgment in Writ Petition No.165 of 1998 is not binding upon the writ petitioner since he was not a party in the said writ petition is equally applicable to the appellant as well. The appellant instituted Writ Petition No.165 of 1998 challenging the inaction of the government in not delivering physical possession despite the direction given by the High Court Division. The appellant did not claim any relief against the writ petitioner in Writ Petition No.165 of 1998. He has acquired no right, title and interest in the property. If he has no interest at all it, is not incumbent upon the appellant to implead him as respondent. Therefore this observation also has no basis at all.</u>

14. On Consideration of the facts and circumstances of the matter, we find substance in the contention of Mr. Khan that the High Court Division on misconception of law and fact made the rule absolute.

15. The appeal is, therefore, allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment of the High Court Division is set aside. Civil Appeal No. 271 of 2003 is disposed of in the terms of the judgment in C.A. No. 270 of 2003.

End.

parties:
Most. Alimonnessa 
(In W.P.No.962/2004)
Most. Razia Khatun 
(In W.P.No.961/2004)
Most.Nurjahan Begum 
(In W.P.No.959/2004)
Most. Aimunnessa 
(In W.P.No.960/2004)
Vs.
The Chairman Rajuk & Others 
(In All the Cases.)
full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan, J: Rules were issued in the above numbered Writ Petitions upon 4(four) separate applications filed by 4(four) petitioners challenging a Memo reflecting the decision of the respondents as per resolution of the special meeting No. 10 of 2003 of the respondents canceling 3 plots out of 4 plots allotted to the petitioners. The Rules were issued in the following terms: 

2. In Writ Petition No. 959 of 2004 the Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order contained in Memo No. RAJUK ESTATE/533/3/ESTHA dated 14.2.2004 (Annexure-F) canceling the allotment of the petitioner's Plot at Nikunja (South) Residential Area, Dhaka shall not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 

3. In Writ Petition No. 960 of 2004 the Rule Nisi was issued upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order contained in Memo No. RAJUK ESTATE/533/1/ESTHA dated 14.2.2004 (Annexure-F) canceling the allotment of the petitioner's plot at Nikunja (South) Residential Area, Dhaka shall not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 

4. In Writ Petition No. 961 of 2004 the Rule was issued upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order contained in Memo No. RAJUK ESTATE/533/4/ESTHA dated 14.2.2004 (Annexure-F) canceling the allotment of the petitioner's plot at Nikunja (South) Residential Area. shall not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 

5. In Writ Petition No. 962 of 2004 the Rule Nisi was issued upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order contained in Memo No. RAJUK ESTATE/533/2/ESTHA dated 14.2.2004 (Annexure-F) canceling the allotment of the petitioner's plot at Nikunja (South) Residential Area, Dhaka should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

6. Since all the writ petitioners have challenged the Memo containing cancellation of their respective plots which were allotted to them as affected persons of that area from where they were displaced, hence all the petitions were heard together, and by a single judgment these 4 Rules are disposed of. 

7. Facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rules are that, the petitioners' father Miazuddin Matbor was the owner of some land in Joar Shahara Mouza, which were acquired vide L.A. Case No. 138 of 61-62. Necessary award was prepared in his name, he received compensation in part. At the time of his demise he left behind his widow, three sons and four daughters, namely, Razia Khatun, Aimonnessa, Alimonnessa and Most. Nurjahan Begum. The four daughters are the petitioners before us. 

8. The Government by publishing the circular published in Daily Ittefaq invited applications from the affected persons for allotment of Residential Plots. The petitioners being heirs of late Miazuddin submitted their applications to RAJUK for allotment of residential plots in their favour. Considering their applications and seeing necessary papers the RAJUK allotted plots of more or less 3 kathas in size to each of the petitioners. Nurjahan Begum Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 959 of 2004 got a plot of 3 Kathas of land which was numbered as Plot no. 8 of Road No. 8. Another petitioner Razia Khatoon being petitioner in Writ Petition No. 961 got allotment of Plot No. 31 of Road No. 8/B. The petitioner of Writ Petition No. 960 Most. Aimunnessa got the plot number 34 of Road No. 3/A. The petitioner of Writ Petition No. 962 of 2004 Mosmt. Alimonnessa got allotment of Plot No. 7 at Road No. 10/A, all the Plots were at Nikunja (South) Residential Area. 

9. After being allotted the plots, the petitioners, as .per the terms and conditions of the allotment deposited full value of the plots as per direction of RAJUK and the possession of the said plots were duly handed over to the petitioners in writ petition no. 959, 961 and 962 of 2004. 

10. No deed was executed and registered between RAJUK and Nurjahan Begum the writ petitioner of writ petition 959 of 2004 and Aimunnessa the writ petitioner in writ petition no. 960 of 2009. But RAJUK entered into an agreement and executed a lease deed with Razia Khatoon the petitioner of Writ petition No. 961 of 2004 and Alimunnessa in Writ Petition No. 962 of 2004. 

11. The petitioners while they had been enjoying possession on their respective plots, all of a sudden were informed by the impugned memo dated 14.2.2004 that the allotment of their plots were cancelled. By the said memo they were informed that in fact out of 4 (four) plots 3 plots had been cancelled and the petitioners would be allotted only one plot. They were also asked to inform RAJUK which plot they would choose to keep in their possession. Thereafter the petitioners sent separate Demand Justice Notices to the respondents asking them to withdraw/ cancel/rescind the impugned Memo but the respondents did not pay any heed to those notices. Thereafter the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the Rule and order of stay. 

12. Dr. Rebeya Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate entered appearance on behalf of the respondents no.1-4 in Writ Petition No. 959 of 2004. 

13. She, by filing an affidavit-in opposition, controverted the material statements made by the petitioner in the Writ Petition, and stated that from an inquiry report dated 17.8.2003 it was found that the present petitioner and her three sisters were allotted 4 plots respectively against their father's award. It was stated that her father was only one awardee and one plot could be allotted jointly in favour of the heirs of the original awardee, herein the present petitioner and her three sisters. The cancellation of the plots was done lawfully on the principle of "one plot for one awardee." As such RAJUK the concerned authority had implemented the Government's decisions lawfully and bonafide to fulfill public demands. She further stated that the Ministry of Housing and Public Works is the controlling authority. They enquired into the matter and found some irregularities. The father of the petitioners received compensation. It was the principle of the authority to allot one plot for one awardee. On 14.2.2004 by its decision RAJUK had only implemented that decision and cancelled three plots of the present petitioners. But the petitioners were asked to chose one plot jointly. She further stated that the plots were not allotted in accordance with law. It was absolutely against the principles of prevailing Rules of RAJUK. 

14. In other Writ Petitions Mr. Mizanur Rahman and Mr. Walilul Islam filing affidavit-in-opposition in Writ Petitions No. 96.0,961 and 962 of 2004 controverted the material statements made in those Writ petitions and adopted the submissions made by Dr. Rabeya Bhuiya. 

15. Mr. Md. Rasheduzzaman Bosunia, the learned Advocate for all the writ petitioners along with Mr. Masud Ahmed Syed in support of the Rule submits that by getting allotment the petitioners acquired a legal right on the plots as bonafide allottee. Without any fault the rights of the petitioners have been taken away by the impugned memo. He further submits that before cancellation of the plots neither any show cause notice was served upon the petitioners nor were they given any chance of being heard, which was violative of the principles of natural justice and as such the cancellation of the impugned memo is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

16. Mr. Rasheduzzaman Bosunia further submits that the respondents after allotting the plots to the petitioners handed over the possession. The full value of the plots were paid to the respondents and as such the petitioners acquired a legal right on the plot and by a stroke of pen their right cannot be taken away and as such the impugned order is liable to be declared illegal and is of no legal effect. 

17. Mr. Rasheduzzaman Basunia further submits that the petitioners were affected persons and each was classified by RAJUK as such, thus each of the petitioners was entitled to get a plot in the area of Nikunja as of their right. As such, the cancellation of the allotment of the plots of the petitioners has been done in clear violation of the established principle of RAJUK and as such the same was done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

18. Since the law points are similar in all the writ petitions, Dr. Rabeya Bhuiyan the learned Advocate submits in favour of the respondent nos. 1-4 in all the writ petitions. She submits that as per the decision of RAJUK only one plot can be allotted to one affected person. Since the father of the petitioners was affected by L.A. Case No. 138/61-62 he was the person who was entitled to get a plot and compensation as well. In his absence his legal heirs can only inherit the property left by him. She further submits that in their applications for allotment of the plots the petitioners did not provide all the relevant facts. In the column of "অংশীদারগণের সংখ্যা" each and every petitioner mentioned "one". In fact all the petitioners were the heirs of the original awardee Miazuddin. She submits that the petitioners got the allotment of the plots by suppression of material facts which is in other words an act of committing fraud and for this fraudulent activity the respondents rightly cancelled the plots allotted in their names. She further submits that since fraud was detected on the part of the petitioners, they did not deserve to get any notice before cancellation of their plots. 

19. We have gone through the writ petitions along with annexures, affidavits in opposition, supplementary affidavits, relevant documents. It appears that the father of the petitioners in all these writ petitions was the affected person. It appears from the list prepared by RAJUK (Annexure-Y) Md. Miazuddin initially was declared as an affected person and the petitioners are his legal heirs which has also been stated in paragraph-4 of the writ petition. Miazuddin died leaving behind his widow Jobeda Begum, 3 sons namely, Md. Abdul Hafiz, M.A. Malek and M.A. Khaleque and 4 daughters namely, Razia Khatun, Aimunnessa, Alimunnessa and Nurjahan. It appears that 8 persons were the legal heirs of late Miazuddin. The property was acquired from Miazuddin, and by acquiring the property the person who was affected was only Miazuddin, no one else. The petitioners and their brothers and mother were. not affected persons at the time of acquiring property for the purpose of receiving any compensation as an awardee. 

20. It appears that the resolution was taken in the 10th Meeting of 2003 of RAJUK following the principle of law. After acquiring property from the persons an award list was
prepared. It is also seen from Annexure-B, the information slip that in respect of C.S. Khatian No. 2161,2162,2180, 2181,2184 and 2185 an award No. 233 was prepared in the name of Miaziuddin and others. Miazuddin received Tk. 9440/- out of total amount of tk. 13,926.50. This is not on the record when Miazuddin died, but it appears that after his death in the name of each petitioner Tk. 402.50 was fixed as award. 

21. Though it is not on the record that under which law Land Acquisition Case No. 138 of 61-62 was initiated, but it is presumed that the said L.A. Case was initiated under the provision of section 93 A of the Town Improvement Act 1953. 

22. As per provisions of section 93A(4)(g)of the said Act, the acquisition procedure ends when the property acquired is finally published by Gazette notification. As per section 93 (A) (5) of the Act, the affected persons or the person interested in the property gets the compensation for such property. It also appears that Miazuddin received major part of his compensation money, it can be presumed that he was properly notified during his life time and after preparing the award list he was given compensation money. At that time the present petitioners were not in the scene and they were not affected persons and as such they were not liable to get any compensation. It appears from the provision of law for acquisition of any land, that the affected persons only get the compensation for the land, crops or any structures standing thereon, and there is no provision to give any plot or any property for being an affected person. It is the practice of RAJUK, when they being the requiring body got the land, from a person, they provide a plot within the area to that person. As per the decision taken by RAJUK they decided to give one plot for one affected person. After allotting plots to the affected person if any number of plots become surplus those plots are distributed amongst the persons according to the quantum of land acquired from the affected persons on pro-rata basis. It does not matter what quantum of land is acquired from each affected person in allotting the plot. Even if a huge quantum of land is acquired from any one person, he would get only one plot as an affected person. It further appears from Annexure-A that every petitioner described herself as the only heir of the affected person, which is contradicted by the petitioners by their own statement made in paragraph 4 of the writ petition. It is admitted by the petitioners that there were 8 persons who inherited the award of the affected person, late Miazuddin. Describing each of the petitioners as sole heir is a clear misrepresentation of fact, but in spite of that the respondents have not totally ignored the claim of the petitioners. In the impugned notice it was simply said that the petitioners were the legal heirs of affected person Miazuddin and they would get only one plot, as if it was alloted to Miazuddin. It has been mentioned by the petitioners that three sons of late Miazuddin had also been allotted plots. Since those matters are not before this Court we shall not go into that and wish to confine our discussion to the plots of the petitioners. The principle followed by RAJUK is that the heirs of late awardee would inherit the plot which the awardee would have received. 

23. Mr. Raseduzzaman during his submission refers one unreported decision pronounced in Writ Petition No. 7566 of 2003,wherein judgment was delivered by a different Bench of this Court on 26.2.2007 and in that decision it was held that-
"RAJUK was under a legal obligation to issue a show cause notice to the petitioners informing them about the irregularities found by the enquiry committee, if any, in allotment of the plot and also about the government decision to cancel the allotment of the plot or any other reason for canceling the allotment of the plot affording the petitioners an opportunity to explain their position."

24. In the aforementioned case no show cause notice was served upon the writ petitioner before cancellation of the plot. In the present case we find that the petitioners by misrepresentation and suppressing some material facts got the allotment which is apparent on the face of the record. We are constrained to say that when the allotment was obtained by dint of fraud, principle of law is "fraud vitiates everything." 

25. Dr. Rabeya Bhuiyan referred to clause 13, of Annexure-C, the allotment letter, in  which it was stated that if any wrong statement is found in the application the respondent reserves the right of cancellation of the plot and also can forfeit the money deposited against the plot. She also refers Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT) Rules, 1969, Rule 10 of which provides as follows: 
"Any application received with false shall be summarily rejected. In case, an allotment is made to any one on the basis of false information in the application and the information is subsequently found incorrect, the allotment shall stand cancelled." 

26. It appears from the record that the fraud has been committed by the petitioners, suppressing some material facts. Since the fraud has been detected it was not required to send any show cause notice to the petitioners before cancellation of the plots. The case referred by the petitioner is quite distinguishable from the present one.
 27. It also appears that in Writ Petition No. 959 and 960 of 2004 no lease deed was executed between the parties and in the other two Writ Petitions being No. 961 and 962 of 2004 lease deeds were executed and registered by the parties. 

28. Mr. Rasheduzzaman submits that since in two writ petitions the lease deeds were registered, the respondents should have gone to the civil Court for cancellation of those deeds in accordance with law. It has been mentioned in the DIT allotment Rules 1969 that "if any information subsequently found incorrect the allotment shall stand cancelled." Misstatement and suppression of facts by the petitioners made the respondent bound to cancel those two deeds. We are of the view that it was not necessary for the respondents to go to the civil court for cancellation of those deeds. As per provision of Rule 10 of DIT Rule 1969, the lease becomes automatically cancelled. 

29. Since it is a lease deed between the public authority and a private party regarding a public property we are of the view that the respondents were not required by law to go to the civil court for cancellation of the deeds especially if it is contended that lease was granted by the lessee without jurisdiction, illegally or beyond the scope of law or on the other hand lease was obtained by fraud. If the deed was executed between two ordinary citizens, of course question of invoking the jurisdiction of the Civil Court for cancellation of the deed arises. 

30. In a lease of a public property for a period of 99 years the ownership always remains with the lessor, in this case RAJUK. Even for the purpose of transfer of any plot it requires permission from the leasing authority to transfer the plots to the new transferee on payment of transfer fees to that authority (RAJUK), which indicates that the leasing authority always reserves the right to take any kind of measure in respect of plots allotted to the persons. At all times the parties remain subject to the conditions specified in the lease deed. Of course this measure must be taken in accordance with law. Law requires at least a show cause notice to be served on the lessee before taking any measure. But if any wrong is detected on the part of the allottee/lessee the authority has the right to take any decision even without serving any notice. In this particular case when fraud has been detected, RAJUK took decision not to allow "that" to be continued. Immediately they have asked the writ petitioners to inform RAJUK which particular plot they wanted to keep as the petitioners were the legal heirs of the affected person late Miazuddin. 

31. Since the allotment of three plots have been cancelled by RAJUK, the RAJUK is duty bound to give back the petitioner money received from them. We are also of the view that the persons who were responsible in classifying and showing the present petitioners as affected persons should be taken to task, so that in future this type of nefarious activities can be prevented. Further, it appears that in 1992 the applications were invited from the affected persons which is evident from Annexure-I of the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner. The contents of the advertisement given by the RAJUK on 27.7.1992 published in the National Dailies runs as follows: 
"মানবিক কারণে উক্ত প্রকল্পে ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত ব্যক্তিবর্গের অসুবিধা সহানুভূতির সহিত বিবেচনা করিয়া মূল বিজ্ঞপ্তির শর্তানুযায়ী তাহাদের প্লট বরাদ্দের আবেদনপত্র অন্যান্য নিয়মাবলী পালনসাপেক্ষে দাখিল করার সময়সীমা আগামী ৩০-৭-৯২ ইং তারিখ পর্যন্ত বর্ধিত করা হইল, যাহা আবেদনপত্রের ফরমে বর্ণিত পেশার (ক) ক্যাটাগরী অর্থাৎ কেবলমাত্র ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত ব্যক্তিগণের জন্য প্রযোজ্য হইবে।"

32. It further appears in Annexure-J of the said affidavit that the petitioners were shown as affected persons, although it is a paper cutting but there is no name of the paper; date of publication is also absent. It appears from Annexure-B that an information slip was obtained from the Dhaka collectorate in which it was mentioned that the subsequent award list was prepared in the name of the petitioners as heirs of late Miazuddin. Each of the petitioners got Tk. 402.50 as compensation. The slip was obtained on 17.8.2000. It appears that vide succession certificate case no. 599/92 the petitioners got their portion of award from the remaining compensation money of late Miazuddin. We have already discussed that it is not on the record when Miazuddin died but from the list of affected persons prepared by RAJUK it appears that only the name of Miazuddin was on the list. But in the subsequent list the petitioners names were included. In our view the petitioners status would be the "heirs of affected persons" but not "affected person". Although the definition of affected person was not given any where but in our view the affected person is the person "whose property was acquired and to whom compensation was paid as affected person." In this case Miazuddin's property was acquired and major portion of compensation money was paid to him and the remainder of the compensation money was paid to the heirs proportionately, and as such no one else but Miazuddin was the affected person. The petitioners and their brothers and mother were the heirs of the affected person. 

33. With the above discussions, we are of the view that since the petitioners do not come within the definition of affected person, they were not entitled to any plot. Since their father was an affected person he was entitled to get a plot, and as heirs the petitioners would inherit only the plot which the petitioner's father would get during his life time. As such the memo issued by the respondents does not suffer any lacking of legal force, and it has been issued by the proper authority. We find no substance in the submission of the learned advocate for the petitioners as well as no merit in these Rules, and accordingly, the Rules are discharged, however, without any order as to cost. 

34. The order of stay granted earlier is hereby vacated.

End.

Farida Begum Minu and Others
Vs.
Abdul Jabbar Being Dead His Heirs Md. Nurul Amin and Others
full_judgment:
Faruque Ahmed, J: This rule at the instance of the defendant petitioners was issued calling upon the opposite parties No.1 and 2 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 22.09.2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 149 of 2002 affirming those dated 31.01.2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 278 of 1993 should not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Short facts of the case are as follows:-The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 as plaintiffs on 24.01.93 filed Title Suit No. 278 of 1993 in the Court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, against the defendants petitioners and the opposite party Nos. 3-9, praying for declaration of title in respect of Ka schedule land and further declaration that Kha schedule Heba deed is illegal, void, inoperatives, not binding upon plaintiffs and for recovery of khan possession in respect of Ga schedule property described in the schedule of the plaint, stating in short that the suit land appertaining to C.S. khatian No. 569, Plot No. 138, measuring an area of land of 2.04 acre and C.S. Plot No. 590 measuring an area of land of 0.33 acre belonged to Wahed Ali and others. The mother of plaintiff No. 1 Chandraban Bibi purchased the land by auction. Thereafter, Chandraban Bibi transferred the land 2.04 acre from the plot No. 138 on 14.09.1949 vide Heba-Bil-Ewaj deed No. 4367 to her two sons Abdul Karim and plaintiff No. 1 Abdul Jabbar. In that deed plot No. 168 has been written erroneously instead of the plot No. 138. Chandraban Bibi had not right, title and ownership over the plot No. 168. The plaintiff No. 1 and his brother owned and possessed the suit land. S.A. khatian No. 667 has been prepared in their names. Plaintiff No. 1 and his brother Abdul Karim transferred 23 decimals land from the plot No. 138 to Intezam and others and they have been owning and possessing that land. Thereafter Government of Bangladesh acquired 89 decimal land from the plot No. 138 by L.A. Case No.159/61-62 Award was prepared in the name of Chandraban, and the plaintiff No.1 and his brother Abdul Karim withdrew the compensation money. Chandraban sold 35 decimals of land from the plot No. 590 to Mather Box and others on 01.09.49 and 85 decimals of land remained in the plot No. 138 which was owned and possessed by the plaintiff No. 1 and his brother Abdul Karim. Thereafter, Abdul Karim died in 1971 laying behind 3 sons, namely, Badsha Miah, Lal Mia and Kokhu Miah and 3 daughters, namely, Samala Khatun, Jamila Khatun and Jahanara Khatun. The defendant No. 4-9 owned 42½  decimals of land from their predecessor, the defendant No. 2,6,7 and 9 sold 21.3333 decimals of land to the plaintiff No. 1 on 23.03.79 vide registered deed No.1053. Defendant No. 4,5 and 6 were minors. Defendant No. 2 was appointed guardian in favour of the defendant No. 4,5,8 by the learned District Judge and with the permission of the Court, defendant No. 2 as a guardian sold 21½ decimals of land in favour of the plaintiff No. 1 on 18.07.1979 vide registered deed No. 3108. In this way the heirs of Abdul Karim sold their 42½  decimals of land. The plaintiff No. 1 has owned .64 decimals of land by way of purchase and gift. The plaintiffs mutated their names and paid rent to the Government and tax to the Municipality and they got Gas line, Water line and paid all rent. The plaintiff approved a plan from DIT (now RAJUK) for constructing building. The plaintiff No. 1 sold .4993 acre of land to others and the rest .1407 acres of land has been owning and possessing by the plaintiff. The defendant No. 1 claiming that he has acquired the suit land from the defendant No. 3 by way of Heva and soon he would enter the suit land. The plaintiff came to known on 16.07.1991. That the defendant No. 3 transferred .13 decimals of land to Nurjahan from the plot No. 138 vide registered deed No. 3061. Nurjahan had no title and interest over the suit land. So her husband the defendant No. 3 could not sell any land from the suit land. The defendant No. 3 has got some land after the death of his wife Nurjahan and he sold the land in favour of the plaintiff No. 1 and his brother Abdul Karim on 10.02.1965. The plaintiffs filed a suit before Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka being Title Suit No. 63/1993 but the suit was filed with formal defect. So the plaintiffs withdrew the suit for filing fresh suit. The defendant No. 3, constructed a building in `Ga' schedule land which is owned by the plaintiff. So the plaintiff has filed this suit.

3. The defendant No. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the materials allegation made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the plaintiffs have no cause of action to file this suit. The suit is not maintainable in its present form. The suit land belonged to Osman Fakir. After the death of 1st husband of Chandraban Bibi, she got married with Osman Fakir. Chandraban Bibi had two sons, namely, Arab Ali Gazi and Kalai Gazi and a daughter Layla Bibi by her previous husband. Thereafter, Abdul Karim, Abdul Jabbar, Noor Jahan and Sohag Banu were born from the wedlock of Osman Fakir and Chandraban, Kalai Gazi died before Chandraban. Thereafter Chandraban died leaving behind two sons Abdul Karim and Abdul Jabbar and two daughters Noor Jahan Bibi and Sohag Banu and the son Arab Ali and a daughter Layla Bibi by previous husband. They have been owning and possessing the land of Osman Fakir and Chandraban. Noor Jahan Bibi died leaving behind only husband Torab Ali. Torab Ali sold all the land which he acquired from his wife, Noor Jahan, sold to Abdul Karim and Abdul Jabber on 10.02.1965 vide registered deed No. 1149 except the land of the plot No. 138. Abdul Karim died leaving behind 3 sons Badsha, Lal Miah and Barek Hossain and three daughters Zamila Khatun, Somela Khatun and Jahanara Begum and a wife Noor Jahan Begum. Abdul Jabbar purchased the land collusively from the minor son of Abdul Karim. He purchased 16½ decimals of land from plot No. 138 on 29.05.1985 by a registered deed No. 1611. Abdul Jabber sold 2½ land to Abdul Awal the son of Sohag Banu from the Plot No. 138 Torab Ali transferred 8 katha of land in favour of defendant No. 1 on 16.07.1991 by a registered deed No. 3061 by way of Heba. Then the defendant No. 1 by way of earth filling spent about 5,00,000/- taka and erected the house on the land. She mutated her name and paid rent to the Government and got electricity, water and Gas line and paid all rent. This plaintiff filed various cases and suits for harassing this defendants. The plaintiff has no right, title and the suit is to be dismissed with costs.

4. The learned trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record decreed the suit. As against that the defendant petitioners preferred Title Appeal No. 149 of 2002 in the Court of the learned District Judge and the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka who heard the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 22.09.2005 dismissed the appeal.

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid appellate judgment and decree, the defendant petitioners obtained the present rule.

6. Mr. Md. Serajul Haq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners placed the revisional application and the impugned judgment and decree and submitted that in the plaint the plaintiffs did not make any statement to the effect that they were in possession of the suit land and the date of dispossession, and that the learned Courts below also did not give any finding to that effect and as such the judgment and decree passed by the learned Courts below are liable to be set aside. The learned Advocate for the petitioners further submitted that the plaintiffs admittedly purchased some land from the contesting defendant No.2 and non contesting defendant No. 4-9, of the disputed plot No. 138 vide registered deed dated 23.03.1979 and 18.07.1979 exhibit-4 and 4 'ka' and that the plaintiffs subsequently got their names mutated and paid government rents vide exhibit-5 ,6 and 6'ka' and as such they were well conversant with the fact that the plot No. 168 were written in the gift deed dated 14.09.1949 exhibit-13, so the present suit though a suit for declaration of title, in fact was a suit for correction of the plot No. 168 in place of 138 and as such the suit for such correction of dag No. is heavily barred by time, but the learned Courts below did not consider this question of limitation at all, and a s such committed error in decreeing the suit and dismissing the appeal. The learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his submission referred to the decision reported in 2 BLC(AD) 134 and 4 BLC 310 wherein it has been held that in a suit for recovery of possession the finding of possession in and dispossession from the suit land is very essential but in the impugned judgment and decree there was no such finding.

7. Mr. M. Hashmat Ullah Sheikh, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, on the other hand, submitted that in the written statement the defendant petitioners said nothing about the question of limitation and no issue was framed on this point and no evidence also has been led by the parties on this point and as such question of limitation cannot be raised for the first time in the revision. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties further submitted that the plaintiffs in their plaint in paragraph No. 12 specifically stated that they were in possession of the suit land all along since 14.09.1949, but subsequently on 15.10.1993 they have been dispossessed from schedule `ga' land. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties further submitted that the finding of fact as arrived at by the learned Courts below being concurrent, in the absence of any misreading or non consideration of the material evidence on record, the impugned judgment and decree .call for no interference by this Court in revision. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties further submitted that though in the deed dated 14.09.1949 exhibit-13 dag number wrongly written as plot No. 168 but the boundary was given correctly of plot No. 138 and as such in case of dispute between plot number and boundaries of the land the boundaries shall prevail and the learned courts committed no wrong in decreeing the suit and dismissing the appeal.

8. On perusal of the judgment passed by the learned trial Court, it appears, the learned trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record found that the plaintiff Abdur Jabbar and his brother Abdul Karim were the owners of plot no. 138 and before that their mother Chandraban Bibi was the owners of plot no. 138 who vide heba-bil-eweaz deed dated 14.09.1949 exhibit-13 gifted the same in favour of heirs two sons Abdul Karim and Abdur Jabbar and in the said deed khatian number was written as 569 and plot number was written as 168, area of land was written 2.04; that in the right side of plot No. 168 in the said deed the word `illegible' was written; that in khatian No. 569 there was no dag as 168; that Chandraban Bibi was not the owner of plot No. 168 of khatian No. 190: that in exhibit-13 plot No. 168 has been wrongly written in place of correct number 138, but the boundary of plot No. 138 was given correctly; that the heirs of Abdul Karim having sold out their entire share in the said plot vide exhbit-4 and 4'ka' the defendants have no subsisting interest in the suit land that except defendant No.1 and 2, other defendants did not claim any interest in the suit land; that the defendant No. 1 and her husband defendant No. 3 got forceful possession in the suit land of schedule-Ga wherein the said defendants did not have any possession earlier. With these findings the learned trial Court decreed the suit.

9. The learned appellate Court, it appears, on consideration of the evidence of P.W.1, 3 ,4 and 5 specifically, as well as the deposition of D.Ws found that the plaintiffs were able to prove their title as well as possession in the suit land and dispossession from `Ga' schedule land and that plot No. 168 was wrongly written in exhbiit-13 in place of correct plot No. 138. Accordingly dismissed the appeal.

<u>10. Thus it shows that though the learned trial Court gave finding regarding title, possession and dispossession as alleged by the plaintiffs and decreed the suit accordingly, but the learned appellate Court though found title of the plaintiffs in the suit land and found that plot No. 168 has been wrongly written in exhibit-13 in place of plot No. 138, but no finding about possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land and their dispossession by the defendants as alleged has been given.</u>

11. The established principle of law is that, in a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession, the plaintiff must prove his title to and possession and dispossession from the suit land. It appears, the learned trial Court gave the finding that the plaintiffs were able to prove their possession and dispossession from `ga' schedule land, but the appellate Court did not give such finding which was very material fur proper adjudication of the matter. So as the evidence of 5 P.Ws and 4 D/.Ws are on record I think it would be proper to consider the deposition on record of the P.Ws and D.Ws by myself and to give a finding regarding possession and dispossession of the plaintiffs instead of sending the case on remand to the learned appellate Court.

<u>12. Accordingly my assessment of evidence is as follows:- P.W.1 Abdur Jabbar in his deposition supported his case as made out in the plaint. He was cross-examined, but nothing contradictory came out in his cross-examination. P.W.2 Haji Din Mohammad Mollah though corroborated P.W. 1 but in cross-examination, stated that the plaintiff No.1 is his Mamato Bhai and the defendants are the heirs of another Mamato Bhai deceased Abdul Karim. He stated that in 1993 in the month of Ashyin/Kartic the defendant started constructing houses in the suit land and the plaintiffs resisted. In cross-examination only there was a suggestion that he is deposing falsely, but nothing material came out to disbelieve him. P.W.3 Abdul Azim stated in his examination in chief that the defendants dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land in October, 1993 and the plaintiffs resisted the defendants. However, in his cross-examination he admitted that he is the son in law of the plaintiff Abdur Jabbar. P.W.4 Md. Abdul Awal in examination in chief stated that both the plaintiffs and the predecessors of the defendants are his maternal uncle. He stated that Badsha Mia dispossessed the plaintiffs from some portion of the suit land in the month of Ashyin/Kartic in 1993. He was cross-examined thoroughly, however, in his cross-examination he admitted that he purchased some land from the plaintiffs and constructed house thereon. P.W.5 Ahmed Hossain is a witness who produced the volume of khatian No. 569.</u>

13. Now let me consider the deposition of the D.Ws. D.W.1 Md. Badsha Miah in his deposition stated the case as made out in the written statement and denied the case of the plaintiff regarding dispossession by the defendants. In examination in chief he deposed regarding the salishnama and proved the shalishnama exhibit-jha. He was cross-examined but nothing material came out. D.W.3 Md. Ashraf Ali corroborated the D.W.1 regarding possession of the suit land by the defendants. He was cross-examined but nothing material came out from his cross-examination. D.W.4 Ahmed Hossain deposed in the Court regarding the volume No. 26 of 1985 wherein the deed No. 1611 was copied. In cross-examination P.W.4 admitted that he purchased some portion of suit dag from the plaintiff who is his mamato vhai.

<u>14. Thus on careful scrutiny of the aforesaid deposition of the P.Ws and D.Ws, it appears, P.W.2 is the of both the parties and P.W.4 also is the of both the parties and as such there is no reason to disbelieve at least P.W.2 and 4 who are common relation's of both the parties. This P.Ws specifically stated about the title to and possession and dispossession of the plaintiffs on 15.10.1993 from the suit land by the defendants. So, in my opinion, the learned appellate court committed no error in decreeing the suit and in dismissing the appeal by the impugned judgment and decree calling for interference by this Court in revision.</u>

15. Accordingly, the rule is discharged however, without any order as to costs and the order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby vacated.

16. Send down the L.C. Records immediately.

End.

vs.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J: This Rule was issued directing the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 28.02.93 passed by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 260 of 1989, affirming the Judgment and order dated 16.9.89 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 265 of 1986, should not be set aside. We are also disposing of the application for mandatory injunction along with this Rule.

2. Plaintiffs are the petitioners before this court. They instituted the aforesaid title suit praying for a decree declaring that the plaintiffs and other co-sharers have easement right in 'C' schedule roads and also for a direction upon the defendants not to block the 'C' schedule roads in any manner whatsoever. After filing the suit they also filed an application under Order XXXIX, rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restraining the defendants from closing the 'C' schedule roads till the final hearing of the suit. An order of maintaining status quo was passed by the court on 30.9.86. It was the case of the plaintiffs that they are the owners of 'A' schedule lands, since 1956 and the defendant opposite parties are owners of 'B' schedule property since 1958. Two 6 feet wide roads which merged with the Tree School Street by-lane from 'A' schedule property are the disputed roads. The plaintiffs and their predecessor-in-interest and other co-sharers had and have been using the said roads for more than 25/30 years, but the defendants were trying to block the same and hence they were compelled to file the instant suit and also file an application for temporary injunction with a prayer for ad-interim injunction.

3. The opposite parties as defendants filed written objection against the application for temporary injunction. Their case was that CS Khatian No. 115 is a big holding containing many plots. CS Plot No. 180 was measuring 2.97 acres of land. The plaintiff petitioners purchased some land from the said plot No. 180 and are the owners of the same. The defendants also purchased some other portions of plot No. 180 and thereby they have become the owners of the same. Other persons also are owning and possessing the balance land of the said plot No. 180. This CS plot No. 180 was never partitioned by metes and bounds and till that date it was in ejmali. The owners by purchase have been enjoying their respective shares by amicable arrangement. If the suit plot is demarcated and partitioned, all the co-sharers will get separate road in their Saham. There is no easement right of the plaintiffs in the disputed roads. The eastern boundary of the defendants is marshy land and the eastern side is the petitioners land. So, the question of plaintiffs using the defendants land for going to eastern boundary of the defendants land, which runs to the southern boundary of the plaintiffs land, does not arise at all and the plaintiffs have not been using the said roads.

4. Before hearing of the injunction matter, on the prayer of the plaintiff, the trial Court passed an order appointing an Advocate Commissioner for local inspection in order to ascertain some points including that whether the electric line, gas line, water and sewerage line have been installed through the disputed roads by the inhabitants of the area including the plaintiffs. However, the learned Advocate Mr. Shikdar A. Salam, as an Advocate Commissioner, went to the locality and visited and inspected the two disputed roads in presence of both the parties and submitted a report on 3.6.89 which shows the through the disputed roads the gas line, electric line, water and sewerage line of the plaintiffs and other co-sharer inhabitants of the CS plot No. 180 have been installed. Against this report the defendant opposite parties also filed a written objection. After hearing the parties, the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, by his order dated 16.9.89 refused the prayer for temporary injunction, although at the time of admission of this suit and on the application of the plaintiffs the trial Court passed an order on 30.9.86 directing the defendants to maintain status quo in respect of the suit lands. Against this order dated 16.9.89 the plaintiffs preferred an appeal which was heard and disposed of by the Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 260 of 1989. However, after hearing the parties the learned Additional District Judge, dismissed the appeal by affirming the order of the learned subordinate Judge, by her order dated 28.2.93. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order of the learned Additional District Judge, the plaintiff petitioners preferred this Revisional application and obtained the rule. From the record it appears that at the time of issuance of the Rule, an order of status quo was passed and the court directed the petitioners to put in the requisites within 24 hours. As the petitioners failed to put in the requisites within 24 hours from the date of the order due to inadvertence and mistake of the lawyer, the order of status quo passed by this court was not effective.

5. Mr. Delwer Hosssain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that in a case like this a local inspection was necessary and for that reason on the prayer of the plaintiffs an Advocate Commissioner was appointed who visited the disputed roads and submitted his report Against the report of the Advocate Commissioner, the defendants also submitted written objection. He submits that without legally considering that report of the Advocate Commissioner the learned Subordinate Judge ought not to have passed the order refusing to grant temporary injunction or maintenance of status quo. He submits that at the time of issuance of the show cause notice in respect of the application for injunction the learned subordinate Judge passed an order for maintaining status quo in this matter. It appears from this application that the Advocate Commissioner visited the disputed roads and had submitted his report stating that the disputed roads are the common roads of the inhabitants of the area and through the disputed roads gas line, sewerage line, electricity connection and water line have been taken by the inhabitants including the plaintiff petitioners. It has been categorically stated in the report that gas line, sewerage line, electric line and water connection were taken through the common roads to the house of the plaintiffs and others of that area.

6. Mr. Md. Moonir, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, submits that since that report of the Advocate Commissioner was not still accepted after hearing the objection, it cannot be considered by this court. No order on the Advocate Commissioner's report was finally passed by the trial Court. But the fact remains that on the order of the court, Advocate Commissioner was appointed who visited the disputed roads and made local inspection in presence of the parties and submitted his report and against which an objection was also filed by the defendants and those are on record. So, prima facie, this report of the Advocate Commissioner may form a strong circumstance along with other materials available on records of this case in support of the allegations of the plaintiff petitioners. Further, the learned Subordinate Judge ought to have considered this report first and thereafter he ought to have proceeded with the hearing of the application for injunction in view of the fact that the court itself had passed an order of maintaining status quo and for appointment of Advocate Commissioner. This is clearly a non-application of mind of the learned Subordinate Judge.

7. We have gone through the Revisional application, counter affidavits and the judgments of the two courts below from which it appears that both the plaintiff petitioners and the defendant opposite parties and others are owners of the land of CS Plot No. 180 by way of purchase. It also appears that CS plot No. 180 comprises an area of 2.97 aceas of land and the plaintiff petitioners purchased some portions of the said plots and opposite parties also purchased some portions of the said plots and some other persons also purchased the remaining portions of the same plot and by mutual arrangement and not by legal partition all these co-sharers by purchase have been using and possessing this CS plot No. 180. In the very written statement of the defendant opposite parties they also admitted the position that till today there was no official partition of the suit property and the co-sharers by purchase are using the same by mutual arrangement. It was also stated in the order of the Appellate Court below that the plaintiffs and the defendants are the co sharers by purchase of the suit plot and unless the legal partition is made there, all the parties have equal right upon each and every inch of the land. So, it is an undisputed fact that CS plot No. 180 is a big plot, part of which was purchased by the plaintiffs and another part of which was purchased by the defendant opposite parties and the remaining portions were purchased by some other purchasers and all of them have been possessing the same jointly by mutual arrangement amongst themselves.

8. Mr. Moonir submits that in a case regarding easement right such an order of maintaining status quo or injunction cannot be granted. We have seen the prayer of the plaintiffs and there are two portions of the prayer one for common right to use the disputed roads and another prayer for directing the defendant opposite parties not to block the 'C' schedule two small roads, Since the suit plot was not legally and finally partitioned amongst the co-sharers and since the prayer in the plaint was made for directing the defendants not to block the suit roads to the prejudice of the plaintiff petitioners, we are of the view that in a case like this the order of maintaining status quo by both the parties should have been the proper order till the disposal of the suit. Both the courts below, prima facie, found that both the plaintiffs, and the defendants are co-sharers by purchase and they are possessing and using the properties by mutual arrangement in a case like this one party should not do anything causing any prejudice and inconvenience to the other party particularly in the common roads and passages.

9. Mr. Delwer Hossain has produced before this court the certified copies of two sale deeds by which some of the defendants purchased some portions of the suit plot No. 180. Registered sale deed No. 4330 dated 23.6.58 is the deed of purchase of defendant No. 2 He produced the certified copy of another registered sale deed No. 4328 dated 23.6.58. It was the sale deed of defendant No. 1. In the schedule of sale deed No. 4330 it was clearly written that on the north side there is six feet wide road for common use and on the southern side six feet wide road given by the purchasers of that plot for their own use. In the other deed also we find in the schedule that there was existing six feet wide common road. Both the deeds were of the years 1958. So, from the two deeds of the defendants it appears that there were two six feet’s wide roads in the suit plot No. 180 since 1958 and with those common roads the defendants purchased the part of the suit plot.

10. Mr. Delwer Hossain has also submitted before us the RS Khatian Nos. 1675 DP and 1623 DP. From these two RS khatians it appears that RS plot No. 1923 is road and RS Plot No. 1927 is also road. When RS operation was made, those two disputed small roads were recorded as roads giving two separate plot numbers, namely, 1923 and 1927. Copy of the RS map was also produced before the court which clearly shows that RS plot No. 1927 is road and RS plot No. 1923 is also a road. One Mst. Ajeri Khatun's name was recorded in DP khatian No. 2054, the name of Rafique Ahmed was recorded on DP khatian No.1662 and the name of one Ekramunnessa was recorded in DP Khatian No. 34 as they all purchased some portions of the aforesaid CS plot No. 180 and in all these Khatians the plot Nos. 1923 and 1927 were shown as roads. So, the aforesaid papers as filed by Mr. Delwer Hossain clearly show that in the recent RS Khatian the two disputed roads were recorded as road vide plot Nos. 1923 and 1927. The opposite parties failed to raise any objection regarding their two registered sale deeds, RS records of right and RS Map showing the two disputed roads as RS plot Nos. 1923 and 1927.

11. Both the courts below considered the case on the point of easement right. But from the facts as described in the plaint as well as in the written statement it appeared that all the co-sharers of the plot had the common right to use the disputed two roads since 1958 in view of the fact that their documents of the year 1958 clearly disclosed in the schedule that there are two six feet wide roads in the area for common use of the inhabitants. Since all the parties, that is, the plaintiffs and the defendants are the co-sharers by purchase and since two roads were used by them and others as common passage, in the matter of granting injunction or passing an order of status quo, the court below ought to have considered this matter from that angle so that the action of the defendants might not have prejudiced the interest of any of the inhabitants of the area including the plaintiffs in using the two common roads which were continuing since the time of their purchase in 1958. But, unfortunately, the courts below have considered the case from a wrong angle.

12. Further, the Lower Appellate Court put much reliance upon the result of a criminal case initiated by the defendants against one Chanu Miah. It was alleged that the predecessor of the plaintiffs was allegedly trying to make a road on the land of the defendants for which the defendants instituted criminal case No. 140 of 1972 in the year 1972 under sections 448 and 332 of the Penal Code. Ultimately that criminal case was compromised in between the parties. What are the terms and conditions of that compromise were not incorporated in the order of the learned Additional District Judge and no evidence was placed before the court as to how and in what terms that criminal case was compromised out of court in between the parties. Such a compromise in the criminal case, the terms of which are not known to us, cannot be ground for refusing the prayer for status quo or temporary injunction in a case like this where the legal partition has not yet been effected amongst the co-sharers of the suit plot No. 180. Rather they are using their respective share by mutual arrangement. So, the findings of the learned Subordinate Judge on this point of compromise of the criminal case cannot be accepted by us.

This court issued a Rule on 17.5.93 and at the time of issuance of the Rule an order of status quo was passed on condition that the requisites would be put in within 24 hours. Mr. Delwar Hossain submits that due to inadvertence of the learned Advocate of the petitioners the requisites could not be put in within the time prescribed by the court. He submits that during pendency of this rule, on 29.5.94 the defendant opposite parties forcibly closed the two west ends of the two disputed roads by constructing brick walls which are six feet’s wide and five feet high and thereby closed the entrance of the plaintiff petitioners through those two common roads. Just after the defendant opposite parties forcibly closed the aforesaid two roads on 29.5.94 in spite of protest, the plaintiffs filed before this court an application for injunction with a prayer for mandatory injunction. In this application for mandatory injunction dated 9.6.94 the plaintiff petitioners have stated in paragraph 11 to the effect that so long, that is, before 29.5.94 the defendant opposite parties did not close the disputed two roads since the institution of the suit in 1986.

13. The plaintiffs came to know that the defendant opposite parties collected bricks, cement and other materials to close the west ends of the two disputed roads with the help of some local miscreants. On coming to know of the above preparation of the defendant opposite parties, the plaintiff petitioners lodged a general diary entry in Dhanrnondi Police Station vide general diary Entry No. 1589 dated 18.5.94. On such general diary entry the Officer-in-Charge Dhanmondi Police Station, visited the spot, verbally warned the parties to wait for the decision of the High Court Division regarding the disputed matter and not to indulge in any forceful action. In spite of that the defendant opposite parties were attempting to close the said two disputed roads by raising brick walls in the west ends. The plaintiff petitioners finding no other way filed an application before the Ward Commissioner No. 50 requesting the Ward Commissioner to interfere into the matter. On receipt of the application the Ward Commissioner issued notices upon both the parties on 27.5.94 directing them to attend his office on 28.5.94 at 07-00 PM with their respective documents and papers. The plaintiff petitioners and the opposite parties appeared before the Ward Commissioner on 28.5.94, but the Ward Commissioner was reluctant to interfere into the matter as the case has been pending in the High Court Division. Taking advantage of this situation the opposite parties with the help of local goonda elements forcibly closed the west ends of the said two disputed roads on 29.5.94 by constructing two brick walls in spite of strong Objection and protest raised by the petitioners and others.

14. Thereafter, the local elites of the area and the inhabitants of that locality tried to settle the matter amicably. 5.6.94 was fixed as a date for holding a salish over the matter, but due to non-co-operation of the defendant opposite parties no salish could he held. Mr. Delwar Hossain now submits that in spite of the best effort of the plaintiff petitioners, they failed to resist the defendant opposite parties from constructing those two new walls in the disputed two roads. Such illegal construction of the walls by the defendant opposite parties completely stopped the plaintiff petitioners and others to use the two disputed roads although the water line, gas line and sewerage line have been taken under the disputed roads to the houses of the plaintiffs. It is submitted that the house of the petitioner No. 1 is attached with southern 6 feet wide road and the house of the petitioner Nos. 2 and 3 are attached with northern side 6 feet wide road. So, the plaintiffs are in great hardship and inconvenience due to the illegal construction of the two brick walls on the two disputed roads. In the circumstances as stated above Mr. Delwar Hossain prays for mandatory injunction.

15. In the counter affidavit dated 6.7.94 sworn on behalf of the opposite parties, it is stated in paragraph 8 that the "defendant-opposite parties never constructed any wall on 29.5.94, but the opposite parties constructed their boundary walls around their respective land after their purchase." It was further stated that the petitioners submitted that" the disputed roads were closed on 29.5.94 that is, more than one month ago and, as such, it proves that they are not facing any inconvenience to ingress and outgress from their houses. "In their other affidavit-in-opposition dated 13.7.94 it is stated that the opposite parties had already constructed the walls and closed the disputed roads and, as such, this Rule is not maintainable. From the above averments made in two counter affidavits by the opposite parties it appears to us that there was no wall on the two disputed roads up to 29.5.94 and the opposite parties constructed the walls on 29.5.94 closing the two disputed roads to the great prejudice of the plaintiffs and others. The opposite parties failed to produce any materials before this court showing as to what urgency led them to construct the disputed two brick walls closing the two small common roads to the prejudice of other co-sharers of the same plot

16. Mr. Moonir has referred to the case of K. Mohideen Ibrahim vs. M Muhammad Abdullah AIR 1978 (Mad) 97. Relying upon this judgment Md. Moonir wanted to submit that the plaintiffs cannot acquire an easement right unless he acts with the knowledge that it is a case of dominant and servant tenement and he is exercising a right over property which does not belong to him. If he enjoys a right under the supposition that he is the owner of the property he does not acquire an easement. But in the same decision it was held that in the case of a common wall, a co-owner is entitled to a reasonable use of the wall owned in common. It appears to us that the aforesaid decision is more helpful for the plaintiff petitioners than the defendant opposite parties in view of the fact that the very intent of the decision is that over a common wall all the co-owners have equally right to use. Here in this case the two common roads which are there since 1958 and the same being recorded in the RS record of rights as roads, should be used by all the co-sharers by purchase of the area and they have the right to use the same and none of the co-sharers has got any right to block or stop the common roads.

<u>17. Mr. Delwar Hossain has given us a further information that after illegally constructing two walls in the west ends of the two disputed roads on 29.5.94, the defendants instituted a new suit namely, Title Suit No; 162 of 1994 in the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka on 5.6.94 for permanent injunction with a prayer that the plaintiff petitioners (who are defendants there in that suit) shall be restrained by way of permanent injunction from disturbing or breaking or demolishing the two walls constructed on 29.5.94 and after filing that suit, the defendant opposite parties obtained an order of maintaining status quo in the matter on 5.6.94. Mr. Delwar Hossain has placed before this court a copy of the plaint of the aforesaid Title Suit No. 162 of 1994 and submitted that the defendant-opposite parties as plaintiffs suppressed all the facts .of the present case in which the trial Court as well as Lower Appellate Court passed two orders and that this revisional application is pending before the High Court Division. He submits that by suppressing all these things and through misrepresentation and by misleading the learned Assistant Judge, the defendant opposite parties obtained an order of status quo. We have gone through the copy of the plaint of Title Suit No. 162 of 1994 and it appears to us that the defendant opposite parties had totally suppressed the facts of the present case right from the court of the learned Subordinate Judge up to the High Court Division where this Revisional application is pending.</u>

<u>Since with regard to these two disputed roads the High Court Division is in seisin of the matter, the defendant opposite patties cannot obtain any other order from any other court in respect of the self-same two common roads by filing a separate suit suppressing all these facts. In such a situation the order of status quo passed in Title Suit No. 162 of 1994 will not have any effect in respect of the two disputed roads and the construction of the two walls on the two disputed roads. It is really unfortunate that though the defendant opposite parties were fully aware of the present case as well as the Revisional application pending before this court, they suppressed everything and filed a separate suit and obtained an order of status quo. This type of misleading the court and suppression of facts are totally disapproved by us. It clearly shows the malafide motive of the opposite parties with regard to a pending proceeding before this court.</u>

18. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record as we have discussed above, we are of the view that this is a fit case where an order of mandatory injunction is required to be issued on making the Rule absolute in this Revisional application. We have perused the judgments of both the courts below and it appears to us that both the courts below committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice and, as such, their judgments and orders cannot be sustained in law. For ends of justice the plaintiff petitioners are entitled to an order of mandatory injunction.

19. In the result, this Rule is made absolute and the impugned judgment and order dated 28.2.93 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 260 of 1989 affirming the judgment and order dated 16.9.89 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 265 of 1986 are hereby set aside. The defendant opposite parties are directed to maintain status quo ante that is, before 29.5.94 in respect of the two "C" schedule roads till the disposal of Title Suit No. 265 of 1986. The defendant opposite parties are also directed by way of mandatory injunction to demolish the disputed two walls, which they constructed on 29.5.94 on the two west ends of the 'c' schedule two roads, within three weeks from date, failing which the trial Court shall execute the order of mandatory injunction by demolishing the two walls on the two disputed common roads as stated above in accordance with law. The order of maintaining status quo passed in Title Suit No. 162 of 1994 by the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka, will not have any bearing in execution of our order of mandatory injunction passed herein.

There will be no order as to costs. Let a copy of this judgment be immediately sent to the trial Court for execution of the mandatory injunction.

End.
