parties:
Tasmina Chowdhury and 12 others ----- Writ Petitioners
Vs.
Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others ----- Respondents
                  [In all the Writ Petitions]
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan J: In all the writ petitions being Writ Petition No. 933 of 1990, filed by Mrs. Tasmina Chowdhury, Writ Petition No. 941 of 1990 filed by Sharif Giyasuddin Khan, Writ Petition No.944 of 1990 filed by Mrs. Nazmun Nahar, Writ Petition No. 945 of 1990 filed by Dr. Ahmed Farukh and Mrs. Zahanara Begum. Writ Petition No. 998(A) of 1990, filed by Abdur Rahman, Writ Petition No. 999 of 1990, filed by Md. Shamim, Writ Petition No. 1022 of 1990 filed by Mrs. Yasmin, Writ Petition No. 1023 of 1990 filed by Mrs. Bilkis Sitara, Writ Petition No. 1024 of 1990 filed Mrs. Azimunnessa, Writ Petition No. 1025 filed by Mrs. Selina Akhtar. Writ Petition No. 1048 of 1990 filed by Md. Motahar Hossain Mojumder, Writ Petition No. 1079 of 1990 filed by Farhad Hossain Khan and Writ Petition No. 1080 of 1990 filed by Sultan Shariar Firoz, Rules Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the respondent No. 1 shall not be directed to rescind, cancel and/or withdraw the notice said to have been published in the Daily Inqilab dated 10-7-89 contained in Annexure-C (Writ Petition No. 941 of 1990 Annexure-F) to the petition touching the title of the petitioner's land as contained in Annexure-B to the petition or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Pending the disposal of the Rules the parties were directed to maintain status-quo in respect of the petitioners peaceful possession of the disputed land.

3. Though the petitioners are different in the Writ Petitions and Rules were issued on different dates the claim of interest of the petitioners in the land are similar and the point of law involved are the same and hence all the Writ Petitions are taken up together for hearing and, as such, heard analogously and disposed up by the same judgment.

4. The facts common to all the writ petitioners are stated below:

The land meaning 18.87 acres was acquired by Dhaka Improvement Trust (now RAJUK) for the construction of a link road from Tejgaon Industrial Area to Gulshan Residential Area in LA Case No. 55 of 1958-59. After construction of the Residential Area link road from Tejgaon Industrial Area certain low lying lands acquired under the scheme remained unused and vacant after completion of the link road from Tejgaon Industrial Area to Gulshan Residential Area. The affected persons of LA Case No. 55 of 1958-59 namely, Abdul Khaleque and eleven others filed Title Suit No. 129 of 1975 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka challenging the validity of requisition and acquisition of lands in the said LA Case No. 55 of 1958-59. The suit having been decreed on 10-4-1976 on declaration to the effect that the Gazette notification of acquisition of land dated 27-6-1960 is void and without any legal effect. After the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 129 of 1975. Abdul Khaleque and 11 others rued petition before the Board of Trustees of DIT, now RAJUK, for mutual settlement and also for abandoning of acquisition under section 92 read with section 93 of Town Improvement Act, 1953. The Board of Trustees referred the application to a Special Committee for detailed examination and to submit its report with recommendation. The Special Committee of DIT, in which the representative of respondent No.1 was present, after thorough examination of the case in consideration of the legal position and in view of the fact that the land on the northern side of the road is not being used or utilised by DIT and is not required for the purpose for which it was acquired the Committee recommended that the Board may consider the prayer for the release of the land in favour of original owner. After evaluation of the report of the Committee a registered deed of agreement was executed between RAJUK and Respondent Nos. 3 and 4 on 2-4-84. The petitioners in the respective Writ petitions purchased some land being a part of Khatian No. B/571 Dag No.565 by different registered sale deeds executed by Respondent No. 4 on 26-6-89 and on different dates as mentioned in the respective deeds and after the purchase developed the same filling earth at a huge cost with the intention to build residential houses there. In January 1990 the attention of the petitioners was drawn to the notice published in the daily Inqilab on 10-7-89 stating that the land is the Khas land of the Government. But no notice was served upon the petitioners asking them to hand over possession of the same to the Respondent No. 1. Thereafter, a registered deed of sale was executed between respondent No. 4 Shah Jalal Housing Limited and Capital Properties Ltd. The petitioner after serving demand for justice notice on the respondents and having not received any reply filed these Writ petitions and obtained the instant Rules.

5 Mr. KS Nabi, the learned Advocate with Mr. Shaheed Alam appeared for the petitioners, Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appeared for the respondent Nos. 1-3 and respondent No.4 has been represented by his Counsel Mr. Moinul Hoque.

6. It is submitted on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned notice dated 10-7-89 has infringed the petitioners' fundamental right to property as contained in Article 42 of the Constitution inasmuch as the said notice is wholly uncalled for, unwarranted and has been made in arbitrary exercise of power and is neither backed by any law nor by anything having the force of law. It is submitted that the acquisition and requisition of lands required by RAJUK is dealt with by Special Statute, namely, Town Improvement Act, 1953 and not by general provision as contained in Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and rules framed thereunder. The notice is not only illegal and contrary to law but also malafide inasmuch as the property has been released and vested in the petitioners pursuant to sections 92 and 93 of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and the respondent No.1 cannot call in question the legality of the release of the property dated 4-2-84. It is further submitted that the right of the property accrued through validly executed deeds of sale in conformity with the relevant provision of laws of Transfer of Property Act, Registration Act, Town Improvement Act 1953, etc. cannot be taken away by means of a mere public notice having not the support of any law. In the face of registered deed of sale only a court of competent jurisdiction on reasonable grounds can call in question for rectification of the deed under the provision of section 39 of the Specific Relief Act.

7. Affidavit-in-opposition and further affidavit have been rued on behalf of the respondent No.1.

8. In the affidavit-in-opposition it is submitted that the CS Plot No.565 is the Khas land of the Government and the respondent No. 4 M/s. Shahjalal Housing Limited cannot execute any deed as owner and, as such, the claim of right and title of the petitioners in respect of the aforesaid land is not legal and valid in the eye of law. The land in question having belonged to the Government in Khas nobody other than the Government can execute any deed of agreement in respect of the same. It is submitted that there is no provision to release the proposed land in question under sections 92 and 93 of the Town Improvement Act of 1953 and the DIT cannot do anything without the consent of the Collector, Dhaka and whatever has been done by the Board is not done as per rule and hence the petitioners cannot get any relief in the present Writ petitions. It is also submitted that the notification dated 10-7-89 in the daily Inqilab issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka stating warning to the general people not to come in contact as purchaser or seller with Puleswari Housing Society as the land in question belongs to the Government in Khas and in that notification there is no mention of the name of the petitioners and M/s. Shah Jalal Housing Society and hence the question of serving notice personally on the petitioner does not arise. In the above context the petitions filed at the instance of the petitioners are not maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution.

9. In the supplementary affidavit it is stated that similar question of fact raised in the Title Suit No. 383 of 1983 (re-numbered as Title Suit No. 83 of 1985) filed by the alleged purchasers Abdul Khaleque Munshi and 9 others as plaintiffs against the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others for declarations of title is pending in the Court of First Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. Same questions of facts have also been raised in another suit being Title Suit No. 217 of 1989 filed by the M/s. Capital Property Limited against the Government was declared and the appeal against the judgment and decree being Title Appeal No.380 of 1990 is pending in the First Commercial Court (Subordinate Judge), Dhaka wherein the appellant, Government has obtained an order of stay of operation of the judgment and decree of trial Court. It is also stated that Title Suit No.129 of 1995 filed by Abdul Khaleque Munshi was decreed ex parte. The suit was filed by Abdul Khaleque, the predecessor of the petitioners suppressing the judgment passed in SA No.685 of 1970 of the High Court Division and that subsequently in CP No. 84 of 1974 the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court affirmed the said judgment of the High Court Division. In the said judgment the petitioner's predecessor Abdul Khaleque Munshi and others were declared as mere bargaders in respect of the suit Plot No. 565 and it was held that they had not acquired tenancy right under the Bhawal Court of Wards Estate. he land in CS Plot No. 565 was acquired by the Government from the then DIT as khas land of the Government and the compensation assessed therefor was deposited in the Government fund in LR Head No. 7 (Photocopy of Judgment in SA No.685 of 1970 by the High Court Division and the photo copy judgment in CP No. 84 of 1974 by the High Co Division are Annexures 1 and 2 respectively). Abdul Khaleque Munshi obtained the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 125 of 1975 suppressing the judgment passed in CP No. 84 of 1974, DIT had no authority to come to a mutual settlement. Sections 92 and 93 of Town Improvement Act empowers DIT to relinquish its claim only when the possession of the property is not taken over and Gazette notification is not published. After delivery of possession and Gazette notification, Deputy Commissioner is the only authority to handle the acquired property as an authorised agent of the Government. The petitioner's predecessors by playing fraud upon the DIT managed the execution and registration of agreement (Annexure-A) which is not binding upon the Government. It is submitted that a number of Civil suits filed by both the parties are pending in different civil Courts and the petitioner's predecessors have also taken recourse to the alternative remedy by way of filing suits and the questions at issue in the said civil suits are essentially the same as that of the present Writ petitions remedy under section 102 is not available. The petitioners knowing full well about the fraud of their predecessors have purchased the parcels of land in dispute and so they are parties to the fraud and that being so, neither the petitioner nor their predecessors, had any right, title, interest and possession in the suit plot which is the khas land of the Government. The Government has legally published the notice in the newspaper in which the name of Capital Property Ltd. was mentioned and, as such, the petitioner has no locus standi to file this petition. In the further supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the Respondent No. 1 the photo copy of the judgment and decree of Title Suit No. 89 of 1982, judgment of SA No. 347 of 1965 have been annexed as Annexure-3-3(a) and 3(b) respectively.

10. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the Chairman, Respondent No. 3 RAJUK it is submitted that the land was acquired in LA Case No. 55/58-59 for the construction and the area of land actually acquired was 18.57 acres and not 14-49 acres as stated. The Dhaka Improvement Trust entered into an agreement with Abdul Khaleque and 11 others and not with Shah Jalal Housing Ltd and Abdul Kalam Azad signed the agreement for the remaining party to the agreement.

11. An affidavit-in-opposition has also been filed on behalf of respondent No. 4 Managing Director M/s. Shah Jalal Housing Ltd which is said to have subsequently been turned to Capital Property Ltd. It is stated that out of the entire disputed acquired land measuring 27.89 acres was shown as Khas land of the Government and the remaining land was handed over to DIT having been acquired by the Government. It is submitted that Abdul Khaleque Munshi and others became the tenants under the Government. The respondent No. 4 filed the photo copy of the certified copy of the plaint (Annexure-1) certified copy of the judgment (Annexure-2) arising out of the suit and the memo of appeal (Annexure-4). In the supplementary affidavit the photocopy of the petition relating to delivery of possession consequent on the agreement by DIT and the map along with the finding of the review committee have been filed making those annexures.

12. In all the Writ Petitions Managing Director M/s. Shahjalal Housing Estate has been impleaded as respondent No. 4 stating that the petitioners became the owners of the portions of their respective land by way of purchase from respondent No. 4. Thus the claims of the petitioners in respect of the land is dependent on the proof of the claim of the respondent No. 4. that the land was free from any type of encumbrance. Though the points involved are similar and the interest of the petitioners and the respondent No. 4 are also similar, the learned Advocate for the petitioners Mr. KS Nabi and Mr. Moinul Hoque, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.4 while arguing approached the case apparently from different angles of vision but their ultimate object is the same.

13. Mr. KS Nabi, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in all the Rules, took us through the petitions, supplementary affidavits, affidavits-in-opposition and supplementary affidavits and further affidavit in opposition filed by the respondent Nos. 1, 2 3 and 4 and submitted that the petitioners acquired valuable right by way of purchasing the lands from the respondent No. 4 M/s. Shah Jalal Housing Limited, who purchased from Abdul Khaleque Munshi, who in turn purchased the same from DIT as per deed of agreement dated 14-2-84 (Annexure-A) and in that view of the matter the impugned notice dated 10-7-89 (Annexure-C) is hit by the petitioners fundamental right as enshrined in Article 42 of the Constitution. The learned Counsel argued that the petitioners had acquired proprietary right secured by sections 92 and 93 of the Town Improvement Act 1953 and read with section 49 of the Registration Act. It is further argued that from the deed of acknowledgment of claim vide annexure A it appears that the Government as well as the Deputy Commissioner were parties to it and, as such, they acted arbitrarily publishing notice in the newspaper on 10-7-89 under section 79 of the Evidence Act and also under the relevant provisions of the Transfer of Property Act and such proprietary right cannot be disturbed by issuance of the impugned notice dated 10-7-89 published in the newspaper. Mr. Nabi then argued that the claim of land by the Government as Khas land and acquisition of property in LA Case No.7/58-59 dated 27-6-60 is inconsistent inasmuch as the Government is not required to acquire land for utilising the same for development purpose by the Government or through statutory body where the land belongs to the Government itself.

14. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the property has been released as surplus unused land under sections 92 and 93 of Town Improvement Act 1953 by a statutory registered agreement for consideration by RAJUK consequent on the resolution adopted in the meeting of the committee held in the chamber of ADC(Rev.), on 23-4-82 in which it was decided to release the property in favour of Khaleque Munshi and others and the petitioners having purchased the land after taking note that the property has been released by due process of law the petitioners are the bonafide purchaser by registered instrument which carry with it the presumption of valid transfer and can only be nullified by the court of competent jurisdiction. Mr. Nabi cited the case decided in WP No. 1041 of 1992 in February 1995 (Jahanara Rashid vs. Government) The learned Advocate also pleaded the effect of promissory estoppel stating that the Government having released 13 acres of land on 2-4-84 by registered deed No. 3092 in favour of Khaleque Munshi cannot now resale and deny the legality of the transfer.

15. In the case of Secretary, Ministry of Industries, Nationalised Industries Division vs. Saleh Ahmed and another reported in 46 DLR (AD) 148 it is held:

"Having taken the decision on agreement the mill in question will be returned to their former owners it is not available to the Government now to say that the decision had been revised. In the factual background the Government is estopped from denying unilaterally that no such arrangement has taken place."

16. It is submitted that after releasing the property by way of the registered deed of agreement by DIT they have got no right to resile on it which is not justified. The Government is therefore, under obligation to abide, by their commitment.

17. The case reported in 43 DLR (AD) 137 has also been cited in support of the contention of learned Counsel for the petitioner.

18. Mr. Moinul Hoque, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent No. 4 Managing Director Jalal Housing Ltd, joined his voice with the petitioners in challenging the notice published on 10-7-89 in the Daily Inqilab vide Annexure-C to the petition but his manner of attack is slightly different from that of the petitioners counsel Mr. KS Nabi. In the affidavit filed on behalf of the respondent No.4 it is stated that the Capital Properties Ltd. has stepped into the shoes of M/s, Shah Jalal Housing Ltd. It is stated that out of the entire land only 27.89 acres were shown as khas and compensation was paid therefor. In the supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of respondent No. 4 the photocopy of the possession paper has been annexed with its map as Annexure I and the report of the Review Committee have been filed. From the report it appears that the question as to how much land of plot No.565 was Khas and how much was privately owned could not be determined otherwise than by a civil suit. In the further affidavit filed on behalf of the respondent No. 4 on 16-2-95 the judgment and decree of TS 89/62 passed by the 1st Subordinate Judge, Dhaka has been annexed. The suit filed against Abdul Khaleque was dismissed on 30-3-64. Title Appeal No. 134 of 1964 filled by Abdul Khaleque and others was dismissed by the same judgment by the Additional District Judge, 1st Court Dhaka. Thus from the lengthy argument of Mr. Moinul Hoque it boils down that the land which was acquired by the Government at the instance of RAJUK was not the khas land of the Government and the acquisition in LA case was declared invalid by the decree of the 4th Sub-Judge Dhaka passed in TS No.129/75 on 24-7-76. The ex parte decree was upheld on appeal on 14-2-84 and hence practically there was no acquisition (5 DLR 81 relevant 84 void ab initio) under section 27 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and under section 27 of the State Acquisition Act has been referred in support of his contention.

19. Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.1, opposed the Rule and contested the claim of the petitioners on various grounds by filing affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit in opposition. In the affidavit-in-opposition it is asserted that the land of CS Plot No.565 was the khas land of the Government and nobody other than the Deputy Commissioner could deal with the property and hence Abdul Khaleque and others and, for that matter, Shah Jalal Housing Ltd. (respondent No.4) has not acquired any title by the deed of agreement, even if entered with RAJUK. The person from whom the petitioners have claimed to have purchased the land having no valid title the question of petitioners becoming the owners does not arise. It was further submitted that in respect of the Khas land of CS Dag No. 565 of Tejkunipara Mouza there was notification on 10-7-89 in the Daily Inqilab by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka giving caution to the general public not to come in contact as purchasers or sellers with Fuleswari Housing Society, the land in question having belonged to the Government as Khas land and in that notification there was no mention of the name of the petitioners and, as such, the writ petitions are not maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution. In the supplementary affidavit it is further stated that on similar question of facts having been raised in Title Suit No.383/83 renumbered as Title Suit No. 83 of 1985 filed by the petitioner's alleged predecessor Abdul Khaleque and 9 others as plaintiffs against the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others for declaration of Title is pending in the Court of 1st Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. Another suit being TS No. 217 of 1989 filed by the Capital Property Ltd., having been decreed the Government. has preferred appeal being Title Appeal No.380 of 1990 and the said appeal is pending in the First Commercial Court Dhaka and in the said appeal Government has obtained an order of stay of the operation of judgment and decree of the trial Court. The suit being TS No. 129 of 1975 filed by Abdul Khaleque Munshi was heard and decreed ex parte. The judgment and decree passed in SA No. 685 of 1970 by the High Court Division affirmed by the Appellate Division in CP No. 84 of 1974 has been suppressed. In the said judgment Khaleque Munshi and others were declared as Bargaders under the Bhawal Court of Ward Estate. It is also stated that land of CS Plot No. 565 was acquired by the Government. for DIT as Khas land of the Government and the petitioners' predecessor by playing fraud upon the DIT managed to get the deed of agreement (Annexure-A) executed and registered in their favour and the said agreement is not binding upon the Government inasmuch as DIT has no authority to execute the same. The learned Deputy Attorney-General referred to the case reported in 71 CWN (Cal) 385 with regard to the existence of alternative efficacious remedy and jurisdiction of the High Court to entertain the case. In the said case it is held:

"Where the question of title to property is involved and there are serious disputes with regard to title to such property the Writ jurisdiction of this Court is not a proper forum for adjudication of such disputed questions of title."

20. In the said Single Bench decision reliance were placed on the Full Bench decision of the said court reported in the case of Abanindra Kumar Maity and another vs. AK Majumdar and others in AIR 1956 (Cal) 273. Reliance were also placed on the case of Tansingh Nathmal vs. The Superintendent of Taxes, Dhubri and others reported in AIR 1964 (SC) wherein it was held:

"Resort to that jurisdiction is not intended as an alternative remedy for relief which may be obtained in a suit or other mode prescribed by statute".

<u>21. In the case of Shafiqur Rahman vs. Certificate Officer, Dacca and another reported in 29 DLR (SC) 232 it is held.</u>

<u>"It is no doubt true that in England the existence of alternative remedy is not a distinct bar to the issue of a writ in the nature of certiorari if the order under challenge is without or in excess of jurisdiction. As has been observed in the case of Muhammad Amir Khan vs. Controller of Estate Duty (1961) 13 DLR (SC) 105, that the rule as to alternative remedy is not a rule of law but a rule by which court regulates its own proceeding and does not generally entertain any such proceeding which can be more appropriately investigated in an alternative forum but in a case where the order is absolutely without jurisdiction and does not involve any investigation of facts or consideration of evidence the necessary relief can be more appropriately and expeditiously given in writ jurisdiction."</u>

22. If is further held:

"If the alternative remedy is adequate and equally efficacious, in that case such an alternative remedy is a positive bar to the exercise of the Writ jurisdiction even though the Writ concerned is in the nature of certiorari".

23. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has also argued that the names of the petitioners were not given in the notification and hence they are not aggrieved persons and for that matter have no locus standito file the Writ application.

24. In the case of Tasbhai Moibhai Desai vs. Roshan Kumar Haji Bashir Ahmed and others reported in (1976) SCC 671 it was observed.

"It is true that in the ultimate analysis, the jurisdiction under Article 226 in general and certiorari in particular is discretionary. But in a country like India where Writ petitions are instituted in the High Courts by the thousands many of them frivolous a strict ascertainment, at the outset, of the standing of the petitioner to invoke this extraordinary jurisdiction, must be insisted upon. The broad guidelines indicated by us, coupled with other well-established self-devised rules of practice such as the availability of an alternative remedy, the conduct of the petitioner, etc. can go a long way to help the Courts in weeding out a large number of writ petitions at the initial stage with consequent saving of public time and money."

Relying on the same decision the learned Deputy Attorney-General submitted that the petitioner's names having not appeared in the notice published they are transfers and, therefore, they have got no right in the present case justifying the issuance of the Writ of certiorari at their instance. On the contrary, the result of the exercise of these discretionary powers in favour of the petitioner will be against public policy.

25. It is also submitted that nothing short of a sale deed could pass title and hence by the alleged agreement with their predecessor, the petitioners cannot claim title under section 54 of Transfer of Property Act. The Town Improvement Act does not authorise respondent No.3 to reliquish the claim of the acquired land in favour of the so-called owner. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further argued that the predecessor of the petitioners having not acquired any interest in the land in question the petitioners cannot also claim any right, title and interest in the same. It is also argued by him that when the question of title to the property is involved and there are serious dispute with regard to title regarding the property in question the Writ jurisdiction is not a proper forum for adjudication of such disputed question of title involving facts. In support of the above contention he relied on the cases reported in 61 Indian Appeal and PLD 1953 Lahore 575.

26. Now let us turn to the stand taken by DIT in regard to the claim of the petitioners. In the affidavit sworn by respondent No.3 it is stated that 18.57 acres of land was acquired in LA case No. 55/58-59 for the construction of the link road between Gulshan and Tejgaon Industrial Area of Dhaka Improvement Trust entered into agreement with Abdul Khaleque and others.

<u>27. Mr. Ziaur Rahman, Khan the learned Advocate appeared for the respondent No.3 RAJUK. Though the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 4 Mr. Moinul Hoque and the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed made lengthy arguments citing a long line of decisions in support of their respective submissions covering a wide range of areas, we do not consider all those as relevant for the disposal of the Rule and therefore, will try to confine ourselves to the relevant issue centring round the moot question raised before us. In the above mentioned 13 Writ Petitions notice dated 10-7-89 published in the daily Inqilab has been impugned by the petitioners. This notice was issued and published in protest against the notice published by M/s. Capital Properties Ltd. on 29-3-89. Neither the Capital Properties Ltd. is a party in the writ petition for it is made known by any of the parties as to what was the notice about as published by the M/s. Capital Properties Ltd. The contents of the notice dated 10-7-89 is in the nature of caution given by the Deputy Commissioner to the intending purchasers in respect of the land of Plot No.565 and nothing more than that. From this it does not appear that the notice has in any way validated the right of any person in any manner whatsoever. In LA Case No.55/CC 58-59 about 18.57 acres of land of Plot No.656 along with 10 other plots of Khatian No. B 572 of Mouza Tejkunipara PS Gulshan formerly Tejgaon, was acquired for the construction of Link Road from Tejgaon Industrial Area to Gulshan Model Town. The area of Plot No. 565 is 77.21 acres and hence it is not known how much land of Plot No.565 was acquired. After the construction of link road certain low lying land remained unutilised and vacant but the quantum of unused land have not been mentioned. It is urged that by registered deed of agreement dated 2-4-84 between respondent Nos.3 and 4 respondent No.4 got unused land measuring about 13 acres in 9 plots including Plot No.565 but how much land of Plot No.565 the respondent has got is not stated specifically. The petitioners are said to have purchased some parcels of land of Plot No.565 from the respondent No A Managing Director M/s. Shah Jalal Housing Limited but in the impugned notice the name of Shah Jalal is not mentioned and the M/s. Capital Property Ltd. which has been mentioned is not a party in the Writ Petitions. Annexure-A (Schedule-B) shows that part of CS Plot Nos. 417, 418, 419, 567,480, 481,482, 565, 560/669 measuring more or less an area of 13 acres of land was to be released as per agreement in favour of Abdul Khaleque, son of late Amjad Ali and 11 others represented by their legally constituted attorney Syed Abdul Kalam Azad, Managing Director Shah Jalal Housing Ltd. The total area mentioned is 77.21 of Plot No.565. Abdul Khaleque son of Late Amjad Ali and others represented by Shah Jalal Housing Ltd. got more or less 13 acres of land in ten plots including disputed Plot 565. In Annexure-A (Schedule-B) there is no mention of the quantum of the land agreed to be released from Plot No.565 and, therefore, the quantum of land agreed to be released in unascertained and unspecific. As the area of land stated to have been released from Plot No.565 cannot be ascertained without physical measurement the dispute remaining as such, we are of the view that such disputed question of fact cannot be decided in a Writ petition. It is necessary to determine how much land of Plot No. 565 is in Khas possession of the Collector and in the possession of the individual owners including the respondent No. 4. This is also a question of fact. From the report of the review committee dated 16-2-93 it appears that TS No. 383 of 1983 of the 3rd Court of Sub-Judge Dhaka subsequently transferred to the 1st Court of Sub-Judge Dhaka and renumbered as TS 83/85 is with regard to the land in plot No.565 brought by and at the instance of Abdul Khaleque Munshi and others and was pending till the submission of the report.</u>

<u>In the case reported in PLD 1964 (SC) 636 it is held:</u>

<u>"The principle is now well settled that a proceeding in the Writ jurisdiction is more in the nature of a summary proceeding in which examination of disputed questions of fact of a complicated nature is not as a general rule undertaken nor investigation of title to property made. It provides means of obtaining a speedy decision in a case where a clear disregard of a statutory obligation or duty has resulted in the infringement or denial of a legal right about the existence of which there is not any reasonable dispute or controversy."</u>

28. Relying on the above view we find that disputed question of facts are involved in the instant case. Writ jurisdiction is not the proper forum for seeking remedy. Moreover, in the notices issued the name of the predecessor of interest M/s. Shah Jalal Housing Ltd. is merely a word of caution to the public used against the M/s. Capital Properties Ltd. who is not a party in the writ petitions.

29. For the reasons as stated above, we are of the view that the Writ is not maintainable and the Rules are liable to be discharged.

In the result, the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule issued at the instance of the plaintiff in Title Suit 80 of 1988 for permanent injunction.

2. Trial Court decreed the suit by its judgment dated 22-11-88. The Subordinate Judge, Maherpur allowed Title Appeal 154 of 1989 preferred by the defendant Government, by its impugned judgment dated 19-6-90 and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit for permanent injunction.

3. Case of the plaintiffs, now petitioners, in short, is that the plaintiffs 1 and 2 are full brothers. Plaintiff 1 took settlement of 2.05 acres land from plot 545/51. Plaintiff 2 took settlement of 0.66 acres land from same plot i.e. 545/51 and so also plaintiff 2 took settlement of 1.39 acre land from plot 15211545/73 on the same date being 10-10-1966 in Settlement Case 1/XII/65-66. Plot 1521/545/73 containing 1.39 acre land is not the suit land. So plot 545/51 is the suit land and area of the suit land is 2.71 acres.

4. Plaintiffs allegation is that although after taking settlement in the aforesaid manner they are in possession of the suit land on payment of rent to the government, the government is trying to give settlement of the suit land to the defendants 1-4 who have made application for the same as landless agriculturist, and the defendants also threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit land. Hence the suit.

5. Defendants 1-4 as well as defendants 6 and 7 filed two sets of written statements and contested the suit. Defendants' case is that, both the plaintiffs who are full brothers jointly took settlement of 0.66 acre land from plot 545/51 and 1.39 acre land from plot 545/73. Total land being 2.05 acres in the aforesaid settlement case on the aforesaid date. So the defendant denies the settlement in respect of 2.05 acres land to the plaintiffs. Defendants' further case is that by forgery, plaintiff created a separate holding being 2746 in respect of said 2.05 acres land showing a separate plot being 545/51 and also shown to have been taken settlement of the same from the government collusively and fraudulently.

6. It is also the case of the government that the defendants 1-4 have already made written prayer for settlement of the suit land of the suit holding to them as landless agriculturists. Defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit contending that the plaintiffs have no prima facie title in respect of the entire suit land and also plaintiffs are not in possession.

7. Further contention of the defendant is that since the question of complicated title is concerned the plaintiffs should have filed a suit for declaration of title and should make the prayer for permanent injunction.

8.Both parties led their respective evidence.

9. Trial Court decreed the suit believing claim of settlement of the plaintiffs on the basis of Exts 1- 1(a). Defendants admit settlement made by Ext. 1 i.e. in respect of 0.66 acres land and 1.39 acres land from the plot 545/51 and 545173. Trial Court found also possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. Trial Court decided title of the plaintiffs in favour of them.

10. Defendant took appeal. The appellate Court wrote out a detailed and precise judgment. Appellate Court found that the plaintiff could not prove even prima facie title over the entire suit land. Appellate Court also opined that the plaintiffs' possession in the entire suit land is not lawful. In fact the appellate Court found title and possession of the plaintiff in respect of said 0.66 acres land only of suit plot No. 545/51

11. In this context, I have heard both the learned Counsels for a reasonable length. Perpetual injunction is to be granted under section 54 of the Specific Relief Act. It reads as follows:

"Perpetual injunction when granted:

Subject to the other provisions contained in, or referred to by, this Chapter, a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favour of the applicant, whether expressly or by implication."

The term 'obligation' has been defined in section 3 of the Specific Relief Act which is as follows:

"Obligation' included every duty enforceable by law."

12. To measure obligation in the present case is to consider whether the defendant government has an obligation towards the plaintiff not to violate the possession of the plaintiff or in other words, not to dispossess the plaintiffs from their alleged possession in the entire suit land.

13. So to get an order of permanent injunction, plaintiff must prove that the government has granted settlement of the suit property to the plaintiff, at least, prima facie and the plaintiffs have got exclusive possession. Decisions in this subcontinent as to granting of permanent injunction is very much divergent decision in the case of Manindra Nath Sen Serma vs Bangladesh, reported in 1984 BLD (AD) 285. In that case, their Lordships of the Appellate Division while considering the question of granting permanent injunction according to Mr. Siddique, have held that even if the plaintiff failed to prove his title, it cannot disentitled him from a decree for permanent injunction if he can prove possession.

14. Reading the whole judgment in respect of that decision, I do not find that the submission of the learned Counsel gets support in the manner as has been made before this court. Facts of that case also differ from the present case. No doubt the headnote of the reported decision also seems to be misleading.

<u>15. In the case of Rafizuddin Ahmed vs Mongla Barman and others, reported in 43 DLR (AD) 215. In para 8 their Lordships have held as under:</u>

<u>"In a simple suit for permanent injunction with regard to a disputed landed property the relief is available to a person who is in possession. The Court may enquire incidentally into the respective claims of the parties to the suit for determining whether the plaintiff has got a prima facie case i.e. whether he is in possession of the disputed property and entitled to the specific relief of permanent injunction. If the dispute involves complicated questions of title the plaintiff must establish his title by filing a regular suit for declaration of title. A simple suit for permanent injunction should not be allowed to be used as a testing device for ascertainment of title."</u>

16. In the present case, question of title no doubt is very much involved and it is complicated. Since the plaintiffs claim settlement of 2.72 acres land, whereas the defendant government admits only settlement of 2.05 acres in two plots, and only 0.66 acres within the suit plot.

17. Appellate Court decided the appeal finding, inter alia, that the plaintiff could not prove  prima facie title and exclusive possession upon the entire suit land.

18. Mr. Siddique, the learned Counsel also cites the decision in the case. of Kalyan Krishna Goswami vs Madhyapara High School and another, reported in 15 BLD, 509 wherein a Single Bench of this court has held in para 19 as follows:

"Now I would like to consider the legal aspect of the case. It appears from the end of the earlier judicial pronouncement that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is to prove exclusive possession of the suit land and incidentally a prima facie title to the suit land. If these two requirements are fulfilled by the plaintiff, only then he is entitled to get a permanent injunction. If we look to section 110 of the Evidence Act we find that this section embodied the well known principle of Roman Law that possession is prima facie proof of ownership and, when therefore, a person is in possession of a property the presumption of ownership is highly in his favour and under section 110 the onus of proving that he is not the owner is on the person who asserts that he is not the owner."

19. Here also the question of prima facie title and exclusive possession have been given topmost priority which are very much lacking in this case from the plaintiffs' side.

20. Mr. Siddique cites the decision in the case of Abdul Kader Mondal and others vs Akbor Mondal and others, (47 DLR 237) wherein the learned Single Judge of this court have decided the principle in granting permanent injunction in Para 8 finding, inter alia, as follows :

"Even if a plaintiff is in possession of land without any title he is entitled to protect such possession through an injunction from the court of law. But such injunction will not debar the true owner from getting his title established and to recover possession thereof in a proper proceeding. The petitioners having proved their exclusive possession in the suit land decree of perpetual injunction in their favour without a prayer for declaration of their title in the suit is valid in law."

But unfortunately, in the present case, the appellate Court as the last and final court of fact has found that the plaintiff could not prove prima facie title in respect of whole land and exclusive possession over the same.

21. A meticulous reading and consideration of judgments of the courts below reveals that the question of settlement of entire suit land to the plaintiffs is very much disputed and it creates a doubt and a legal lacuna over the title of the plaintiffs.

22. Mr. Neogi, the learned Assistant Attorney-General supports the judgment of the appellate Court citing the decision in the case of Md Shah Jahan and others, vs Mir Hossain and others, reported in 17 BLD (AD) 218, where in para 7 of the decision their Lordships have held as under:

"The trial Court dismissed the suit. On appeal by the plaintiff the appellate Court as the final court of fact, reversed the judgment of the trial Court and decreed the suit on proper assessment of the evidence on record. Since the findings of the appellate Court do not suffer from any legal infirmity nor are they vitiated by any procedure affecting the merit of the case, the case is concluded by findings of fact and it calls for no interference under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure".

In the case of Belayet Hossain vs Nurul Alam Mir and others, reported in 42 DLR (AD) 20. In para 7 of that decision it has been held as follows:

"A person in wrongful possession of property is not entitled to be protected against the lawful owner by an order of injunction and a trespasser is not entitled to perpetual injunction against the owner of a property."

23. Government is admittedly the owner of the suit land. The plaintiffs could not prove their title and exclusive possession in the instant case.

<u>24. Illegal possession in whatever manner it has been obtained if not found legalised otherwise such as by adverse possession or by subsequently acquiring title, it cannot be protected.</u>

<u>25. In the case of Rafizuddin Ahmed vs Mongla Barman and others, reported in 43 DLR (AD) 215 it has been held that when the dispute involves complicated question of title, plaintiff must prove his title by filing a suit for declaration of title.</u>

26. Mr. Siddique submits that the DW 1, the Tashilder has admitted settlement of the suit land to the plaintiffs and their possession. But from the documentary evidence that is the Ext 1 series which are the title deeds of the plaintiffs they could not prove their settlement of the entire suit land. So, the oral evidence of the DW 1 cannot be accepted as barred under sections 91 & 92 of the Evidence Act. Therefore, Tahsilder's evidence is of no legal substance.

27. For the reasons and discussions made above, I find no substance in this revision and as such the Rule is liable to be discharged. In the result, the Rule is discharged with cost, the suit is dismissed. Send down the records of the courts below at once.

End.
