parties:
Abdul Quader Chowdhury ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Sayedul Hoque & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of the judgment and decree of reversal passed by the learned District Judge, Noakhali.

2. The opposite parties Nos. 1 to 11 hereinbefore me instituted Title Suit No. 564 of 1985 for declaration that order passed by the defendant No. 2 the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Rev.) cancelling the lease of the plaintiffs on 15.8.85 is void, illegal and not binding on the plaintiffs. The case of the plaintiffs-opposite parties was that the land in suit measuring 78.23 acres in plot No. 123 of Mouza Char Wapda was recorded in a block during Diara Survey in the names of the different persons on the basis of their title and possession. The land of plot No. 123 is a reformed land and subsequently recorded in khatian No.1 as khas land of the Government. The Government settled the said land measuring 78.23 to the different persons including the plaintiffs in perpetual lease. They paid the salami after execution and registration of the Kobuliats and the lease-hold lands were recorded in their names and sub-plots Nos. 5, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19 and 20 were created in the names of the lessees. The plaintiffs were in possession on the basis of their respective settlement on payment of salami and rents. But the father of the petitioner collusively and fraudulently got 32.50 acres of land out of 78.23 acres recorded in his name without any title and possession therein. The petitioner thereafter started Miscellaneous Case No. 100 of 1975-76 and obtained shaham by influencing Circle Officer (Rev.) on 23.10.75, 31.10.75 and 10.1.76 in respect of 32.5 acres of land out of the plot No.123 wherein the plaintiffs were not made parties. The plaintiffs instituted a suit for permanent injunction in the Court of Munsif, 1st Court, Sadar, Noakhali against the petitioner and others and also filed an application for temporary injunction restraining the defendants not to proceed with the demarcation of the land on the basis of shaham as granted in the Miscellaneous Case No. 100 of 1975-76. The prayer for injunction was rejected by the learned Munsif loading to Miscellaneous Appeal No. 188 of 1976 which was dismissed by the lower appellate Court on 24.11.1974. Thereafter the petitioner also filed an application on 20.6.85 for cancellation of the lease created in favour of the plaintiffs before Mr. MA Karim, the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali and S.A. Petition Case No. 20 of 1985-86 was started and the Additional Deputy Commissioner by his order dated 15.8.85 cancelled the lease of the plaintiffs.

3. The defendant No. 3, petitioner herein contested the suit by filing written statement. His case was that his father Idris Miah was the owner in possession of 32.50 acres of land on the east side of block 81/123 comprising 78.23 acres of land. But as the said land as wrongly recorded in the name of the Government in khas of Khatian No. 1 his father filed objection case before the Objection Officer on 23.10.68, which was allowed and 32.50 acres of land was recorded in the name of his father by opening a separate diara Khatian No.100 noting 6 annas 13 gondas share in plot No. "423 and on his prayer Miscellaneous Case No. 100 of 1975-76 was started for demarcation of the land and separate shaham for 32.50 acres of land in plot No. s1/123 was allowed by the Circle Officer (Rev.) and he had been possessing the land as a tenant under the Government. The plaintiffs collusively got settlement of the land. As they acquired no title to and possession in the suit land on the basis of the lease the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.) legally cancelled the lease by his order dated 15.8.85.

4. The learned Assistant Judge dismissed the suit holding that the Additional Deputy commissioner legally passed the order Dated 15.8.1985.

5. The plaintiffs against the judgment and decree of the trial Court preferred Tide Appeal No. 10 of 1989 in the Court of District Judge, Noakhali who allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge and decreed the suit.

<u>6. Mr. Ruhul Amin-II, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule submits that the learned District Judge wrongly relying upon inadmissible evidence, Ext. 7, the written statement filed by the Government in Title Suit No. 63 of 1976 found that the Government admitted the lease of the plaintiffs and their possession in the disputed land. In repelling this contention Mr. Ruhul Amin appearing for the opposite parties contends that the written statement being a public document within the meaning of section 74 of the Evidence Act the learned District Judge did not commit any error of law in putting reliance upon Ext. 7. I find force in the contention of Mr. Ruhul Amin. The learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that the court of appeal below committed illegality in basing its finding on the basis of inadmissible evidence, the Commissioner report submitted in Title Suit No. 63 of 1976 which was a piece of evidence in tit suit and can not be used as evidence in this suit in the absence of the sketch map and without examining the Commissioner. He cited the decision in the case of Sunder Vs. Hint and others, 1936 Lah 138 in support of his contention. In the facts and circumstances of the present case the principle laid down in Sundaes case has little application in as much as objection as to admissibility of evidence is to be taken at the first instance. In this case no such objection was raised either in the Court of first instance or in the lower appellate Court. The report can also be relied upon as the same was official document and was prepared in due course. Therefore, the contention of the learned Advocate fails and the District Judge has not committed any error of law in placing reliance upon the report.</u>

7. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that it took into consideration the documentary evidence namely, at A, certified copy of the objection petition filed by M Idris Miah challenging the correctness of Ithatian No. 81/123 in objection case No. 472 of 1968 recording 78.23 acres in the name of the Government; Ext. A(1), certified copy of the order in the said case for opening a separate Khatian in the name of Idris taking out 32.50 acres from Khatian No. 81/123. Ext. A(2), the certified copy of the order dated 28.3.197 of the Settlement Officer dismissing the appeal against the order dated 23.10.1968 passed in the Objection Case No. 472 of 1968. Ext. A(14), order dated 15.8.1985 of the Additional Deputy-Commissioner cancelling the lease of the plaintiffs passed in SA petition Case No. 20 of 1985-86. Ext. B, certified copy of the Khatian recording 32.50 acres of land in the name of Idris Miah in Dag No. 81/123. Eats.A(6), Ext. D the certified copy of the judgment and decree of the Title Suit Flo. 63 of 1976 showing that the suit was dismissed against the petitioner on contest and on appeal by the plaintiffs the decree of the Munsif was affirmed. He also found that Ext. E, Ext. E(1), E(2), the certified copies of the plaint in Title Suit No. 468 of 1986, Title Suit No. 467 of 1980 and in Title Suit No. 466 of 1980 and Ext. A (15), Ext. A(16) and Ext. A(17), the certified copies of the judgments in Title Suit No. 468 of 1980, in Title Suit No. 467 of 1980 and in Title Suit No. 466 of 1980 showing dismissal of the suits instituted by the father of the plaintiff No. 2 Kala Miah and plaintiff Nos. 3 and 9 against the father of the defendant No. 3. The Trial Court also considered Ext. C series the rent receipts showing payment of rent in the name of the plaintiffs father and Ext. F Barga Kabuliats executed by the Bargadars in favour of Idris Miah in respect of 32.50 acres of land. It also considered the evidence of both the PWs and DWs.

8. The learned Assistant Judge further found that Shamsul Hoq opposite party No. 5 and Bazlul Karim, husband of the opposite party No. 11, were Government servant and they fraudulently obtained the settlement in their favour of the land measuring 2.50 acres in violation to the Government Circulars. The Assistant Judge further found on the basis report of the Surveyor that the land of the defendant No. 3 situates on the eastern side of Plot No. 81/123 and he held that Khatian 100 was correctly opened in the name of the defendant No. 3 on the basis of the order dated 23.10.68 of the Objection Officer and the order dated 20.8.1974 of the Settlement Officer. Upon such findings the learned Assistant Judge held that the kabuliats executed by the plaintiffs in favour of the Government are paper transaction in as much as the Government having had admitted the title of the defendant in the disputed land can not subsequently settle the same with the plaintiffs. But this finding of the trial Court has been reversed by the lower appellate Court with cogent reasons on consideration of the evidence on record.

9. The lower Appellate Court on the basis of the report submitted on 9.2.1980 by the Commissioner appointed in Title Suit No. 63 of 1976 found that the land of DS Plot Nos. 22, 23, 24 of Khatian No. 162, DS Plot Nos. 93, 94, 95, 94/1 of Khatian No. 539, Plots Nos. 50, 51, 70 of Khatian No. 537, Plots Nos. 71, 72, 91, 96 of Khatian No. 538 and DS Plots Nos. 49, 52 and 69 of Khatian No. 536 of No. 258 Mouza Char Jubilee which was claimed by the father of the defendant No. 3 does not correspond to the land of the Diara Block Plot No. 81/123 and accordingly held that the order passed on 23.10.1968, Ext. A(a), in objection case No. 471 of 1968 was without any basis as the land of Idris Miah was not identical with the suit land. The learned District Judge also observed on the basis of Ext. A that while claiming the title and possession of the disputed land Idris Miah did not furnish the quantity of the land covered by his alleged pattan nor he disclosed the date when he took the settlement of the land appertaining to DS Khatian Nos. 162, 536, 537, 538 and 539 as his raiyati land which he alleged was incorporated in Block Plot No. 81/123 or Mouza Char Vvrapda. He also found that from the certified copy of the order dated 23.10.68, Ext. A(1) passed by the Objection Officer there was nothing to show that Idris Miah ever produced any paper in support of his claim of pattan from the Ex-land lords but Khatian No. 100 was opened in the name of Idris Miah for 32.50 acres of land showing 6 annas 13 gonads share in Plot No, 8'623. On consideration of Ext. 7, the lower appellate Court also found that. Diara Khatian No. 100 opened in the name of Idris Miah was illegal, collusive and without any basis and the Government claimed the entire 78.23 acres recorded in diara block Plot No. 81/123 as the Government khas land out of which the Government settled the land in dispute in perpetual lease to the different persons including the plaintiffs obtaining kabuliats from them and the claim of Abdul Kader Chowdhury, defendant No. 3 is not identical with the land in suit appertaining to Plot No. 81/123. The learned Judge on consideration of Ext. A found that Idris Miah did not furnish any particular about his pattani land in the objection case and in the written objection Ext. 7(A) in Title Suit No. 63 of 1976, the defendant No. 3 for the first time disclosed particulars of land of their settlement. It appears on the basis of an application filed by the plaintiffs, the learned Munsif appointed a survey knowing Advocate Commissioner for the purpose of investigation who submitted his report on 9.2.80 but the learned Munsif without accepting the report dismissed the suit. The learned District Judge on perusal of the report found that the Advocate Commissioner on relayment found that the land of DS Plot Nos. 22, 23, 24, 93, 94, 95, 94/1, 50, 51, 70, 71, 91, 69, 49 of No. 258 of Mouza Char Jabilee does not attract the land of Diara Block Plot No. 81/123. On consideration of this material evidence the learned District Judge held that the objection Case No. 472 of 1968 was allowed without any basis and it did not create any legal right in favour of Idris Miah. The learned District Judge further found that while on the basis of the lease the plaintiffs were in possession Abdul Kader Chowdhury filed the Miscellaneous Case. 100/75-76 for allotment of separate shaham from Block Plot No. 81/123 and got an order made in his favour and that order necessitated in institute of the Title Suit No. 63 of 1970 on 21.1.76 against Abdul Kader Chowdhury and others for permanent injunction followed an application for temporary injunction not to proceed with the demarcation of the land in pursuant to shaham allotted to the defendant No. 3 Abdul Kader Chowdhury in the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No. 100 of 1975-76. Against the said order the plaintiffs preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 188 of 1976 and prayed for temporary injunction which was rejected by Mr. Amiya Bhushan Podder, District Judge by his order dated 30.11.76 and the appeal was subsequently dismissed by another Subordinate Judge on 24.11.74. The learned District Judge further noticed that due,to observation made in Title Suit No. 63 of 1976 several suits were filed which however were dismissed on different dates and against the decree of dismissal of Title Suit No. 465 of 1980 Title Appeal No. 11 of 1989 was preferred and during pendency of that appeal in respect of 27.50 acres of land, the defendant No. 3 petitioner herein started SA Petition Case No. 20 of 1985-86 and obtained an order 15.8.85 from the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), Noakhali cancelling the lease made in favour of the plaintiff. On consideration of the aforesaid evidence the learned District Judge held that the order dated 15.8.85 of defendant No. 2 was illegal.

The finding of the possession of the plaintiffs was based on consideration of the evidence of PWs. So far finding as to possession is concerned the learned District Judge also observed that the trial Court found fault with some of the witnesses who failed to detail about when they got possession. The learned District Judge very correctly observed that the lessor having had admitted possession of the tenants it is idle to embark upon an enquiry as to how and when they got their first possession. The learned District Judge further found that the defendant No. 3 in his cross-examination stated that he did not file any map in Misc. Case No. 100/1975-76 nor the Surveyor was examined who demarcated the land in favour of the defendant No. 3. He has also considered the evidence of DW 2 Belayet DW 3 Fazal Haque who were bargaders, of defendant No. 3 Abdul Kader Chowdhury and on consideration. of their oral evidence he held that defendant No. 3 has no possession and the plaintiffs were in possession as of right since 1970 as lessees in the suit land and he reversed the finding of the trial Court. The finding of possession based on legal evidence is binding upon High Court Division.

10. It is contended on behalf of the petitioner further that the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.) legally cancelled the lease inasmuch as the plaintiff opposite party No. 5 and the husband of the plaintiff opposite party No. 11 are not entitled to get lease of the Government khas land in view of the Government Circular dated 13.2.1963. From a plain reading of section 76 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is not possible to hold that the same creates any bar to grant lease to the Government servant. The Circular dated 13.2.1963 issued by the Government having had no force of law the cancellation of the lease by the Additional Deputy-Commissioner (Rev.) on the basis of the same was absolutely without any jurisdiction and in doing so he has transgressed his limit. In this respect it may be observed that section 147 of the State Acquisition Act provides forum for appeal from an order of revenue authority. Nothing could be placed before me by the petitioner to show that the Additional Deputy-Commissioner had any such jurisdiction to pass the impugned order upon an application filed by the defendant No. 3. The petitioner placing reliance upon the decision in the case of Satyendra Kishore Roy Vs. Ramendra Kishore Roy, 7 BCR 227 (AD) however argues that the Government servant is not entitled to get settlement of khas land. A careful reading of the judgment shows that the learned Judges observed in that case that the Government servant got lease of the khas land practicing fraud and observed" in view of the fraud which has subsequently been revealed vitiating the transaction such delay is no bar to its cancellation". Therefore, the facts of that case, being distinguishable from the facts of the instant case the principle laid down in that case does not apply here. It also seems to me that the learned Judges did not express any opinion as to whether that circular has any force of statutory law rather the observation was made with regard to violation of the law and fraud practiced by the lessee in obtaining the lease. In the instant case before me there is nothing on record to show that the plaintiffs obtained the lease practicing fraud upon the authority. Mr. Ruhul Amin for the opposite parties, on the other hand, relied on the decision in the case of Nazi Nurul Islam Vs. Serajul Islam and others, 4 BCR 1984 (AD) 401 wherein it has been held that the circular is a mere departmental guide lines having no statutory force. The learned Advocates at the Bar could not place before me any thing to show that the Additional Deputy-Commissioner (Rev.) had power to cancel the lease.

11. For the aforesaid discussion, I do not find any substance in this Rule. The judgment and decree passed by the lower Appellate Court, accordingly, is affirmed.

12. The judgment made in the Civil Revision No. 110 of 1989 will govern the judgment of Civil Revision No. 111 of 1989 in view of the facts that the points involved are identical except that Civil Revision No. 111 of 1989 arises out of the suit for declaration of title only on the basis of settlement of the disputed land from the Government. When the foundation of the title of the plaintiffs has been found to be legal in this Rule the same also applies in the Civil Revision No. 111 of 1989. In view of my finding in Civil Revision No. 110 of 1989 I hold that the learned District Judge rightly reversed the decision of the trial Court and set aside the judgment and decree declaring the title of the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 465 of 1980. Accordingly, the judgment and decree made in Tittle Appeal No. 11 of 1989 is hereby affirmed.

In the result, both these Rules are discharged.

No order as to cost. The connected stay orders are hereby vacated.

End.

full_judgment:
This Second Appeal has been directed against the judgment and decree dated 25.4.66 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 158 of 1950 setting aside those passed by the Munsif, First Court, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 567 of 1946 on 31.3.54.

2. The present appellants were defendants in the trial court and the respondents were the plaintiffs.

3. The plaintiffs brought the suit for a declaration of their easement right of pathway over Plot No. 1 and 2 and drain in plot No. 3 and 4 to the land mentioned in the schedule to the plaint. The suit was also for their 12 annas maliki right in plot No. 2 and 4, the removal of obstruction placed on plot Nos. 1 by the defendants and for a permanent injunction to restrain the defendants from interfering with the plaintiff's right in the suit land.

4. According to the plaintiffs their houses and those of the defendants are on the same plots. The houses of the plaintiffs are on the southern side and the houses of the defendants are on the northern side of the plots. Plot No. 1 is a pathway running from south to north across the eastern side of the homestead of the defendants. Plot No. 2 is another pathway running along the northern border of the defendants homestead. Plot No. 1 meets Plot No. 2 on the northern border of the homestead of the defendants. Plot No. 1 is a continuation of the pathway which originates from the homestead of the plaintiff. Plot Nos. 3 and 4, which are drains, run along the western side of Plot No. 1 and southern side of plot No. 2. The predecessors of the plaintiffs as well as of the defendants used to live in the same homestead and they were related to each other. The suit land was not partitioned and both the plaintiffs and their predecessors had of right claimed and enjoyed the pathways and drains without interruption for a period of about 150 years. Defendant No. 1 used the western latrine of the plaintiffs without their permission and plaintiff No. 9 took objection to this and as a result a quarrel took place resulting in an assault on the plaintiff No. 9 who brought a criminal case against the defendants and during the pendency of the criminal case, the defendants erected a shed, planted certain plants and erected a mud wall in Aswin 1353 BS. Then a proceeding u/s 133 CrPC was started by the plaintiffs when the suit land was thus obstructed, the plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of easement right over the suit land.

5. Defendants No. 1, 2, 9 and 11 contested the suit by filing joint written statement. They denied all the allegations of the plaintiffs. According to the defendants they are owners of the homestead and the land in suit. Plot No. 1 is a part and parcel of their homestead. It is not and was never used as a pathway by the plaintiffs or by their predecessors. Plot No. 2 is also a part of their homestead and it is their private pathway. The plaintiffs or their predecessor did not use this plot and acquired no right therein. The plaintiffs have no Maliki right to the suit and they have also no right over the drainage in Plot Nos. 3-4 which are their own drains. The defendants thus denied the easement right of the plaintiffs in the suit land.

6. The trial court considered the evidence and other document and decreed the suit in part. It was decreed that over Plot Nos. 1 and 2 the plaintiff had right of easement for a pathway but their claim for malike right relating to Plot Nos. 2 and 4 and their right of drainage in Plot Nos. 3 and 4 was dismissed.

7. The defendant No. 1 preferred an appeal against the said judgment and decree and the plaintiff also filed a cross-objection. After hearing the appeal and the cross-objection the appellate court below allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and sent the case on remand for retrial to enable the plaintiff to bring the representative of the plaintiff No. 14 on record. The court also directed that a fresh judgment and decision should be given in the suit. Accordingly a fresh decision by another trial court was given dismissing the suit of the plaintiffs, and finding that plaintiffs acquired no right of way or drainage in the suit land.

8. Against that decision the plaintiffs preferred an appeal and the appellate court below dismissed the said appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court. Thereafter the plaintiffs preferred Second Appeal No. 142/1959. The High Court allowed the appeal and sent back the case on remand to the lower appellate court for re-hearing with the following observations.

"I accordingly allow the appeal in part and set aside the judgment and decree of the lower Appellate Court so far as they relate to the pathway over Plot Nos. 1 and 2 and sent the case back to that court for re-hearing of the appeal on the question of pathway in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made above."

Thus the trial court, the lower appellate court and the High Court were all of the decisions that the plaintiffs had no maliki right in Plot Nos. 2 and 4 and no right of drainage over Plot Nos. 3 and 4. The High Court sent the case on remand to lower appellate court only to consider whether the plaintiffs have right of way over Plot Nos. 1 and 2.

9. Admittedly there was a local investigation in this case and there were 2 reports—one by pleader commissioner and the other by the trying Magistrate and ADM. After considering these reports and the sketch map of the suit land, the appellate court on remand found that the Plot Nos. 1 and 2 are used by the plaintiffs as a pathway for their going to the mosque, the latrine and the paddy filed. The court also found from the reports that the nature of the plot No. 1 was deliberately changed and that although the house of the defendant was originally east facing, it was subsequently converted into nor facing for the purpose of the suit. From the deposition of PWs 3, 5 and 7 the court found the existence of the pathway and its use by the plaintiff for a long time. PWs 3-5 and 7 appear to be independent witnesses and there was no reason as to why they should depose falsely against the defendants. Accordingly, after considering the reports of the pleader commissioner and the trying Magistrate and ADM as also the evidences of PWs 3-5 and 7, the appellate court below found the easement right of the plaintiffs over Plot Nos. 1 and 2. Accordingly, the appeal was allowed in part by the lower Appellate Court by its judgment and decree dated 26.4.1946. It is against this that this Second Appeal was filed.

10. Mr. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury the learned Advocate for the appellants has submitted that the claim of the plaintiffs to have right of easement over the Plot Nos. 1 and 2 having not fulfilled the requirement of section 15 of the Easement Act, they are not entitled to a decree and the lower appellate court having not considered the provisions of section 15 of the said Act have committed illegality. In this connection he submitted that according to the explanation 2 of section 15 of the Easement Act, a plait having not mentioned as to when the obstruction was created and the suit having not been filed within 1 year from the creation of such obstruction, it s barred by limitation and the courts below having not given a decision on the question of limitation their judgments and decrees are bad in law. The lower appellate court ought to have considered this legal question of limitation when the case was sent back on remand by this court. Section 15 of the said act reads as follows:

"Where the access and use of light or air to and for any building have been peaceably enjoyed therewith, as an easement, without interruption, and for twenty years, and where support from one person's land or things affixed thereto has been peaceably received by another person's land subjected to artificial pressure or by things affixed thereto, as an easement, without interruption, and for twenty years, and where a right of way or any other easement has been peaceably and openly enjoyed by any person's claiming title thereto, as an casement and as of right, without interruption and for twenty years, the right to such access and use of light or air, support or other easement shall be absolute."

From the reports of the pleader commissioner and the trying Magistrate and ADM as also from the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs it is clear that the plaintiffs and their predecessors enjoyed the right of way over Plot No. 1 and 2 peacefully and openly without interruption for the last 20 years. It cannot be said that the requirement of section 15 of the Easement Act has been fulfilled. Explanation No. II in the said section 15 of the Easement Act provides as follows:

"Nothing is an enjoyment within the meaning of this section unless where there is an actual cessation of the enjoyment by reason of an obstruction by the act of some person other than the claimant, and unless such obstruction is submitted to or acquiesced in for one year after the claimant has notice thereof and of the person making or authorizing the same to be made."

From the record it appears that the cause of action arose on 5.10.46 and the suit was filed on 23.12.46. According to Mr. Chowdhury, the cause of action arose on the date when the first obstruction was created and the plaintiffs filed a criminal case and thereafter they also filed an application under section 133 of CrPC and that the criminal case and the proceeding under section 133 CrPC having taken place much earlier than the date of cause of action as mentioned in the plaint, the trial court as well as the lower appellate court ought to have held that this is not the actual date of cause of action. According to him, if the date on which the first obstruction was created and consequently the criminal case. Its well as the criminal proceeding under section 133 of the CrPC were filed was mentioned then the present suit would have been hit by the provision of the explanation given in the said section 15 of the Easement Act. In the trial court issue No. 2 was as follows:

"Is the suit barred by limitation?"

It appears that this issue was not pressed and as such it was not at all touched by the trial court and as such the appellate court also did not discuss the point. It also appears that the High Court while sending the case on remand to the lower appellate court to re-consider the question of casement right of the plaintiffs over Plot Nos. 1 and 2 did not feel the necessity of going into the question of limitation. Mr. Chowdhury submits that in the remand order by the High Court the words" in accordance with law" means that the question with regard to easement right over Plot Nos. 1 and 2 is to be decided not only in the light of the observations made by the High Court but also in accordance with law and the words" in accordance with law" means that the lower appellate court ought to have considered the question of limitation as also the question of maintainability. So this case should be again sent on remand to consider these law points. Mr. Chowdhury, however; could not show me the date on which the first obstruction was created consequent upon which the criminal case as well as the proceeding under section 133 of the Criminal Procedure Code was started. Ext-C is the application under section 133 CrPC and was filed on 25.3.47 in the Court of ADM Sylhet praying for an injunction and this was filed after the suit was filed, In view of the fact that the proceeding under section 133 CrPC was filed on 15.3.47 after filing of the suit and in view of the fact that the issue of limitation was not at all agitated by the defendants themselves either in the trial court or in the lower Appellate Court or in the High Court I am not inclined to consider this point after a period of 45 years or send the case on remand to the lower court for another round of legal battle, particularly when the High Court, while sending the case on remand to the lower Appellate Court, limited the scope to consider and decide the easement right of plaintiffs to Plot Nos. I and 2 only.

11. It is also argued by the learned Advocate for the appellants that in the application under section 133 CrPC the pathway was described as a "cattle pathway" for the petitioners as well as villagers for going to the grazing ground but in the plaint the plaintiffs mentioned it as their own ground of the petitioner's pathway for going to their own grazing ground. This, according to Mr. Chowdhury is a departure and making out a new case.

12. It has been already found that the application under section 133 CrPC was filed after the suit had been filed. So the question of making out a new case in the suit does not arise. Moreover, the application under section 133 CrPC is a general application without making any mention of the Plot No. etc. But one thing is clear that the petitioner Abdur Razzak himself filed it and signed it and he did not men on that he is filing it on behalf of others.

13. The other submission of Mr. Chowdhury is that Ext-2A (which are the reports of trying Magistrate and ADM) speak of customary right and not prescriptory right whereas the said suit has been filed for a right of prescription only. Customary right under section 18 of the Act has been defined as follows:

"An easement may be acquired by virtue of a local custom. Such easements are called customary easements."

<u>14. Customary easement is different from prescriptory easement in that in order to establish the right of customary easement it is not necessary to show that it has been enjoyed from time immemorial or even for a time over 20 years. A customary easement is in favour of a class or community and cannot be in favour or an individual whereas in the case of the prescriptory easement it is essential that it was for a period of 20 years or more. From Ext-2 to 2A, I do not find any materials to conclude that the trying Magistrate and ADM are speaking of any customary right. They have discussed the right of easement of the plaintiffs over the suit land by their user for over 20 years. The reports clearly speak of right of easement by prescription and not of customary right.</u>

15. The next submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants is that the suit is hit by Order No. 1 rule 8 CPC as it has not been filed in representative character. The contention of the learned Advocate is that in the application for a proceeding under section 133 CrPC, the plaintiffs mentioned about the other villagers and the suit ought to have been filed by the plaintiffs not only for selves but also on behalf of others. I have already found and stated above that the application under section 133 CrPC was filed after filing of the suit. It is clear that it was for all these people who were close to Plot Nos. 1 and 2 and who were as a result of obstruction confined in their houses. Thus this Rule has no application in this case. Moreover, this point was never raised by the defendants in the courts of the day after 45 years of the filing of the suit, particularly, when the application under section 133 CrPC was filed after the filing of the suit.

For the reasons stated above the judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge Second Court Sylhet on 25.4.66 in Title Appeal No. 158 of 1954 are upheld and the Second Appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

parties:
Mosammat Monowara Begum ------ Appellant 
vs. 
Syed Ashrafuddin & ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C J: This appeal arises from Civil Order No. 177 of 1984 disposed of by a Bench of the High Court Division, Barisal (Mr. Justice M.H. Rahman and Mr. Justice Syed Misbahuddin Hossain) on 2nd September 1984.

2. Appellant filed Title Suit No.15 of 1984 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit land. Appellant's case, inter alia, is that property "ka" Schedule land belonged to one Abdul Malek who sold it to Jahanara Begum, predecessor-in interest of defendant-respondent Nos. 3-13 and respondent Nos. 14-15 in equal shares. Jahanara Begum and respondent Nos. 14 and 15 amicably partitioned 195 sahasrangsha out of suit plot Nos. 874 and 875 in three equal parts and Jahanara Begum got '065 sahasrangsha from extreme northern portion and the remaining portion was received by respondent Nos.14 and 15 keeping the land of suit plot No. 873 ejmali along with other jointly purchased land. Jahanara Begum constructed pucca wall on three sides of her portion and while she had been possessing the suit land peacefully she transferred '065 lands to the appellant by a registered kabala for Tk. 50,000/- on 29th April 1981.

3. Since the purchase the appellant has been possessing the suit land through her tenant after raising dwelling hut and other structures thereon and has mutated her name. She has been paying rents and taxes for the suit land.

4. Appellant has come to learn that respondent Nos. 14 and 15 transferred '144 land from plot Nos. 874 and 875 to respondent Nos. 1 and 2 by kabalas dated 15th June 1978, 16th June 1978 and 23rd September 1978. They claimed amicable possession in plot Nos. 874 and 875 including the land purchased by the appellant from Jahanara Begum. They instituted Title Suit No. 141 of 1981 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal for recovery of possession under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act on the allegations that they have been forcibly dispossessed by the appellant on 29th April 1981. Appellant contested by filing written statement but lost the case. A revisional application was filed by the appellant before the High Court Division, Barisal Bench, being Civil Revision No. 19 of 1983. The Rule was, however, discharged on 29th November 1983. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1983 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal for execution of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 141 of 1981 for eviction of the appellant. Appellant thereafter filed the aforesaid title suit, namely, Title Suit No.15 of 1984. Appellant also filed an application under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restraining defendant-respondents Nos. 1 and 2 from prosecuting the Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1983 and also for evicting the appellant's monthly tenant and from disturbing the peaceful possession of the tenant till disposal of the suit.

5. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 contested the application for temporary injunction by filing written objection. They denied the right, title, interest and possession of Jahanara Begum, appellant's vendor, in the suit land. They contended that they had purchased the suit plot Nos. 873, 874 and 875 from respondent Nos. 14 and 15 by registered kabala’s and were possessing the same till they were forcibly dispossessed by the appellant on 29th April 1981. After dispossession respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed Title Suit No. 141 of 1981 for recovery of possession. They got decree which was confirmed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 19 of 1983. Thereafter they filed Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1983 for execution of the decree. Appellant filed Title Suit No. 15 of 1984 only to frustrate the decree passed in Title Suit No. 141 of 1981. It was asserted by them that as the suit was not maintainable the application for temporary injunction was, therefore, liable to be dismissed.

6. By his judgment and order dated 22nd July 1984 the learned Subordinate Judge, Barisal rejected the prayer for temporary injunction. Appellant preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 94 of 1984 before the District Judge, Barisal. Appellant filed an application for temporary injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 and section 151, C.P.C. for restraining respondent Nos. 1 and 2 from executing the decree. By his order dated 29th July 1984 the learned District Judge passed an ad interim order of stay till the disposal of the injunction matter. Subsequently, by his order dated 19th August 1984 the learned District Judge rejected the prayer for temporary injunction and vacated the order of stay. In doing so he placed reliance on a decision reported in AIR 1955 All. 64 holding that temporary injunction cannot be granted against executing a decree passed in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act.

7. Appellant preferred an application under section 155 of the Code of Civil Procedure, being Civil Order No. 177 of 1984, before the High Court Division, Barisal Bench. The learned Judges of the High Court Division who heard the application summarily rejected it on 2nd September 1984.

8. Being aggrieved appellant moved this Court and obtained special leave to appeal on 28th October 1984. Terms of special leave are: "Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioner argues that the learned District Judge rejected the petitioner's prayer for injunction on an erroneous view of law holding that the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession is not contemplated in the back ground of a decree passed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. He has further argued that the learned District Judge in taking the aforesaid erroneous view relied on the decision reported in AIR 1955 (Allahabad) 64, which was over-ruled by another decision of the said court in the case reported in AIR 1972 (Allahabad) 418. The learned Counsel argues that the High Court Division did not apply its judicial mind in considering the point of law raised on behalf of the petitioner and committed an error in summarily rejecting the petitioner."

<u>9. The main contention in this appeal relates to whether the decree obtained by respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in Title Suit No. 141 of 1981 which was filed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is executable. If it is found not executable in view of the appellant's application for temporary injunction she is entitled to succeed, on the other hand if contrary conclusions are reached as the Courts below have done, the prayer for temporary injunction restraining respondent Nos. 1 and 2 from executing the decree obtained by them in the aforesaid suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act cannot be granted. Let us consider if a decree obtained in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is enforceable or not. To determine this, relevant provisions of law and decisions cited by the learned Advocates need consideration. Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act provides as follows:</u>

<u>"9. If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise that in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit 3 recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit.</u>

<u>Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.</u>

<u>10. A person who has been dispossessed from his immovable property without his consent or illegally can institute a suit under the provisions of this section and obtain a decree on proof of his claim to possession of such property. The judgment-debtor in such a case may, if aggrieved, institute a suit to establish his title and on obtaining a decree can recover possession of the property in question.</u>

<u>11. As already mentioned, respondent Nos. 1 and 2 obtained a decree for recovery of possession in Title Suit No. 141 of 1981 and put the decree into execution in Title Execution Case No. 3 of 1983. The aforesaid suit, if may be mentioned, was contested by the appellant upto the High Court Division but with no effect. On her failure to get any relief against the decree obtained by respondent Nos. 1 and 2 she filed Title Suit No. 15 of 1984 for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and also filed an application for temporary injunction restraining respondent Nos. 1 and 2 from prosecuting the Title Execution No. 3 of 1983. From facts so far disclosed, it appears that the appellant's prayer for temporary injunction cannot be granted, the reason being that it would lead to interference with and ultimately frustrate the order of the Court which was passed in the suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act enabling respondent Nos. 1 and 2 to recover possession of the land in question. The proposition that respondent Nos. 1 and 2 should be restrained by an injunction from recovering possession of the suit land in execution of the decree obtained by them in the suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act cannot be accepted also for the following reason as appears from a reading of the judgments in this suit and proceedings arising there from.</u>

<u>12. Though appellant has filed Title Suit No. 15 of 1984 for establishing her title to the suit land which she is expressly empowered to do, the question of title to the same was also considered by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 19 of 1983 arising from Title Suit No. 141 of 1981. Findings on title to the suit land went against the appellant. We are not dealing with the question how far those findings would be binding on the appellant in Title Suit No. 15 of 1984, but for refusing relief to the appellant in the present case those findings are worth consideration.</u>

<u>13. So far as the decision reported in AIR 1955 All 64 is concerned, the principles laid down therein lend support to the view that no injunction can be granted to a person against whom a decree has been passed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act restraining the decree-holder from executing the decree, the reason being that if an injunction is granted on the prayer of the judgment-debtor the object and purpose of the suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act will be frustrated. Section 9 enables a person to recover possession of his land from one who took the law into his own hands and forcibly dispossessed him otherwise than in accordance with law. If the judgment-debtor against whom a decree has been passed under section 9 can establish his title in a suit subsequently filed by him, he can no doubt get relief on the basis of his title so found in such suit. In the aforesaid case it was held that the defendant in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act must first surrender possession to the decree-holder in execution of the decree obtained by him in such a suit. No injunction can be granted on the plea of title to restrain the execution proceedings, because this tends to deprive the decree-holder of the fruits of the decree obtained by him.</u>

For the reasons stated above, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

parties:
Sarwarjan Bhuiyan and others ------- Petitioners.
Vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration & Land Reforms, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka and others ------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Kazi EbaduI Hoque, J.: This rule, at the instance of the petitioners Sarwarjan Bhuiyan and 4 others, has been issued calling upon the respondents namely, Government of Bangladesh and others, to show cause as to why they should not be directed to make over vacant possession of the disputed land as described in the schedule of the petition to the petitioners.

2. Case of the petitioners, in short, is as follows: The lands of CS Plot Nos. 677, 680 and 681 originally belonged to Wazir Bibi and by inheritance; transfer and abandonment of the tenancy Shamsun Nahar Begum, Syed Mohammad Abdul Motaleb and Abdul Hamid became owners and possessors of the same. Thereafter Abdul Hamid orally gifted his share to his cousins, petitioner Nos. 1-3. Similarly Syed Mohammad Abdul Motaleb orally gifted his share to the petitioner Nos. 4 and 5. Shamsun Nahar Begum died leaving petitioner Nos. 1-3 as her son and daughters and only legal heirs to inherit her share. On 10.4.1950 an area of 32.50 acre of land was requisitioned in LA Case No. 29 of 1949-50 including 0'10 acre of CS plot No. 680, 0'13 are of CS plot No. 681 being parts of these plots and entire 0'28 acre of CS plot No. 677 of Mouja Dhanmondi owned and possessed by the petitioners for Diplomatic Colony. Thereafter on 24.1.51 some area of requisitioned land including the said land of the petitioners  were de-requisitioned but possession of the same was not delivered to the petitioners or their predecessors-in-interest. There- after by Gazette Notification dated 4.10.1951 said requisitioned land was acquired under section 5(7) of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948. By order dated 5.5.1952 payment of compensation in respect of CS Plot Nos. 677 and 680 was stopped. By Gazette Notification dated 11.11.1954 original Gazette Notification dated 4.10.1951 was amended deleting "for Diplomatic Colony." Thereafter 20 acres of the said acquired land was made over to the Bangladesh Scientific and Industrial Research Council in 1955 and remaining 12.50 acre of land remaining unutilized must be deemed to have been de-requisitioned. The land of the petitioners is still lying vacant though covered by the boundary walls of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research. In spite of petitions filed by the petitioners and their predecessors-in-interest possession of the disputed land was not made over to them. Thereafter on the application of the petitioners by letter dated 21.12. 1982 Senior Member, Martial Law Vigilance Team recommended to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka to take steps to rectify the irregularities in including 12.50 acres in the Gazette Notification for acquisition by another Gazette Notification as the same was de-requisitioned in 1951. Thereafter by Memo dated 6.3.1983 Section Officer of the Ministry of Law and Land Reforms asked the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) to submit a report with a map and in reply thereto by Memo dated 10.5.1983 Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) forwarded a map to the said Section Officer showing the area of acquired and de-requisitioned land including petitioner's said land. But the Government did not take any steps to restore vacant possession of the disputed land to the petitioners in spite of receipt of the said report and map. Thereafter on the application of the petitioners Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms called for a report from the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka who by Memo dated 29.11.1984 stated that 12.50 acre of land out of 32.50 acre of land was withdrawn from acquisition but possession of the said de-requisitioned land was not restored to the owners thereof and disputed land of the petitioners are lying vacant within the boundary walls of Bangladesh Council for Scientific and Industrial Research. But instead of restoring possession of the disputed land to the petitioners Government again by Memo dated 6.11.1986 asked for another report in consultation with the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research and with their opinion in the matter. Thereafter by Memo dated 20.10.1986 Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka informed the Government that an area of 6.27 acre of land in addition to 20 acre of allotted land lies within the boundary walls constructed by the Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research. But the respondents having failed to restore possession of the disputed land which was de-requisitioned the petitioners served notice dated 14.3.1987 demanding justice in the matter to put the petitioners in possession of the disputed land. The respondents are legally bound to restore possession of the disputed land to the petitioners.

3. The rule is being contested by the respondent Nos. 1 and 4 by filing separate affidavits- in-opposition denying material allegations. Their common case is that Wazir Bibi had no Khas possession in the disputed land and she had only rent receiving interest therein after settling the same with tenants, and heirs of Wazir Bibi inherited only rent receiving interest and no notice under section 57(1) of the Bengal Tenancy Act was given to the Collector by Shamsun Nahar Begum and others and they did not take possession of the disputed land. The story of gift is false, concocted and malafide. The petitioners did not acquire title and possession in the disputed land and award of compensation for the requisition and acquisition of the same was not prepared in their names. The land of CS Plot Nos. 677, 680 and 681 was not de-requisitioned. Notice of de-requisition of part of CS Plot No. 680 was issued in the name of Alep Ali and not the petitioners who had no right, title and interest therein. But subsequently entire 32.50 acres of lands were permanently acquired by Gazette Notification dated 4.10.1951 and as such question of de-requisition and delivery of possession of the disputed land to the petitioners does not arise. On the request of the Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, in short, BCSIR, government by letter dated 18.10.1955 decided to transfer 20 acres out of 32.50 acre of acquired land for its regional laboratories at Dhaka and subsequently leased out the same to the BCSIR by deed dated 10.12.1956 and possession of the land was duly delivered to BCSIR. As BCSIR could not accommodate all their constructions within the said 20 acres of land they requested for allotment of further 10 acres of land but the Government allotted 7.60 acres of additional land out of the said acquired land by Memo dated 26.8.1957 and handed over possession of the same to the BCSIR including the disputed land. After allotment and delivery of possession therein BCSIR constructed several buildings in the said land. As the disputed land was not de-requisitioned question of restoration of possession to the petitioners does not arise at all. Report submitted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka to the Ministry on 10.5.1983 is incorrect and suppression of facts. The petitioners managed to prepare the said report and the map attached thereto in illegal collusion with the staff of Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka. Similarly report dated 29.11.1984 of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka is also biased and incorrect by misrepresentation and suppression of facts. Report dated 20.10.1986 of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka is also biased, incorrect and obtained by undue influence and misrepresentation of facts. BCSIR is not in possession of any land beyond the land allotted to it the petitioners are not entitled to restoration of possession in the disputed land which was never de-requisitioned rather permanently acquired and allotted to the BCSIR and in its possession after construction of buildings therein.

4. The petitioners filed two affidavits-in-reply to the said affidavits-in-opposition stating that they are the owners of the disputed land and title of their predecessor was recorded in CS Khatians in respect of Plot No. 681 and declared in respect of Plot Nos. 677 and 680 in Title Suit No. 32 of 1950 and LA Collector also admitted their predecessor's claim to compensation by correcting the awards.

5. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioners submitted that after de-requisition of the disputed land Deputy Commissioner is under legal legal obligation to restore possession of the same to the petitioners as the rightful owners of the same.

6. Mr. AF Hasan Ariff, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 1 submitted that there was no de-requisition and the land was acquired by Gazette Notification and vested in the Government. Even if any notice to de-requisition was issued that was not given effect to by restoration of possession and subsequently acquired by Gazette Notification. Moreover, the petitioners having no right, title and interest in the disputed land cannot claim restoration of possession.

7. Mr. SC Das, learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 4 submitted that the disputed property was not requisitioned from the petitioners and their right, title and interest therein is disputed and as such the petition at their instance is not maintainable as this Court cannot enter into deciding disputed question of fact regarding title of the petitioners. Moreover, the petition suffers from inordinate delay. He submitted that possession of 7.60 acres of land including disputed land was made over to respondent No. 4 as far back as in 1957 and the respondent No. 4 constructed buildings over the same at huge cost and after 35 years status quo cannot be disturbed.

8. In course of hearing the arguments the petitioners have filed an application to issue fresh Rule against the respondents to show cause as to why acquisition notice dated 24.9. 1951 published in the Dhaka Gazette dated 4.10.51 (Annexure-C to the writ petition) should not be declared to have been issued and published without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and why they should not be directed to cancel the same.

9. We shall dispose of this application in course of our judgment.

10. It is an admitted fact that an area of 32.50 acre of land including the disputed land was requisitioned by the respondent No. 2 Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka on 10.4.1950 in LA Case No. 29 of 1949-50 under the provisions of section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act and subsequently acquired under the provisions of section 5 of the said Act by notification dated 24.9.1951 published in the Gazette dated 4.10.1951 for the Diplomatic Colony at Dhanmondi but by notification dated 13.10.1954 published in the Gazette dated 11.11.1954 the said purpose of acquisition was deleted. It is also admitted that an area of 20 acres of land out of the acquired 32.50 acres was allotted and leased out to the respondent No. 4, BCSIR for construction of its laboratories in 1955. It is not denied by the petitioners that in 1957 Government allotted another area of 7'60 acres of land including the disputed land to the respondent No. 4 and delivered possession of the same to the respondent No. 4. Admittedly, the disputed land is within the boundary walls of the respondent No. 4. Petitioners contended that the disputed land is lying vacant but the respondent Nos. 1 and 4 on the other hand contended that the disputed land is covered by constructions within the boundary walls of the respondent No. 4.

11. It is not the case of the petitioners that the disputed land was requisitioned from their possession or from the possession of their predecessors Shamsun Nahar and others or that the notice of de-requisition of the same was served on them. To obviate the said difficulties to claim the disputed land the petitioners have set up case of oral gift followed by delivery of possession in their favour and inheritance from the alleged owners. But the respondent Nos. 1 and 4 denied the same in their affidavits-in-opposition.

<u>12. It appears from the certified copy of the CS Khatians annexed to the affidavit-in-reply that land of CS Plot No. 681 belonged to Uzir Bibi, Nejamat Ali and others. It also appears from the certified copies of the judgment and decree passed on 26.12.52 in Title Suit No. 32 of 1950 of the 3rd Court of Munsif, Dhaka annexed to the affidavit- in-reply that title of Shamsun Nahar and others in the compensation awarded in respect of lands of CS Plot Nos. 677 and 680 was declared. It also appears from the order dated 5.2.52 in LA Case No 29 of 1949-50 annexed to the affidavit-in-reply that award for compensation in respect of CS Plot Nos. 677 and 680 was corrected in favour of the said Shamsun Nahar, Abdul Mutalab, Abdul Aziz and Abdul Hamid, predecessors of the petitioners in pursuance of the aforesaid judgment and decree. But there is no assertion by the petitioners that after correction of the award no payment was made to those awardees Shamsun Nahar and others. There is nothing on record to show that the petitioners were admitted as owners of the disputed land by the respondents who dispute their claim of title and possession therein. We cannot examine and decide the title of the petitioners in the disputed land in writ jurisdiction. Moreover, it is the function of the Deputy Commissioner to decide the claim of compensation under section 7A of the said Act or the Civil Court. Similarly it is the function of the Deputy Commissioner under section 8 of the said Act to decide the claim of any persons for restoration of the land. Only when the Deputy Commissioner exercised the jurisdiction without lawful authority this Court can exercise the same.</u>

13. Certified copies of the notices of de-requisition (Annexure  'B' and 'B(1)' to the petition show that the order of requisition was withdrawn in respect of part of Plot No. 680 without specifying the area in the name of Alep Ali against Serial No. 157 and part of Plot No. 681 without specifying the area in the name of Jibunnessa against Serial No. 124. We have examined the original records of L.A Case produced before us by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. It appears that notices were issued under rule 10(2) for release and restoration of the requisitioned property to 150 persons on 24.1.1951. Original notice corresponding to Annexure 'B(1)' in the name of Jibunnessa and some others is in the file, but no original notice corresponding to annexure 'B' in the name of Alep Ali is in the file. But in the original de-requisition notices neither the name of the petitioners nor the name of their alleged predecessors Shamsun Nahar and others appeared. From the original notices we do not find any such insertion 'ADC (LA) M/s. Sarwarjan Bhuiyan and others as noted in the heading portion of Annexure B(1)'. It further appears from the said de-requisition notices that last paragraph regarding date and time of delivery of possession has been penned through. In Annexure  'B' and "B(1)' also there is nothing to show that any date and time was fixed for delivery of possession of the de-requisitioned land. After examining the original records which is very old, partially torn and damaged it is difficult to brush aside the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the certified copy (Annexure-B) is wholly manufactured one and insertion of name of Sarwarjan Bhuiyan and others in Annexure-B(1) is an interpolation which is not in the original. We have already noticed that in 1952 LA Collector passed necessary order for correcting the award in the name of Shamsun Nahar and others in pursuance of a decree passed by the Civil Court in their favour. So, in 1951 no notice for de-requisition could be issued in the name of the petitioners who claim to be transferees and successors of the said Shamsun Nahar and others.

14. The learned Advocate for the petitioners placed before us certified copy of the order sheet in LA Case No. 29 of 1949-50. Order dated 06.01.51 is as follows:

"Seen the report of Kgo Mvi. A Hamid submitting the list of plots to be de- requisitioned. As possession of the land was not taken and delivered to the requiring authorities, issue de-requisitioned notices under rule 10/2 stating that requisition orders issued have been vacated,"

15. Thus from the above discussion we are of view that some land was de-requisitioned by notices dated 24.1.1951 but as no possession was taken over from the owners thereof there was no delivery of possession to them in pursuance of the said notices of de-requisition. No such notice of de-requisition was also issued in the name of the petitioners or their alleged predecessors-in-interest Shamsun Nahar and others in respect of the disputed land.

16. Petitioners have not stated the date and year when their predecessor Shamsun Nahar died leaving behind them as their legal heirs to inherit her share in the disputed land and Syed Mohammad Abdul Motaleb and Abdul Hamid gifted their share therein to them. Though the petitioners claim that they prayed for restoration of possession in the disputed land on 4.3.1960 there is nothing to substantiate the same except their assertion. It appears from order dated 1.2.69 from the Order Sheet of the said LA Case No. 29 of 1949-50 that KGO was directed to demarcate the boundary of the acquired land on 8.2.69 and from order dated 13.2.69 it appears that KGO demarcated the boundary of part of CS Plot No. 681 of Dhanmondi (one of the disputed plots) on R 69 and it further appears from order dated 22.2.69 at petitioner No. 1 Sarwarjan Bhuiyan and staff of BCSIR were present on 8.2.69 at the time of demarcation of the said boundary. So it is clear that the petitioners did not claim the disputed land even in 1969 when the boundary line of acquired part of CS Plot No. 681 was demarcated. It is only in 1982 the petitioners became vigilant and filed application before the Martial Law Vigilance Team claiming the disputed land. Thereafter queries were made by the Government from the Deputy Commissioner following recommendation of the Senior Member, Martial Law Vigilance Team on 21.12.82 and several reports were sent by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka, last one being dated 20.10.86. In this report it has been stated that there is 26.27. acres of land within the boundary walls of respondent No. 4 BCSIR with several buildings thereon. In the said report it has also been stated that notices to de-requisition of 12.50 acres of land were issued on 24.1.1951 but possession was not made over to the owners. But we have already seen from the LA record that there was no question of delivering possession of the de-requisitioned land to the owners as no possession was taken over from them. So it is clear that the observation in the said report regarding non-delivery of possession of the de-requisitioned land is contrary to the record of the LA case. Thus, we find that the petitioners failed to explain how, when and by whom possession of the disputed land was taken over. But it is an admitted fact that the disputed land stood acquired by Gazette Notification dated 4.10. 1951 and the respondent No. 4, BCSIR is in possession of the same since 1957.

17. The learned Deputy Attorney-General faced with the difficulty that some notices of de-requisition were issued in this case submitted that the notices of de-requisition were not given effect to by the authorities as is evident from the subsequent action of the Government in acquiring the entire requisitioned area of 32.50 acres by Gazette Notification published on 4.10.1951. He further contended that since the petitioners did not challenge the vesting of the disputed land by the aforesaid Gazette Notification dated 4.10.1951, they cannot claim restoration of possession.

18. To meet this objection the petitioners have filed the application in course of the hearing as already noted for issuance of fresh rule challenging the said Gazette Notification.

<u>19. From the record it is seen that the petitioners are residents of Elephant Road, Dhaka and the Laboratory, residential, school buildings, etc. of the respondent No. 4, BCSIR are also situated at the Elephant Road, Dhaka and the respondent No. 4 is in possession of the disputed land since allotment of 7.60 acres of land in their favour by the Government in 1957 by construction of several buildings thereon, in the view and within the knowledge of the petitioners without any objection from them at any time. It is only in 1982 the petitioners woke up from their slumber and started filing applications to the different' authorities for restoration of possession but failed. Petitioners claim for restoration of possession in the facts and circumstances of the case suffers from laches and inordinate delay and they cannot now be allowed to disturb the status quo regarding possession in the disputed land after such long period of time. Extraordinary remedy provided by writ petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution is for speedy relief and is for the vigilant and not for the indolent ones like the petitioners and is to be sought immediately after the grievance is caused. It is well settled law that laches and delay disentitle one to such remedy. The petitioners having not sought the relief immediately after their grievance arose rather having acquiesced in the matter as far back as in the year 1969 they cannot now be allowed to claim the disputed land.</u>

20. Petitioner's application for issuance of fresh Rule Challenging the acquisition of the disputed land, in our view, also suffers from laches and inordinate delay. In that view of the matter their belated prayer for issuance of fresh Rule challenging the said Gazette Notification dated 4.10.1951 cannot be entertained.

21. Decisions in the case of Haramba Chandra Vs. Province of East Pakistan, reported in 15 DLR 452, Md. Ismail Vs. Government of East Pakistan, 21 DLR 267 and Meheruddin Vs. Bangladesh, reported in 30 DLR 426 relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioners have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of this case.

22. In the facts and circumstances as discussed above, we find no merit in the case of the petitioners.

23. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

The application for fresh Rule is rejected.

End.
