AKM Faruque ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Works and others ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Anwarul Hoque Choudhury, J.: This Rule arises out of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and is directed against an allotment letter bearing Memo No. 5817 dated 30.8.1987 issued by the Assistant Commissioner Settlement, Ministry of Works, Dhaka.

2. It is the case of the petitioner along with five others that they were allotted a piece or parcel of land measuring 400 square yards each for residential purpose situated at Mouza Senpara Parbatha under Police Station Mirpur being plot No. 5 Road No. 6 Block E section 2 by lease deed dated 17.5.79. Amaster plan was prepared and sanctioned by the competent authority for construction of houses of the allottees of different blocks and the said master plan was approved by the authority long ago in 1967. The allotted plots with their respective numbers were in Block E and F and a permanent vacant space in between Block E &F was kept for maintaining the residential character of the area and for the civic amenities of the residents of Block E &F. The petitioner and the other allottees of the area after their plan was passed by the Dhaka Improvement Trust constructed their residential houses in those leased out plots and the petitioner's house is situated in front of the eastern side facing the vacant space in between Block E &F of the Master plan of the Mirpur Housing Estate. The vacant space in between Block E &F of the Section 2 in fact was preserved in the Master plan for proper sanitation, light and ventilation and for free air for the residents of the area.

3. It is the further petitioner's case that subsequently for purpose of development of civic amenities of the residents of the areas the vacant space in between was handed over to the Dhaka Municipal Corporation in 1982 and since then the vacant space is in possession of the Dhaka City Corporation and the petitioner and other owners of the houses of the said block are enjoying the said vacant space kept in between the blocks for their passage to the their plots. While the petitioner and other allottees of the said blocks have been enjoying the said vacant space as their passage and other amenities the petitioner and other residents very recently came to know that at the instigation of some interested quarters the respondents in violation of the terms of the aforesaid lease deed and in breach of the public duties and obligation and also to the detriment of the civic amenities of the residents of both Block E and F of. Section 2 made plotting of the said vacant space and purported to have allotted those to different persons including the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 who are going to construct their houses in the said vacant space by blocking the main entrance of the petitioners and causing other inconvenience of light and air. The petitioner and other allottees made representations to the Ministry of Works and other authorities stating that the allotment of plot in respect of vacant space as in the  master plan is unjustified and illegal and further  requested the authority not to allot any plot, but to no result.

4. It has been further the case that the petitioner also thereafter sent a demand justice notice on 14th January, 1991 but no action has been taken in this regard by the respondents. It has been the further case that the new allottees being respondent Nos. 4 and 5 has constructed the house pursuant to the impugned order on the vacant space just in front of the house of the petitioner and other allottees blocking the main entrance of the house and also obstructing the light and air of the petitioner's house, and it is prayed that the respondents be restrained by an order of injunction by this court which was granted at the time of the issuance of the Rule.

5. We have heard the learned Advocate Mr. Md. Awlad Ali appearing in support of the Rule, who having taken us through the master plan of the Mirpur Housing Estate as appended to the writ petition, the approved plan of the house of the petitioner and the allotment letter by which petitioner's plot was leased out to him by the Works Housing/Settlement Department and also other papers on record, submitted that the master plan would clearly show that the vacant space was kept in between the block minus the road that are necessary as vacant space for affording passage and other amenities to the residents of the blocks and, according to the learned Advocate, this would amount to a representation made by the lessor, namely the Housing Settlement in the Ministry of Works and they would be legally bound to honour that representation which created an expectation that the vacant land would remain vacant because of which expectation the allottees took their respective plots on lease. Those would create right to the petitioner to insist that the vacant plot is utilised by keeping it vacant as was in the master plan on the basis of which expectation the petitioner would have a locus standi to challenge any change in the master plan made by violating the expectation and the representation made by the lessor initially at the time the plots were leased out and any deviations from it would be a violation of a promise which has been acted upon the lessor, hence need be restrained by this court.

6. According to the learned Advocate, this violation would not be a mere violation of any contractual obligation but a vested right arising out of equity which would not depend on contractual obligation but mutual trust. He further submitted that the petitioner's boundary, opening to the eastern side of the plot which is the vacant plot in the master plan and if now that vacant plot is leased out to anyone else he would be deprived of the entrance in his plot which would render the plot unfit for any residential purpose and that would cause a violation of the terms of the lease agreement by which the lessor and the lessee are bound.

7. The learned Advocate further submitted that on the plea of rehabilitation new plots were created behind the back of the allottees by unauthorised person changing the entire master plan which can only be done by the Government in the Ministry of Town Planning and in the instant case any sub-division of plots were unauthorised and having unauthorisedly injected in to the main master plan the sub-division of the plots are without lawful authority and further this sub-division would make the area completely uninhabitable, unhealthy, without free passage and flow of basic air and light to which light and air the petitioner has a vested right.

8. Respondent No. 2, namely the Assistant Commissioner of Settlement, Ministry of Works, Dhaka contested the Rule by filing an affidavit in opposition wherein the material allegations made in the petition have been denied asserting that the master plan prepared for the Mirpur Housing Estate in the year 1967 had many a time been altered and rectified with the approval of the proper authority. In the instant case as per approved plan of the authority the disputed land in question which is the vacant land in between blocks E & F as in the original master plan being within control of Housing Settlement and Ministry of Works having vested in the Government were subsequently alloted to the new allottees. That land in between Blocks E & F is in fact a rehabilitation zone and not kept as permanent vacant space for any light and air. The vacant land as a matter of fact has been allotted making new plots to the "affected people" and for their rehabilitation. Those new plots have in fact been styled and named as rehabilitation residential plot Nos. 5 and 5/2 and this rehabilitation lot 5/1 and 5/2 and the eastern side of original plot No. 5 and covering a portion of the vacant space has been allotted to respondent Nos. 4 and 5 and the matter has been approved by the appropriate authority and it has been approved by the land allotment committee in its decision dated 22.8.85 which decided the allotment of the said plot, situated in Section 2 Mirpur Road No. 6 with the consent of the Ministry of Law and Justice. Thereafter the deed of agreement has been registered in favour of respondent Nos. 4 and 5 bearing deed No. 2584 dated 30.7.89 and respondent Nos. 4 and 5 had been officially and physically handed over the possession of the said plots on 4.4.90. It has been further stated that this has been done by supplementary revised plan approved by the Chief Engineer of Housing and Settlement and this has been annexed as Annexure-2 in the Affidavit-in-opposition. According to the respondent No. 2, the vacant land had not been kept permanently in the master plan but it was kept for further accommodation of affected people of the area from whom the original lands were acquired for rehabilitation zone and in fact those plots were numbered as rehabilitation plots being Nos. K(1), K (2), K(3), K(4), K(5), 5(1) and 5(2). It is the further reply of the respondent No. 2 that all the carpetted, metalled concreted roads has been handed over to Dhaka Pourashava in the year 1982 and it was done for the purpose of maintenance of those roads in the residential area but the disputed land in question, the vacant land in between E and F Block where no roads had been constructed by the Housing Estate or by the Municipal Corporation at any point of time is not maintained as road by the Municipal Corporation and it has been the further case of the government that the land in question has been turned into residential plot and has been allotted subject to the approval of the concerned higher authority of the Housing Settlement It is the further case of the government that there are four roads crossing the disputed land in question being 5(1) and 5(2) and original plot No. 5 and its passage has never been blocked by the new plots in question. In front of the plot of the petitioner there is Road No. 6 and on the back of the plot is road No. 8 which is also the passage of plot No. 1 and plot No. 3, the road being in the north and the south. It is the further case that the petitioner in plot No. 5 instead of making the north and the south side, where these road Nos. 6 and 8 are situated as the front side of their plot, had shown the eastern side vacant land as the front side of his building which has no legal basis and his construction plan also did not show that.

9. Respondent Nos. 4 and 5 also opposed the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition and Mr. A Y Salehuzzaman, the learned Advocate who appeared for both of them, submitted that after the plots had been leased out to them respondent Nos. 4 and 5 have already constructed houses thereon at a cost of Taka six lac accordingly to a plan approved by the RAJUK, dated 23.9.90 (Annexure-Y) and the construction of the said house is completed in December, 1990 and the photo copy of the enquiry report in support thereof given by the Administrative Officer has been annexed as Annexure- Y (1) to show that it was so completed. It has been further stated that there is a road running north to south in between Block E and Block F of section 2 of the Mirpur Housing Estate, Block E lies to the west of the said road. There were several plots adjacent west of the said road within that block. These vacant plots were subsequently divided into eight sub-plots and were allotted to persons including the present respondent Nos. 4 and 5. These sub-plots were never permanent vacant space and the allotment has not changed the residential character of the plots. The revised plan has been annexed in their affidavit as Annexure J to which reference will be made at the relevant portion of the judgment.

10. Respondent No. 6 Dhaka Municipal Corporation appeared and filed an affidavit-in-opposition and was represented by Mr. AQM Shafiullah, the learned Advocate who was present at the time of argument of the case.

11. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the petitioner and also for respondent No. 2 and respondent Nos. 4 and 5 and also Dhaka Municipal Corporation and we find that in the instant case the dispute is over the creation of new sub-plots by means of a revised plan adding to the master plan and leasing it out to new allottees by the appropriate authority, namely Housing and Settlement Department from whom the petitioner AKM Faruque is also one of the lease holders being plot No. 5 of Section 2, Mirpur Housing Estate, which is adjacent to the newly created sub-plots No. 5(1) and 5(2). We have examined the master plan of the Mirpur Housing Estate which is annexed to the main writ petition by the petitioner being Annexure-'B'. From a reading of the said master plan it is seen that the said plan clearly mentioned where it is required to mention such as Road, Market, police station, wide road Graveyard, Lake, Playground etc. The vacant space in between Blocks E and F is not earmarked to be any road or market land or police station or mosque but just vacant and in front of which long vacant space at both ends there is a road marked as road in the master plan and in between the other blocks the crossing roads are numbered as Road No. 4, 5 and 6, 1,2,3, and Road No.8. This vacant space kept by the original framer of the plan in 1967 had not been marked for any particular purpose. The vacant land vested in the government within the residential zone are to be utilised for residential purposes by the government or for other amenities thereto. It appears that thereafter new plots were created terming them as rehabilitation plots in the said zone as or housing Estate within the master plan adding to the master plan. The new plots have been created on the same line one after the other, in a chain on the vacant side in between block E and F being new plot No. A(1), A(2), A(3), A(4), A(5) and in the chain thereafter, a new plot was created as "Police Station" and below that another two plots were created being plot Nos. 5(1) and 5(2) by keeping road No. 6 in front of plot No.1, 5, 5(1) and 5(2) as in the original plan, It is further seen from the revised plan Annexure-2 to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the Government at page 21 that in spite of the creation of plot Nos. 5 (1) and 5(2) on the part of eastern vacant side there is still 13 feet vacant space left after new plot on 5(1) and 5(2), from the other block. The petitioner can, so it appears, yet enter his plot from two ways namely Road No. 6 on the north and road No.8 on the south but vacant space of 13 ft. on the east would now be available to plot Nos. 5(1) and 5(2) because plot No. 5 shall have common boundary with Nos. 5(1) and 5(2) on the western side. This new site plan, clearly described to be a revised site plan and plots marked as rehabilitation plot. Those are created on the old vacant area starting from Mirpur Avenue No.1 ending in road No. 2 which covers in between a large number of other plots on the eastern side coming to main A venue and those plots are all in the vacant space in between. It is further seen that after creating the new plot A(l), A (2) and A(3) on the eastern north, facing the Avenue side, there is yet a vacant space of 40 ft at that end but at the bottom only 13 ft vacant space. We have examined the letter issued from the office of the Chief Engineer Housing and Settlement Estate and the letter for approval has been marked as an Annexure, which question of approval and non- approval has not been challenged in the original writ petition though it has been attempted to be agitated at the time of hearing of the petition and as that would be a question of fact not originally agitated in the petition we are not inclined to go into those facts and also for the reason that a plan once made is always capable of being revised thereafter by the marker and there is no bar to any revision or alteration and in the instant case the lease agreement with the new allottees having already been executed by the Directorate of Housing and Settlement and the established fact having been that the new allottees already with sanctioned plan from RAJUK had constructed their building in those newly leased out plots and the completion of the said construction by respondent Nos. 4 and 5 having been certified after local inspection, which is also in the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent Nos. 4 and 5 and when we have no reasons to doubt such a certificate given by an officer, in course of his official duty when presumption of its correctness under the Evidence Act would be evident, the question of sanction would not be relevant.

<u>12. Initially, a question arises as to the locus standi of the petitioner in moving this writ petition challenging the allounents of plots belonging to the government to a person it considers desirable for the purpose of writ jurisdiction. A person to move this court under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, need be an aggrieved person and an aggrieved person has often been described as a person against whom a decision has been pronounced illegally and which deprived him of something or refraining something or affected his title to something allowed to him by law. This would not include a person who had been merely disappointed of a benefit, which he might have received if some other order would have been made. This concept has since been enlarged and modified to enable a person who has been denied even of an expectation, created in the mind of the aggrieved person by the representation of the other, namely the Government functionary because of which expectation created by representation, the aggrieved person had changed his position to his disadvantage by acting upon it which he would not have acted but for the representation, a writ would lie to assert that expectation to be honored.</u>

<u>13. In the case of Mian Fazal Din Vs. Lahore Improvement Trust, Hamidur Rahman, J in delivering the judgment for their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan reported in 21 DLR (SC) 225 on a similar matter of re-allotment of plots within Gulberg residential area, Lahore, on the application of an allottee, observed in the relevant portion of the judgment, thus:</u>

<u>"It is clear from the above that the right considered sufficient for maintaining a proceeding of this nature is not necessarily a right in the strict juristic sense but it is enough if the applicant discloses that he has a personal interest in the performance of the legal duty which if not performed or performed in a manner not permitted by law would result in the loss of some personal benefit or advantage or the curtailment of a privilege or liberty or franchise."</u>

<u>The learned Judge further observed, thus:</u>

<u>"This principle governing an appeal cannot be invoked in the present case, particularly since the abandonment of a privilege or facility undertaken to be provided by the Improvement Trust cannot but have prejudicially affected the residents of the locality who had come to live therein not only on the expectation but on the representation contained in the Scheme, as sanctioned by the Government that such a facility would be provided. The deprivation of such a facility would, in our opinion, confer a sufficiently valuable right upon the residents of the Scheme to enable them to maintain an application for enforcing the Trust to discharge its obligation of executing the Scheme as sanctioned by the Government."</u>

14. In that case under report the contention was that the scheme has been changed without the approval of the Government and in the scheme the area which has been earmarked as Market in the master plan had been changed and realloted for the establishment of the Mosque for the Shia community and an allottee of one of the plots of the said Gulberg area challenged the allotment by writ and in that judgment their Lordships of the Supreme Court dismissed the leave application on the ground that the power of modification under the General Clause Act is there with the authority who made the original master plan and minor modification of the master plan would not need sanction of the Government or republication of the scheme in any newspaper, finding that the Mosque or market proposed to be constructed on the plot will not be restricted to any sect and it is not proposed to build an Imam bara on the said plot but a mosque for all the Muslims and not restricted to any particular sect and the appellant would not suffer any serious prejudice by the creation of the mosque dismissed the same.

15. In the instant case we have examined one further thing over and above the fact that the master plan did not earmark any mosque or market as in the Gulberg's case in the vacant area as quoted above, the lease agreement executed between the parties, namely the present petitioner Mr. AKM Faruque and the respondents, stipulated in clause No. 3 that the construction to be made on the demised property shall not cover more than two thirds of the area of the demised property and within three years from the date of commencement of the lease or within such further time as the lessor may allow in his discretion, the tenants shall complete building on the demised property, a house with all necessary out houses, boundary marks, drains and appurtenance for the purpose of a residence including a septic tank of a pattern approved by the Authorised Officer under Building Construction Act. and sub-clause 4 of clause 23 provided that the lessor has the right and is entitled to change the layout, outside the premises let out to the tenants, at all times and in any manner he may deem fit provided that in so doing none of the bye-laws relating to sanitation, light and ventilation are infringed and the residential character of the colony is not interfered with. It is further provided in clause 28 that if there be any dispute as to the terms or conditions or as to the reasonableness of anything contemplated to be done or decided by the lessor, the decision of the officer appointed by the lessor in his behalf shall be final and binding upon the parties and no civil suit shall lie.

16. It is thus seen that the lessor who is the Assistant Commissioner Settlement, Ministry of Works and Urban Development representing and on behalf of the President of People's Republic of Bangladesh, reserved the right of changing the plan, let out permanently, at all times and in any manner as it deemed fit but not to change the residential character of the colony in the process or to impose any restriction on any light, sanitation and ventilation.

17. In the instant case the new plots were created in the vacant space not earmarked for any particular purpose in the master plan, left vacant for the purpose of rehabilitating the affected owners and it appears that a good number of plots have been created in the revised plan and it is leased out to genuine persons who desire rehabilitation and affected persons of which respondent Nos. 4 and 5 are two and it is leased out to them for residential purposes only and there is nothing to show which has changed the residential character of the colony. It is also seen that even after rehabilitating these two plots enough vacant space is left and there is no question of interference with any light and air and we also find that by keeping vacant plots no representation had been made in the master plan to the tenants initially that those would be used for a garden or for children parks or playground, for the petitioner to be materially prejudiced in his expectation. Neither, it has changed the residential character of the colony. not obstructed the light and air of the resident allottees, nor prejudiced any representation, promise or expectation what is done by the lessor in the instant case, namely the Directorate of Housing and Settlement, had been done with lawful authority having all powers to change or modify the master plan in public necessity and public interest, providing residential plots to others who are equally deserving person, to receive a government allotment like the petitioner. The petitioner stands on no super category of citizen for any extra privilege, denying right of other citizen of the country, namely a right of having a plot in government owned residential area which has been acquired finally by the requiring body for the purpose of alloting those to deserving persons in the city for constructing a residential house.

18. We however, observe that one statement in the petition does not seem to tally with the records and it is the assertion of the petitioner that he has constructed a building in plot No.5 and its entry is now blocked. On an examinations of the said plan as submitted by the petitioner before the DIT for sanction we find that in the lay-out as done in that plan a wide road is shown in front of his building to be constructed on plot No. 5 and from a reading of the master plan it appears that in front of the house there is in fact a road and on the back side of the house there is also a road but in the plan submitted before the DIT a road has been shown to exist also on the side of the house which is not a road in the master plan but showed as a vacant land. Only because the petitioner's Engineer would show the vacant land as a road would not make the vacant land in the master plan to be a road on the side of the building as shown in the building plan submitted to the DIT but in any case that road shown on the side of the building is incorrect and it is also incorrect that the side of his building is blocked because the entry of the building as shown in the plan is not from the side but from the main road and creation of the new plots has not blocked petitioner's entry to his house.

19. We find no substance in this Rule which is thus discharged.

The stay granted earlier by this court as to the construction of the building of respondent Nos. 4 and 5 is hereby vacated.

End.

Mr. Syed JR Modassir Hossain, DAG with Mr. Fazlul Hoque AAG  -------  For the Petitioner.

parties:
Bangladesh  ------- Petitioner 
Vs. 
Md. Aslam and others.  ------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Qazi Shafiuddin, J.: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-9 to show cause why the judgment and decree dated 28.2.1981 and 6.3.1981 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet, in Title Appeal No. 229 of 1976 reversing those dated 21.8.76 and 28.8.1976 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Additional Court, Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 3 of 1976 should not be set aside.

2. Short relevant facts leading to the filing of this revisional application is that, the opposite party No. 1, as sole plaintiff, filed Title Suit No. 29 of 1971, in the 1 st Court of Subordinate Judge, against the petitioner and others for a declaration of his Junglebari Abadkari right on reclamation and confirmation of possession therein and also for permanent injunction. The said suit on transfer was renumbered as Title Suit No. 3 of 1976. During the pendency of the said title suit plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 2-9 filed a petition under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure to be impleaded as plaintiffs in the said suit. The prayer was allowed. The plaintiffs assert that the land in question originally belonged to Baraura Tea Company Ltd. within Rashidpur Tea Estate. The plaintiff No. 1 took lease for the year 1360 BS on annual rental thereof. Plaintiffs assert that after taking Amaldari from the Manager of the said Tea Company and clearing the jungles, plaintiff No. 1 was possessing the same without any interruption or obstruction. That defendant No. 1, Government of Bangladesh, served a notice of eviction under Act 10 of 1953 and being threatened he filed TS 218 of 1968. The said suit was dismissed on contest. Thereafter, the said plaintiff No. 1 preferred an appeal which subsequently was withdrawn with the leave of the Court to file a suit afresh.

3. The case of the petitioner Government is that the land originally belonged to Rashidpur Tea Estate Co. and the said Tea Estate Company surrendered the excess of khas land including the land in the suit and the Government took over the same. Compensation of the surrendered land including the suit land was also assessed. That the plaintiff is in unauthorised possession of the suit land. So notice was issued for his eviction and that the land having been vested in Govt. in pursuance of wholesale acquisition of tenancy, vested in the Government and the Government acquired the same free from all encumbrances.

4. The learned trial Court upon hearing the parties and perusing the evidence oral and documentary dismissed the suit on the findings that the plaintiffs had no right, title or interest in the suit property and they had also acquired no right by way of adverse possession and accordingly he dismissed the suit. On appeal by the plaintiffs-appellants the learned Appellate Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court and allowed the appeal.

5. Mr. Syed JR Modassir Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the petitioner, submits that the Court of appeal below committed an error of law in not adverting to the findings of the learned trial Court with proper and sound reasonings. Mr. Hossain argues that the learned Court of Appeal below has committed serious error of law in not considering the basic documents filed by the defendant Government such as Exhibits 'A', 'B', 'H' and 'K' which would positively indicate that the land in question and all the land surrendered to the Government by that Tea Estate as excess of khas lands had vested in the Government. Mr. Modassir Hossain also argues that there are errors of law on the face of record and as such the impugned judgment and decree must be set aside.

6. Mr. IN Dev, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties, has raised a question as to the revisional powers of this Court vis-a-vis the powers of this court under the unamended section 100 CPC. It is desirable that this question should besorted out at the outset before entering into the merit of the ease. Mr. IN Dev further lays stress that this Court under the present revisional power cannot transgress the power vested under the unrepealed section 100 CPC.

7. It is academic to dwell on the powers of this Court under the unrepealed section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure but it is worthwhile to discuss and give an outline of the powers of this Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, now as it stands, runs as follows:

"The High Court Division may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any Court subordinate to the High Court Division and in which no appeal lies thereto, and if such subordinate Court appears to have committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, the High Court may make such order in the, case as it thinks fit."

8. By the Ord. No. XLVIII of 1983 amendment the words "apparent on the face of the record" in the decision it has been substituted by "resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice", and further beyond the old section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure stood in the form.

9. The High Court may call for the record of any case which has been decided by any Court subordinate to such High Court and in which no appeal lies thereto, and if such subordinate Court appears-

(a) to have exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law, or

(b) to have failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested, or

(c) to have acted in the exercise of the jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity the High Court may make such order in the case as it thinks fit. It appears that the section at that time applied to jurisdiction along the irregular exercise or non-exercise of the same.

10.	 So a bare reading of these three stages, would reveal what radical changes in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been brought about. It needs be borne in mind that while section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure dealt with jurisdiction of the Court, powers under section 1 00 of the Code of Civil Procedure remained unaffected. An appeal under the unrepeated section 100 was provided from every decree in appeal by any subordinate Court on any of the following grounds:

(a) the decision being contrary to law or some usages having the force of law.

(b) the decision having failed to determine some material issues of law or usage having force of law.

(c) a substantial error or defect in the procedure provided by Code of Civil Procedure or any other law for the time being having force of law which may possibly have produced error or defect in the decision of the case upon the merit.

(d) appeal from an appellate decree passed ex-parte.

Thereafter powers under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure was squeezed and limited to "errors of law on the face of the record". Section 100 was omitted by Ord. XLIX of 1978 with effect from 1.6.79. Litigants could only invoke the jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure when no appeal lies against any order or decree. But with the repeal of section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure and re-enactment of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in its new garb, the powers of the High Court has increased to a large extent. Now under the newly amended provision as made in section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, the grounds for interference has been stretched from jurisdictional point of view for stretching and superseding the errors on the face of the record into errors of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

<u>11. The framers of law might have in their minds the effect of repeal of section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code and squeezing or curbing the powers of the High Court and thereby an attempt might have been made to make room for interference in case error in the decision has occasioned a failure of justice. The strict binding effect of concurrent findings of facts, "however erroneous the same might be, in revision, the same could not be interfered with has been diminished to a large extent by introducing the words "error in the decision occasioning failure of justice." "Error in the decision" coupled with, occasioning a failure of justice would lead the High Court to a larger scope of jurisdiction in mitigating the causes of failure of justice. Now the High Court in the interest of justice may go into the question of fact in revision to a limited sense to ameliorate the injustice that the subordinate Court might commit occasioning failure of justice. The term" occasioning failure of justice" has a far-reaching significance. It invests the High Court with wide power not only to go into the question of law but also to the question of fact in search of fact and to make scrutiny and analyse and if necessary to assess evidence for itself for its own satisfaction, how, to what extent such failure of justice has been perpetrated.</u>

12. The deleted appellate power under section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code haunts the High Court and the Court seeks after the truth in a bid to redress the errors resulting in the failure of justice. Therefore, it appears that the present section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code has made amends to a large extent, the loss incurred due to the absence of section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code.

13. Now coming to the question on merit let us now concentrate to observe how upon being faced with the pleadings of the parties, the evidence on record both oral and documentary, the court of appeal reacts; whether the court below proceeds in accordance with law or commits errors of law in the course of the trial occasioning failure of justice or commits an error in procedure affecting in the decision occasioning any failure of justice.

14. In the plaint, the plaintiff No.1 Md. Aslam as the sole plaintiff averred that he is the 16 annas owner of the suit land and had acquired the same from the Rashidpur Tea Estate on receipt of rent-receipts for clearing jungle and bushes and had been exercising "Abadkari Amaldari right". That on the expiry of the said Amaldari right on 29.9.1955, the plaintiff wrote to the Manager for renewal of the settlement and the Manager granted Amaldari letter dated 15.10.55 and thereafter by Amaldari letter dated 1.10.1957 renewed the term. He asserted that he himself acquired such right and settlement was taken in his name and he paid the rents by himself. That subsequently he filed Title Suit No. 218 of 1966 and ultimately withdrew the suit and appeal at the appellate stage with permission of the appellate Court to file a suit afresh. And he filed the present suit for a declaration of his Junglebari Abadkari right by reclamation as well as right by adverse possession and that the defendant had no right in the suit land and confirmation of possession. He also made a prayer for permanent injunction against the Government. It may be noted that the Rashidpur Tea Estate or for that matter the Baraura Tea Company Limited is not made a party in this suit.

15. During the pendency of the suit, by a petition under Order 1 rule 10, plaintiffs Nos. 2-9 have been added as plaintiffs by way of amendment of the plaint by order dated 8.3.1974.

16. Allowing the amendment of plaint by adding the petitioners as plaintiffs Nos. 2-9 and decreeing the suit by the appellate Judge in their favour, the learned Judge virtually committed a serious error in procedure in placing the plaintiffs Nos. 2-9 (with conflicting interest with the sole plaintiff) in the category of plaintiff and thereby violated the procedure of the Code of Civil Procedure when specific provision is made to transpose the plaintiff or defendants in their respective positions. Since plaintiff Nos. 2-9 have conflicting and divergent claim to title with the plaintiff No.1 they could be placed in the category of defendants and not as plaintiffs. There is an error in procedure and the learned Judge acted with material irregularity which vitiated the proceedings or affected the decision resulting in miscarriage of justice.

17. PW 1 Abdul Latif in his deposition stated that the lands in the suit in question were acquired by way of settlement by all the nine plaintiffs, rents were paid by them and they jointly possessed the lands. He further filed a registered partition deed dated 5.4.72 showing the suit lands were divided amongst all the nine plaintiffs on different shares mentioned in the said deed. The partition deed is made Ext.7.

18. Mr. JR Modassir Hussain argues that the new claim and new allegations raised subsequently which are inconsistent with the pleadings of the plaintiff made in the plaint is prohibited under Order 6 rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code. He alleged that the learned court of appeal below committed error of law in allowing these inconsistent pleas with the pleadings and erred in law in allowing the appeal and decreeing the suit by acting contrary to the provision of law.

Order 6 rule 7 runs as under :-

"No pleading shall, except by way of amendment, raise any new ground of claim or contain any allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings of the party pleading the same."

<u>19. The plaintiff must not make any departure from the earlier pleadings made in the plaint so as to bring into existence any new claim or raise any new ground or plea which are quite inconsistent, incongruous or a departure from the earlier stand or pleas. The Court will not allow either party from making any departure from the earlier pleadings set forth in the plaint or written statement. Plaint and written statement are the foundation of the claim of the plaintiff and the defendant; any deviation from the earlier stand would surely land the other side into serious dislocation and by Order 6 rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code the same has been made prohibited.</u>

<u>20. In the case of Kazi A. Khaleque Vs. Kazi Eazlur Rahman and others, reported in 34 DLR 278, a Division Bench of the High Court held., "No pleading except by way of amendment, shall raise any new ground or claim or contain any allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings of the party pleading the same. After the parties have filed their pleadings, they will not be allowed to depart from the pleadings or raise any new allegations of facts inconsistent with the previous pleadings. The Court will not allow any party to make out a new case not made out in their pleading."</u>

21. The Court of appeal appears to have acted illegally and beyond the power vested in it by allowing the plaintiff to make out a completely new case and to make out a new pleading inconsistent with his earlier pleadings made in the plaint and further the Court erred in law in decreeing the suit beyond the scope of the prayer made in the plaint.

22. Let us now have a look to the rent receipts which Mr. IN Dev terms as documents of title filed in support of the plaintiffs claim to title.

23. Ext. 1 is a rent receipt for the year 1360 BS dated 29.9.1953 bearing the signature of the issuing authority, Manager, Baraura Tea Company Ltd. in the name of Md. Aslam.

Ext. 1 (a) another rent receipt in an ordinary typed paper dated 15.10.1955 signed by Manager, Reshidpur Tea Estate for the year 1361 BS.

Ext. 1(b) is certified copy of yet another rent receipt dated 7.10.1957 for the year 1362 BS showing payment of rent on 7.10.1957.

Ext. 2 is a letter dated 15.9.1955 leasing out the property for two years.

24. These are the papers considered by the learned Judge in support of title of the plaintiff. The plaintiff asserts that by granting these rent receipts 'Abadkari Amaldari' right has been acquired by him.

25. These rent receipts were not formally proved by anybody although the same are marked as exhibits.

26. The plaintiff has filed the suit with the assertion that the plots in dispute were settled with him on the basis of the rent receipts granted by the Baraura Tea Company who was a rent receiver. It is found by the learned Judge, and also contended by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties that the said rent receipts were acted upon and the plaintiff held over the possession by acquiring Abadkari Amaldari right. It is to be noted that this Abadkari Amaldari right is unknown or unrecognised by the State Acquisition &Tenancy Act. Section 2 of the Act defines various types of right or tenancy recognised by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. By the word 'Amaldari' it is meant a writ authorising the grantee to take possession and there by Amaldari at best one can gain a possessory interest without any semblance to title.

<u>27. Section 101 of the Evidence Act, requires that the plaintiff who wants the Court to believe that the alleged receipts have created any right or title in his favour or any legal right or liability has been created by virtue of such settlement by way of those rent-receipts, it is the plaintiff who has to prove the same in a legal manner as provided under the Act. Whether these rent receipts were genuine or represented true and correct state of things, the burden of proving such things heavily lies on the plaintiff. It is to be noted that no witness has been examined to prove the rent receipts, the alleged signature of the Manager of the Tea Company Limited or the contents of such rent-receipts. Without such proof the rent-receipts Ext. 1, 1(a), 1(b) and Ext. 2 cannot be accepted as legally proved or exhibited. The learned Judge thus has committed a serious error of law in taking into consideration and based his decision on the rent-receipts in matter of title which 'affected the merit of the casco Mere filing a rent receipt or a private document without formal proof thereof and without proving the contents of such documents cannot fulfill the requirements of section 101 and section 103 of the Evidence Act. Therefore, in my view, by Ext. 1, 1(a), 1(b) and Ext. 2, the plaintiff has acquired no title.</u>

28. In support of my view, it would be profitable to quote the observation and decision of the Appellate Division made in the case of Ajirannessa Vs. Saper Mia, reported in 30 DLR (SC) 41 which runs as follows:

"In this case the plaintiffs have come to the Court with the assertion that the disputed land was settled with them by the owners of the land on the basis of the Kabuliyat Ext. 3(a) and produced the Dakhilas Ext. 4 series in proof of the fact that the Kabuliyat was acted upon on subsequent payment of rent in pursuance of the said settlement. According to section 101 of the Act, as referred to above, it is for the plaintiffs to prove that as a matter of fact, settlement was granted by the owners of the land and the rent receipts Ext. 4 series were really genuine and represented the correct state of things, as the plaintiffs desire the Court to believe on the said assertion. The burden of proof as to the genuineness of the dakhila Ext. 4 series is undoubtedly upon them in the absence of any legislative provision to the contrary. There having been no legislative enactment requiring the dakhilas, Ext. 4 series, which had been formally proved at the trial of the suit, to be accepted as genuine documents, merely on proof thereof there is no question of shifting the onus upon the defendants. The learned Judges of the High Court appears to have been under a misapprehension as to the real effect of formal proof of a document in a Court of law. A private document cannot be taken notice of and marked as an exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may, however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a person as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There may be cases where the law requires that the contents of a particular document shall be presumed to be correct unless they are rebutted by adducing evidence by a party who disputes their correctness, as has been provided in section I03B of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a landlord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. The learned Judges of the High Court have apparently made a mistake in taking the view that as soon as the rent receipts have been proved the primary onus of the plaintiffs has been discharged and the defendants having failed to produce any rebutting evidence the said rent receipts should have been accepted as genuine and relied upon. The onus of the plaintiffs cannot be discharged until the Court is persuaded to accept the position that there had been payment of rent by the tenant and acceptance thereof by the landlord, as a matter of fact on the basis of the disputed rent receipts. In this case both of the Courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or of procedure which had affected the merits of the case."

29. Apart from this, there is another aspect namely sub-lease is prohibited under section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which runs as follows:

"From the date of publication of notification under sub-section A(3) of section 17 or under sub-section (1) of section 31, no person shall sublet any land in his khas possession in the area to which it relates and under sub-section 2 of section 75A, any sub-letting made in contravention of sub-section (1) of section 75A shall be null and void."

Sub-section (2) of section 75A came into force on 22.9.56 by Act IV of 1956 making the subletting null and void in case of contravention of sub-section I of section 75A. Lease or sub-lease of any khas land prior to 29.9.56 would revert back to the original owner as being null and void but those made after that date would definitely revert back to the Govt. At any rate, the plaintiff who claims his right and title to the property in suit on the basis of these rent receipts acquires no title. The properties go back to the Baraura Tea Company Ltd. or to the Government even if these rent receipts were at all found to be valid. The plaintiff is placed in between Scilla and Charibdis, on the one side the Baraura Tea Company Ltd. who surrendered the excess of khas lands including the suit plots (and Government accepted the same) and on the other, the Government who has already acquired the same leaving nothing for the plaintiff to gain. Similar view has been expressed in the case of Abdur Rashid Vs. Abdus Samad, reported in 33 DLR 260.

<u>30. Ext. 2, the alleged basic lease letter granted by the Rashidpur Tea Estate dated 15.9.1955 leasing out the suit property for a period of two years is hit by section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act as not being registered. Unregistered lease deed of immovable property from year to year is inadmissible in evidence for lack of registration.</u>

31. This view finds support from the decision in the case of Abdul Majid Vs. Nabiruddin, reported in 22 DLR 360.

32. Mr. JR Modassir Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the petitioner, submits that Court of appeal' below committed an error of law in not taking into consideration the material documents filed by the Government in support of their claim. He submits that Exhibit 'A', statement of excess lands of the Tea Estate surrendered under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to the Government under Memo No. 989/SA dated 29.8.74;

Exhibit 'B' the certificate in Misc. Case No, 9 of 1972 under sub-section 4(a) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 by ADC (Rev.) Sylhet;

Exhibit 'H' papers surrendering excess khas land of Baraura Tea Company Ltd. to the Government signed by Manager of the Company and the CO Revenue, Bahubai dated 24.4.65 and Exhibit 'K', the compensation assessment rolls by the Government were not taken into consideration by the learned Appellate Judge and thereby the Government has been seriously prejudiced. It appears from the judgment of the learned appellate Court that he did not take into consideration these material papers and documents which are said to be the foundation of the Government's claim to title and which are set forth in the pleadings of the Government. This is a serious allegation as this touches the merit of the case. Omission to consider such vital documents affects the merit of the case.

33. State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force by publication of notification No. 4829 LR dated 2nd April, 1956, published in the Dhaka Gazelle Extraordinary dated 2nd April, 1956. The Government have acquired by notification in the official gazette all the interests of land of rent receivers as specified in the notification in the respective Taluks, Tenures, holding or tenancy and all interest in any estate, Taluk or holdings in the khas possession of the tenure holders. UR4er sub-section

(1) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Government acquires interest of the proprietors, tenure holders and rent receivers including khas lands (beyond the retainable limit) by publication of notification from the date mentioned therein and these interests vest in the Government absolutely free from all encumbrances. By Exhibit 'R' Baraura Tea Estate through their Manager surrendered the excess khas land to the Government. The learned trial Court found that the excess land so surrendered by Baraura Tea Co. Ltd. in favour of the Government was duly accepted by the Government and compensation assessment' roll was also published. Rent-receivers having khas lands in the capacity of a rent receiver are stripped of their excess khas lands on the very moment of the publication of notification under sub-section 1 of section 3, and the same vests in the Government absolutely free from all encumbrances. It may be noted that the lands in schedule of the plaint falls within surrendered excess khas land. It may also be noted that the records of right and the compensation roll were prepared in the name of the Baraura Tea Company and not in the name of the plaintiff. Had the plaintiff occupied the lands in question as a rayati or under rayati, record of right or the compensation roll would also have been prepared in his name and the Baraura Tea Company would definitely have excluded the plots in question from the lands surrendered as in the statement Ext. 'H'.

34. The scheme of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, would reveal that special provision has been made in Chapter II of Part-II of the Act in regard to acquisition of rent-receiving interests and special provision for acquisition of the interests of certain rent-receivers. According to this provision, rent-receiving interest can be acquired by notification under section 3 of the Act even before the general provisions of the aforesaid Act have been given effect to. Before acquisition of the interests of the rent-receivers and tenure holders or Taluks or rayati or the khas lands of the tenure holders or rent-receivers, preparation of the record of rights is necessary. Thereafter, the compensation assessment roll is prepared and published in order to give effect to such provision of law. Sub-section 2(a) in section 3 of the Act was introduced by amendment empowering the Government to publish notification in respect of rent-receiver by name with reference to areas where such interests exist in the manner the Government might determine and notifications were issued District-wise but the rent-receiving interests and vesting of khas lands in the Government shall vest in the Government with effect from 14.4.1956 in terms of those notification issued.

35. Therefore, the plaintiff's assertion that he has acquired title on the strength of Ext. 1, 1(a), 1(b) or Ext. 2 has absolutely no legal basis when the same are put to legal test and scrutiny.

36. As to adverse possession claimed by the plaintiffs in matter of acquisition of title, it is to be borne in mind that in order to acquire title by exercise of adverse possession, the same must be open, hostile and within the knowledge of the real owner for over statutory period of limitation. The learned appellate Judge declared title in favour of the plaintiff by adverse possession against the Tea Company who is not even a party in the suit and the Tea Company long before has been divested of its right, title and possession by surrendering the excess khas land in favour of the Government and thereby extinguished all its right and title. But as against the Government the learned appellate Judge did not utter a word, although Government is the defendant No.1 and the real contestant over the suit lands. As against Government the limitation for acquisition of tide by adverse possession is 60 years which is a far cry for the plaintiff to establish. The finding of the learned Judge is palpably wrong.

37. Mr. Hossain argues that the learned Court of appeal below has not controverted the findings of facts arrived at by the trial Court while reversing the same. It is a settled principle of law that the Court of appeal below must take into consideration the findings of facts arrived at by the trial Court with due application of mind. The Court should assess the evidence and come to a positive finding of his own. In case of disagreement on any issue of fact, the learned appellate Court should take the same all the more seriously giving better and sound reasoning in support of such altered findings. On a consideration of the rent-receipts and other papers of the plaintiffs the learned appellate Court found the plaintiffs as tenants under the Tea Company. But the learned Judge lost sight of the background of the case as well as the nature of documents of the .plaintiff produced and the attending circumstances under which the said papers were made public and also cogent reasons given by the learned trial Court. The learned trial Court disbelieved the papers filed by the plaintiffs on the ground that these papers were collusive and never saw the light of the day inasmuch as although the plaintiff Aslam filed a title suit being Title Suit No 218 of 1968 which was dismissed on contest and also filed an appeal before the appellate Court but these papers were not filed before the courts in support of his claim. This non-disclosure is a fact to be taken into consideration. Also the fact that PW 1 Abdul Latif who used to serve in the Baraura Tea Company in collusion with the staff might have manufactured these papers could not be brushed aside.

38. Upon consideration of the points raised, it is crystal clear that the learned Court of appeal below has committed serious error of law resulting in error in the decision which ultimately caused miscarriage of justice occasioning failure of justice. Therefore, his judgment and decree are liable to be set aside.

39. The Rule is accordingly made absolute.

40. It is hereby ordered that the judgment and decree date 28.2.81 and 6.3.1981 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet, in Title Appeal No. 229 of 1976, reversing those dated 21.8.1976 and 28.8.1976 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Additional Court, Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 3 of 1976, is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge are affirmed and maintained.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 153 of 1978
lawyer:
