Syed  Shamsur Rahman ------ For Respondent
parties:
Shahabuddin & ors ------Appellant
Vs.
Saijuddin & ors ------Respondent
full_judgment:
Anwarul Hoque Chowdhury, J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 26.7.74 passed by the Additional District Judge Khulna reversing those passed by the learned Munsif Second Court Bagerhat on 25.9.72 in Title Suit No. 716 of 196.

2. Plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the plot No. 1292 of khatian No. 66 and prayed for for injunction restraining the defendant from interfering with plaintiff's possession in the suit land on the allegation that the suit jote belonged to the father of plaintiff No. 1 and plaintiff No.2 in equal 8 annas share by inheritance which was sold to defendant No. 1 by two kabalas dated 29-1-37 and 3-5-38 respectively. But their sale deed did not include plot Nos. 1290 and which they got by exchange from one Jalaluddin and others prior to C.S. operation. They have been living there by erecting house and the defendant had not title and possession of the same that being so the defendant No. 1 had no right to lease out of the land. It was their further case the defendant No.1 on their asking leased out to them plot No. 1292 of khatian No. 66 and executed a patta on 28-2-45 as to plot No. 1292 and delivered possession to them and in the said patta defendant fraudulently inserted the plot No. 1290 and 1291 of Khatian 65 covering the area of 2'46 acres instead of plot No. 1292 which was agreed to be leased out by the registered patta.

3. The defendant's case is that plot No. 1292 which is the disputed plot including. plot of 1291 and 1304 of Khatian 65 belonged to Jalauddin and others in korfa under the jote recorded in khatian No. 63 in the name of Kalimuddin Shaikh. The Babus purchased the jote of khatian No. 65 but the said was subsequently purchased in auction by one Baru Bibi. It was the further case of the defendants that Baru Bibi after having gone into khas possession of the same sold it to one Saila Bala by registered kabala dated 11-8-38 and the said Saila Bala thereafter leased out to defendant no. 1 by a registered kabuliyat (Ext. C) dated 19-3-40 1'52 acres of plot no. 1290,1291 and 1261 and they had been in possession of the same by erecting Basa Bari on plot no. 1292. The further case of the defendant that the aforesaid lease was taken in the banami of his minor son and that he never leased out to the plaintiff at any point of time the plot bing no. 1292 and there was no talk of leasing out the same at the time of the patta dated 28-2-1945 and there was no fraudulent insertion also in the said Kabuliyat as alleged. The defendant's further case is that the plaintiff forcibly entered into his homestead in plot no. 1292 and erected huts there and are in possession thereof. The land has been rightly recorded in his name and the plaintiff has no case.

4. The learned Munsiff on a Consideration of the evidence on record found this.Suit land was in fact settled with the plaintiff and that they are in possession and upon that finding decreed the suit. On appeal the said was reversed and the judgment and decree of the trial court Was set aside and the suit was dismissed. As against that this appeal has been preferred by the plaintiff before this court.

5. Mr. M.A. Aziz, the learned Counsel appearing in support of the appeal having taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and the evidence on record pas contended that the learned Additional District Judge has erred in law in reversing the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif and had failed to apply his judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and specially that of the Pleader Commissioner's report as to possession. He has further argued that the learned court below was also wrong in holding that in matters like this When the allegation was a mistaken entry and description of the property written in registered document can only be rectified under Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act when in Inc was competent for the court to correct the error provided under proviso (1) of the Section 92 Evidence Act.

6. Mr. Syed Shamsur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents of the other hand has argued that the judgment and decree as passed by the learned Additional District Judge need not be interfered by this Court in appeal because the court in arriving at the finding that there was nothing to prove any fraud on record or mistaken description of the property inadvertently by the parties concerned it can not be said to be finding falling under proviso (1) to Section 92 of the Evidence Act and that being so plots described in a registered document being the terms of the contract cannot be varied by oral evidence between the parties and the document need be read as it is found written, expressing the intention of the  parties in executing the document. He further submits that there was no question of fraud or mistake in the case as the document clearly recited the plots to be plot nos. 1290, 1291 total area being 2'46, under khatian no 65. (and that being so plot no. 1292 covering an area of 2'86 each is more than the area of 2'46 as in the disputed kabuliyat cannot be read into because in that case it will change not only the plot numbers but also the area of the land leased out and there cannot be mistake on both the counts and thus he submits that the court of the learned Additional District Judge was correct in holding that the plaintiff is not entitled to the relief sought for. Mr. Rahman, the Advocate argued also on the point of limitation.

7. In the instant case, the point for consideration is whether the terms of the document as to disposition of property, evidenced by the registered patta dated 28-2-45 executed by defendant no.2 purporting to lease out plot no. 1290 under khatian no. 65 of an area of 1'14 (Bastu) and an area of 1'32 of plot no. 1291 (Bilan) in total an area of 2'46 of land could be read as only plot no. 1292 covering an area of 2'86 acres of land instead of 2'46 acres under khation no. 66 as urged by the plaintiff in the instant suit. There is no dispute that a patta of this nature dated 28-2-45 existed and there is also no dispute that plaintiff 1 and 2 did ask the defendant no.1 to lease out to them certain property on an agreed salami. What was disputed was that according to the plaintiff the said plot, agreed to be leased out by the defendant no. 1, was plot no. 1292 covering an area of 2'86 decimals of land under khatian no 66 when according to the defendant it was plot no. 1290 and 1291 covering an area of 2'46 under khatian no.65 as it is in fact written so in the patta in black and white.

8. Under the provisions of law when the terms of a contract or of a grant or of any disposition of property has been reduced to the form of a document, no evidence shall be given in proof of the terms of such document except the document itself and secondary evidence of the said would only be admissible when the original is lost or it is beyond the control or jurisdiction of the parties or of the court. When a document is produced in Court for proving the terms of the document by producing the original or the certified Copy of the same, nothing can be read into the said document, which is not there as the terms of the document cannot be varied, contradicted or added by extrinsic oral evidence unless the evidence is lead to show the invalidity of the document itself caused by fraud, intimidation, illegality, want of due execution, want of capacity of any contracting party, failure of consideration and of mistake of fact or law. This type of evidence would be admissible in evidence because that Will not contradict, vary or modify the terms of the document but rather it would make the very document invalid being executed by fraud or intimidation. It would also be possible to give evidence to show any mistake of fact' crept in to the document while describing the property.

<u>9. This mutual mistake as to description would call for rectification of the document which need to have been effected by filing a suit for rectification within the prescribed period of limitation as provided under section 31 of the Specific Relief Act before the appropriate forum on payment of the proper court fees. The said stilt under the said Specific Relief Act be filed subject to the restriction as provided under the said Act as to the exceptions of persons against whom a document would not be specifically enforced, particularly against a bonafide purchaser for value without notice of the mistake. That is however also the common sense view of the matter because a bonafide purchaser for value in good faith would be acting to his detriment on the misrepresentation of the description stated in a document which would be rectified subsequently to his disadvantage.</u>

10. In the instant case however the question is whether there was any fraud in executing the document as alleged by the plaintiff or just a bonafide mistake without fraud calling for rectification. There is a presumption of good faith in human transaction and therefore he who alleges fraud or bad faith need to prove the same by leading evidence to the satisfaction of the Court as to the existence of a fraud which would invalidate the document itself to the extent of the fraud committed. It is again the settled principle of law that a finding of a court as to the existence of fraud or the non-existence of the same would be a question of fact and not a question of law. It would be a question of law if however it could be shown that in arriving at that conclusion, as to the existence of fraud or mistake of fact, a wrong inference was drawn by a non consideration of the evidence on record or by a misreading of the same, thereby, causing the wrong inference to be drown in coming to a wrong conclusion, as to fact. This could only also be shown by showing that there was a misreading of a document which is a title document, causing a wrong inference. In the instant case the dispute is related to Ext, 4, being the patta, dated 28-2-45 and it is the title document. On a reference to the said patta it is seen that the said document written in Bengali referred to plots no. 1290 of khatian no. 65 and not a plot under khatian no. 66 and the said plot is described to be 1'14 decimals and the nature of the land is described as Bastu. It also includes plot no. 1291 under khatian no.65 covering an area of 1'32 decimals and the nature of the land is described to be Bilan and the total area of the land leased out of those plots, is described to be 2'46 acres of land. Plaintiff claims this plot to be only plot no. 1292 covering an area of 2'86 under khatian no. 66. So appears that the mistake as alleged by the plaintiff would refer not.only to the plot numbers but also to the area involved to a considerable extent. It 4 also change the khatian because plot no. 1290 a 1291 stands in khatian no. 65 and the area of the 2 plots in total is recorded in that khatian to he 2.55 decimals where according to the plaintiff plot 1292 would cover 2.86 acres. This is not a mistake of minor description but this is a mistake which in total in nature specially in view of the allegation I made by the plaintiff that plot no. 1290 and 1291 could not be taken from the defendant because those were their own properties from before the lease of their own property. This was not, thus. a mistake of fact as to description but a deliberate fraud committed by the defendant while inserting the plots already belonging to the plaintiff..

11. So. what in fact agreed to be leased out? Is there any evidence to that effect. I find none. Nor Me court below could find any such oral agreement. prior to the execution of kabuliat proved by evidence conclusively by the plaintiff. How then the fraud was proved.

12. In matters like this circumstantial evidence as to the subsequent dealing with the property would be also relevant in proving the conduct of the parties to the transaction, operating as an estoppel. It appears that the relevant khatian had long been recorded in the name of the defendant as to disputed-plot no. 1292. Is not in the name of the plaintiff and to his knowledge. There is noting on record also to show that the plaintiff had ever paid any rent to the defendant as their lessee as it would have been done if he was in fact a tenant, a lessee as to plot No. 1292. It is true that nonpayment rent alone will not extinguish or disprove a tenancy but when it is a question of the very existence of the status of a tenant payment of rent would be relevant as conduct subsequent of the parties concerned. It was the plaintiffs case that he came to know for the first time about the insertion of the wrong plot in the to at the time the lands were recorded in S.A. an in the name of the defendant, about 12 years after the document was duly executed and duly registered on 28-2-1945. What prompted the plaintiff to sleep all these years only to file the instant suit in the year 1969 to correct a mistake crept in a document registered in 1945. It is plaintiffs allegation that after the erroneous recording he has come to the court for a declaration of title by filing a suit in the year 1969 A.D. Of course, it is true, that the plaintiff will not be compelled to come to a court of law and file a suit for declaration that there was a wrong recording in the S.A. Khatian, immediately, after it was so recorded because he would be entitled to wait till his possession if any would be invaded and time would run from that date. in the instant case the court of appeal below found that as to that attempt of dispossession also there was no evidence on record to the effect that the plaintiff was threatened to be evicted from plot No.1292 by the defendant in Jaishta 1376 B.S. corresponding to 1969 A.D. So, the learned Court of appeal below found that there was neither a mistake of fact nor there was anything on record to show that any fraud was committed by defendant No. 1 upon the plaintiff in executing the kabuliat dated 28-2-45 which he was in fact seeking to rectify by this suit for declaration of title in the year 1969 which is more than 20 years after the alleged fraud. In that view of the matter the finding that there was no fraud or mistake in executing the document could not be said to have been arrived at by the learned Court of appeal below illegally. The said finding.of fact need not be disturbed by this Court in Second Appeal as there was no misreading of the patta or evidence by the courts below.

13. It is not a case of adverse possession and none fought out the suit on such an issue. Further, though an entry in khatian is not an evidence of title, it would be a prima facie evidence of possession. Possession is so recorded in the Government record in the name of defendant No. 1. and not in the name of the plaintiff. This the court of the first instance filed to take into consideration, as to the presumption of possession that would arises in favour of the defendant in view of the entry in the S.A. Khatian and the pleader Commissioner report has not rebutted the said presumption in proving, that the plaintiff was in possession of the instant homestead plot to the exclusion of the defendant. Further, a Pleader Commissioner's report is not binding upon the court. It is like any other evidence and need be considered in the light of the circumstances of each case.

<u>14. It is found by the Court of appeal below that a suit like this, would amount to rectification of a document and hence could only be done by a suit filed under section 31 of the Specific Relief Act and not by a suit for declaration of title as was done in the instant case. That view however do not seem to be correct. Because a court of law, as a court of equity would not allow a person to be relegated to a separate suit for rectification of mistake in a document. which came into effect by mutual mistake after possession delivered to plaintiff because a court of law would always be competent. even in a declaratory suit to correct the mistake even when the plaintiff does not bring a separate action for the rectification of the instrument within 3 years but only a declaratory suit much after a suit for rectification is barred.That will be the total and combined effect of proviso 1 to Section 92 of the Evidence Act read with Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act, basing on the doctrine of part performance read with Section 53A of the T.P. Act. In such a case the limitation will run from the time the mistake or the fraud was discovered and not from the date of the very execution of the document (Ref. Sukhdev-Vs- Ram Narain A.I.R. 1930 Allahabad 387, Sayamma-Vs-Venkata A.I.R. 1931 Madras, 783).</u>

<u>15. That being the position, I do not find any substance in this appeal. which is accordingly dismissed. The judgment and decree of the court of appeal below are upheld. In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs only before this Court.</u>

<u>Send down the records as expeditiously as possible.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Md. Nurul Huq with AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner
Sajjad Ali Khan, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Kalipada Saha being dead his heirs: Narayan Chandra Saha and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Faridpur in Title Appeal No. 198 of 1981 dated 13.8.84 affirming those of the learned Munsif, Sadar, Faridpur in Title Suit No. 505 of 1978 dated 10.7.81.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted a suit for declaration of his title in the suit land comprising an area of .03 acre. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that the land was recorded in RS Khatian No. 253 of Mouza Cerakhali, Madhukhali under PS Boalmari and was held and possessed by the predecessor of the plaintiff by way of settlement from Pannu Kumari and others since prior to revenue settlement operation. The plaintiff's predecessor had been possessing the suit land by constructing his dwelling hut and a shop and the land was recorded in his name. Lalit Mohan Shaha died leaving plaintiff as his sole heir who had been possessing the same on payment of rent by rent receipt. A certificate proceeding was started against the predecessor of the plaintiff and the suit land was auction sold. The plaintiff paid the certificate dues and released the suit land. The defendant No. 3 issued a notice dated 1.8.78 directing the plaintiff to surrender possession of the suit land and the same was received by the plaintiff on 11.8.78 although he had no right to issue such notice for eviction of the plaintiff. The suit land was wrongly recorded in khas land of the Government and the notice to surrender possession was illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff and the defendants have no right to get possession of the suit land. At the time of preparation of record of rights the land was recorded in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiff but subsequently it was changed and the name of the Government was inserted and brought the land in the khas khatian of the Government.

3. The defendant's case is, that the suit land situates within the periphery of Madhukhali hat and bazar. At the time of wholesale acquisition Madhukhali hat and bazar was acquired by the Government under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and since then it was managed by the Government on yearly lease. The suit land was correctly recorded in the khas khatian of the Government during the SA operation and the plaintiff has got no right, title and interest in the suit land.

4. The learned Munsif considering the facts, circumstances of the case and reading evidence on record dismissed the suit of the plaintiff and decreed in favour of the defendant and on appeal the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Faridpur affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree the plaintiff preferred this revision before this court.

5. Mr. Md. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the Mudhukhali hat was acquired by the Government under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 during the wholesale acquisition of such hats. The disputed plot belonged to a tenant and he did not come without the provision of section 3 and section 20 of the said Act and the tenant's interest was not acquired by notification of any final publication of the compensation assessment roll. He submits that it indicates that this is a distinct plot outside the hat, the defendant No. 3 served notice under section 5 of Ordinance No. XXIV of 1970 for surrendering the land to the Government illegally and without jurisdiction and as such the plaintiff petitioner is not bound to surrender the land nor the plaintiff can be evicted on such a notice. He further submits that plaintiff filed this suit for declaration of his title in respect of the suit land because the land was illegally recorded in khas khatian of the Government and also to remove the clouds of his title in the land but the learned Munsif due to his misreading of evidence on record and also without considering some of the material evidence dismissed the suit and on appeal the learned Subordinate Judge, Faridpur affirmed the judgment and decree without considering those facts, circumstances of the case and evidence on record according to law.

6. Mr. Md. Nurul Huq, also submits that this disputed plot is a distinct plot separated from the hat khatian and hat plots and more so it is not within -the periphery of Madhukhali hat He submits that the plaintiff was possessing the suit land on payment of rent by Ext. I series since the time of his predecessor-in-interest and released the land from auction sale on payment of certificate dues by DCR Ext. 2. The learned Courts below gave stress on the proximity and periphery of the suit land to the hat. In order to make the point clear be referred to 22 DLR 715 where it has been held:

"It often happened that private persons raise shops near about a bazar or a hat but mere proximity to a hat would not make it as building in a hat. It must be clearly shown that the disputed property is in a hat or bazar"

7. He also referred to 34 DLR (AD) 103 wherein periphery of hat or bazar has been described in the following terms

"Periphery of hat or bazar was within the bounds of any land of hat or bazar. But the land which is not physically attached to the hat or bazar nor shown as such in any settlement record could be treated as within the periphery of the hat or bazar. If the hat is separated by an intervening space from the plot on which the bazar is situated the word 'periphery' cannot be constituted to have brought the appellant's plots within the definition of hat or bazar."

8. He submits that in this case the disputed land is in plot No. 255 under RS Khatian No. 253 of mouza Gerakhali of Boalmari PS and to the north of the plot there is another plot 255/720 under khatian No. 202 and thereafter to the north of this latter plot the hat plots situate. Thus the suit plot is intervened by another plot which is attached according to the deposition of DW 1, the Tahsilder of the Government and he deposed that the hat comprises of four plots namely RS plot Nos. 292, 296, 431 and 267/734. Thus he submits that it is evident that the suit plot does not fall within the hat plots nor attached and within the periphery of Madhukhali hat. This aspect of the material evidence was not assessed by the learned Subordinate Judge on appeal and also by the learned Munsif.

9. He further submits that only consideration which was misread and misinterpreted by the learned court below in respect of the following pleadings of the plaintiffs in the plaint:

“অত্র আদালতের এলাকাধীন থানা বোয়ালমারী অনুর্গত গাজখলী মধুখালী মৌজার পূর্ব্বে বিধি পান্নাকুরারী গং মালিকাধীন বার্ষিক ২.০০ টাকা সদর কর আর এস ২৫৩ নং খতিয়ানে যে একটি জমা লেখা যায় তাহাতে বাদীর পুর্ব্বাবর্তী আর এস জরিপের বহু পুর্ব্বে হইতে প্রজানিযুক্ত থাকিয়া তৎপর ঐ স্থানে বাজার শুরু হইলে তথায় দোকান ঘর উত্তোলনে তথায় ব্যবসা করিয়া আসিতে থাকে।”

10. The learned Advocate submits that in this case the learned Subordinate Judge misread and misconceived the words “এইখানে বাজার শুরু হইলে” as it means where bazar was started in the locality or area because the bazar was started within the aforementioned 4 plots as specified by DW 1 in his deposition and the disputed plot which was recorded in the name of the predecessors of the plaintiff was on different plot under a different khatian intervened by another plot under another khatian as mentioned above. So he totally misread and misconstrued the pleadings of the plaintiff in the plaint. In delivering judgment the learned Subordinate Judge erred in holding that:

"In the above statements plaintiff himself admits that bazar was held in the suit land and his predecessor, raised a shop therein"…………….."These above statements amply prove that the suit land and his predecessor, raised a shop therein"…………………."These above statements amply prove that the suit land is within the Madhukhali hat or bazar. A pleading is serious production of facts. Any admission in the pleading is fatal to the party concerned. So in this instant case the plaintiff has no scope of escaping from the hat and bazar."

11. In this respect the learned Advocate referred AIR 1926 (PC) 29 wherein it has been held:

"The whole conduct of the case can scarcely be scrutinised with the strictness with which a case would be scrutinised in this country. That allowances must be made is abundantly clear from the history of the proceedings in this case, because it is apparent when the proceedings are looked at that really both the plaintiff and the defendants floundered as to their real case, and that the court quite rightly took upon itself to straighten out the whole matter and try to discover what the real question between the parties was."

12. So in view of the above submissions and the decisions cited by the learned Advocate I find that the case of the plaintiff is, that the suit land since the predecessors-in-interest of the deceased plaintiff was in his possession and he possessed the same by constructing a hat on the land and thereafter when the Madhukhali hat was started- in the locality or in the nearby area he built a shop on the plot. He paid rent by Ext I series and released the land from auction sale on payment of certificate dues by LCR Ext. 2 The pleading of the plaintiff does not contain within the few lines of the plaint but it comprises the entire of it and to clear any ambiguity the plaint should be read entirely. The said plot does not fall in the hat plots and this is specific plot and nor even it is within the periphery of the hat as it is intervened by another plot and not within the circumference of hat plots. So, the notice under section 5 of the Ordinance XXIV of 1970 is illegal and the land was wrongly recorded in the khas khatian of the Government.

13. The learned Advocate appearing for the Government submits that under Order VII rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code plaintiff is required to specify and describe the suit plots. In support of his submission he referred 42 DLR 432. I have seen the schedule of the plaint that the suit plot has been described specifically in the language that the disputed schedule is in the district of Faridpur, PS Boalmari under mouza Cerakhali, Madhukhali PS the plot No. 255 recorded in RS Khatian No. 253 comprising an area of .03 acre. So there is no ambiguity in respect of the suit plot and there would be no difficulty if a decree is passed and more so the deceased plaintiff and his heirs are in possession of the suit land and living there by constructing hat and' a grocery shop attached to his residential house.

Next point raised by the learned Advocate is that the suit is barred by limitation because the suit was not filed within 6 years of the date of knowledge from the Tahsil office when his rent was not accepted as the land was recorded in khas khatian of the Government

14. The learned advocate in reply submits that the defendant did not raise this point of limitation in their pleadings in written statement nor at the time of hearing before the learned trial Court and the learned lower appellate Court and no issue-in respect of this point was framed and here also before this court the point is not raised by specific assertion against the plaintiff petitioner through any counter affidavit. He asserts that defendant No. 3 issued a notice on 1.8.78 directing the plaintiff to hand over possession of the suit land and the same was served upon the plaintiff on 11.8.78 and that the defendant No. 3 has no right to issue such notice for eviction of the plaintiff. He submits that the suit was filed on 8.9.78 after the date of notice of eviction as mentioned above and the date of notice was the cause of action in this case and so it was within time.

<u>15. This submission and the assertion of the learned Advocate of the plaintiff petitioner is not challenged by the opposite party. So I find no objection of limitation was raised in the written statement nor during hearing in the trial Court nor before the lower appellate Court and also here before this court by filing any counter affidavit. So at this moment this point raised by the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party is not sustainable in law and cannot be considered at this stage.</u>

16. I perused the supplementary affidavit of the plaintiff petitioner and found that as many as 10 cases were instituted by the owners of the plot Nos. 301, 253, 252, 311, 303, 393/725, 304, 310, 271, 274, 432, 434 and many other plots which are in close proximity of the four hat plots on receiving notices to surrender their lands to the Government and in all these cases decrees were passed in favour of the plaintiffs and against the Government by the trial Court and no appeal was preferred by the Government

17. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the material evidence which were not considered by the courts below and in view of the above discussion and the rulings cited above, I am of the view that the learned lower appellate Court and the trial Court totally misconceived the facts and circumstances of the case and also material evidence on record and so they came to an erroneous decision in the disputed plot and the plots where hat is situated.

18. In the result, therefore, I make the Rule absolute, set aside the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Faridpur affirming those of the Munsif, Sadar, Faridpur and pass the decree in the suit land declaring title of the plaintiff. The entering of the suit land in the khas khatian of the Government was wrong and I direct for necessary correction.

19. In the facts and circumstances of the case the parties will bear their respective costs.

Let the records be sent down to the lower courts.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Mahmudul Islam, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
None appears ----- for the Respondents.
parties:
Alhaj Mohammad Rahimuddin Bharsha ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh represented by the Secretary to the Ministry of Works and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque, J.: In this Rule the respondents have been called upon to show cause why the notification No. SRO 365-L/86 dated 23.9.1986 published in the Bangladesh Gazette, Additional Issue (Annexure "A") to the petition so far as it relates to House No. SW(F)4 Gulshan Model Town, Dhaka and Memo No. Shakha-9/AP/ 675 dated 12.5.1988 (Annexure "A(1)") to the petition should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Case of the petitioner is that he is, a citizen and permanent resident of Bangladesh; that Plot No. 4 of Block No. SW(F) of Gulshan Model Town was leased out by the respondent No.2 to one Abu Zahid Md. Omar by a registered deed of lease dated 13.2.68 (Annexure "B"); that the said Abu Zahid Md. Omar constructed a house in the said plot and was in possession thereon; that while in such title and possession the said Abu Zahid Md. Omar entered into an agreement with the petitioner to sell the said house hereinafter referred to as the disputed property to him and obtained necessary permission from the respondent No. 2 on 11.3.85 (Annexure "C"); that thereafter the said Abu Zahid Md. Omar by registered deed of sale dated 27.3.85 (Annexure "E" to the petition) sold the disputed property to the petitioner at a consideration of Tk. 16 lakh and made over possession thereof to the petitioner and since then petitioner has been in continuous and peaceful possession of the disputed property; that thereafter the petitioner applied to the respondent No. 2 for mutation of his name in place of name of the vendor and by the Memo dated 28.4.86 (Annexure "F") his name was mutated; that the petitioner left Bangladesh for the United Kingdom for treatment on 8.9.86 and returned to Bangladesh on 6.10.1986; that the petitioner submitted a revised plan for modification of the house with the authorised officer of respondent No. 2 on 14.3.1987 and the said authoritsed officer, 2 days thereafter informed the petitioner that the disputed property has been included in the list of abandoned properties published in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 23.9.86 (Annexure "A"); that thereupon the petitioner filed an application on 19.4.87 to the Secretary, Ministry of Works for excluding the disputed property from the list of abandoned properties (Annexure "I"); that Ministry of Works by Memo' dated 2.1.88 (Annexure J) informed the petitioner that the Ministry of Works has nothing to do in the matter since the petitioner did not apply to the Court of Settlement within 108 days; that on the same date i.e., on 2.1.88, the petitioner filed another application (Annexure "K") to the Minister-in-Charge of Ministry of Works requesting him to exclude the disputed property from the list of the abandoned properties, that the respondent No. 1 by another Memo dated 12.5.88 (Annexure A(1) refused to exclude the disputed property from the list of the abandoned properties; that the disputed property was owned and possessed by a citizen of Bangladesh before purchase by the petitioner and since the petitioner has been in title and possession of the same it cannot be treated as an abandoned property; that no notice was ever served upon the petitioner or his vendor to show cause why the disputed property should not be treated as abandoned property; that respondents had no materials before them for their prima facie satisfaction that the disputed property is an abandoned property and the disputed property cannot come within mischief of abandoned properties and, as such, inclusion of the disputed property in the list of abandoned properties (Annexure "A") is illegal, void and without lawful authority; that respondent No. 1 used to keep respondent No. 2 informed about the DIT Plots which respondent No. 1 treated as abandoned property; that the disputed property was not treated as abandoned property when petitioner's vendor was in possession and the petitioner purchased the disputed property relying upon the permission granted by the respondent No. 2 for sale of the same by the vendor to the petitioner and as such the respondents are stopped from treating the disputed property as abandoned property; that the petitioner was in the United Kingdom when the impugned Gazette notice was published on 23.9.86 and after his return he was not told by anybody about the publication of the aforesaid list and as such he was totally unaware of the fact of the disputed property in the said list till he was informed about the same by the authoriscd officer of respondent No. 2 on 16.3.1987; that the petitioner thereafter approached the respondent No. 1 to exclude the disputed property from the list of abandoned properties; that though the respondent No. 1 excluded from such list properties which were wrongly included in the list but refused to exclude the disputed property from the list of the abandoned properties; that time for filing the application before the Court of Settlement had expired before the petitioner learnt about the inclusion of the disputed property in the list of the abandoned properties and, as such, he has no remedy otherwise than by way of an application under Article 102 of the Constitution; that by letter dated 12.5.88 respondent No. 1 asked the petitioner to surrender the possession of the disputed house and as such the petitioner filed this petition challenging the legality of the inclusion of his house in the said Gazette notification and notice to surrender possession.

3. Though the notice of the Rule was served on the respondent No. 1 on 12.12.88 no appearance has yet been made on behalf of the respondent No. 1. Although respondent No. 2 had entered appearance on 19.6.1990 but no affidavit-in-opposition has been filed nor the learned Advocate on behalf of the respondent's appeared at the hearing of the Rule.

4. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Advocate along with Mr. Mahmudul Islam, Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner. Learned Advocate placed before us all the annexures and relying on the said documents submitted that the vendor of the petitioner as well as the petitioner himself has always been citizen and permanent resident of Bangladesh and had and has always been in possession of the disputed property and the petitioner is still in possession of the same and as such there is no reason for treating the disputed property as abandoned property. Even no notice as contemplated under section 4 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance 1985 (Ordinance No LIV of 1985) was issued or served upon the petitioner or his vendor and as such inclusion of the disputed property in the list of abandoned properties on 23.9.86 is without jurisdiction and of no legal effect. The learned Advocate further submitted that inclusion in the said list of the disputed property which did not answer the description of the abandoned property within the meaning of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 affected petitioner's fundamental right guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution. The learned Advocate further submitted that though alternative remedy to go to the Court of Settlement within the period of 108 days from the publication of the list in the official Gazette has been provided under section 7 of the said Ordinance petitioner's property not being an abandoned property within the meaning of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and no notice having been served upon him treating the disputed property as an abandoned property and in the peculiar facts and circumstances of this particular case that the petitioner having no means of knowing about the inclusion of the disputed property in the list of abandoned properties before 16.3.87 when the time for filing a case before the Court of Settlement had already expired the petitioner had no efficacious remedy before any other forum and as such the petitioners petition is maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution.

5. It appears from the registered lease deed dated 13.2.68 in favour of the petitioner's vendor that the petitioner's vendor Abu Zahid Mohammad Omar, son of late Kazi Abdul Wadud of village Paigram Kashba, PS Fuitala, District Khulna by profession Government Servant took lease of the disputed plot from the respondent No. 2 by the said deed. It further appears from Memo No. DIT/OD (E)/808-3(3)2-P dated 11.3.85 of the respondent No. 2 that the said lessee was granted permission to sell the disputed property of the petitioner at a consideration of Taka 16 lakh, It also appears from the registered deed of sale dated 27.3.85 that the said lessor sold that disputed property to the petitioner at Taka 16 lakh and delivered the possession of the disputed property to the petitioner. It also appears from the endorsement in Passport No. E 514156 that the petitioner left Dhaka Airport on 8th September 1986 and arrived at Heathrow, London on 9.9.86 and returned back to Dhaka on 6.10.86.

6. Since the allegations made by the petitioner are supported by the documents referred to hereinabove have not been controverted we have no option but to hold that the petitioner's vendor, a citizen of Bangladesh, was in possession of the disputed property till he sold the same to the petitioner by a registered sale deed dated 27.3.85 obtaining due permission from the required authorities concerned. Further, allegation of the petitioner that he has been in possession of the disputed property since his purchase on 27.3.85 has not also been controverted. Moreover, inclusion of the disputed property in the Gazette Notification dated 23rd September 1986 in the "Kha" list of the abandoned properties under section 5(1)(b) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance 1985 (Ordinance No. LIV of 1985) as a building in respect of which possession has not been taken over by the Government and also Memo No. Sakha-9/ AP/675 dated 12.5.88 of the respondent No. 1 directing the petitioner to surrender possession conclusively show that the petitioner is still in possession of the disputed property.

<u>7. In the above facts and circumstances when the petitioner as well as his vendor are citizens of Bangladesh and the disputed property had been in possession of petitioner's vendor till his sale to the petitioner and the petitioner is still in possession of the same without a notice under the provisions of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and Rules made thereunder the said property cannot be treated as an abandoned property, Petitioner's assertion that no notice was served at any time to treat the disputed property as an abandoned property having not been controverted we have no option but to hold that inclusion of the disputed property in the list of the abandoned properties published on 23.9.86 in pursuance of section 5 of the aforesaid Ordinance is without jurisdiction.</u>

8. Article 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh provides that subject to any restrictions imposed by law, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property, and no property Shall be compulsorily acquired, nationalised or requisitioned save by authority of law. So petitioner as a citizen of Bangladesh has right to hold the disputed property owned by him unless such right is restricted by any law or acquired or nationalised by the authority of law. We have already found that the property owned by the petitioner does not answer the description of abandoned property and inclusion of the same in the list of the abandoned properties is without jurisdiction.

<u>9. In the case of Fazlul Huq Chowdhury Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 30 DLR 336 a Division Bench of this Court held as follows regarding maintainability of a writ petition without availing of an alternative remedy:</u>

<u>"But we think that an application under Article 102 of the Constitution lies, even where an alternative remedy is available, if the impugned order is ex facie void for want of jurisdiction or is violative of any provision of the Constitution."</u>

<u>10. Irrespective of the fact that the petitioner had any alternative remedy inclusion of the disputed property in the list of abandoned properties by the respondent No. 1 in the Gazette notification dated 23.9.86 having been found to be without any jurisdiction, such notification in respect of the disputed property certainly is in violation of petitioner's right to hold property under Article 42 of the Constitution. As such the petitioner's petition to enforce such fundamental right is maintainable under Article 102(1) of the Constitution. Moreover, from the facts stated in the petition and the documents annexed thereto we are satisfied that the petitioner had no knowledge about the inclusion of the disputed property in the list of the abandoned properties till 16.3.87 when he came to know about the same and when the time for filing the case before the Court of Settlement had already expired. As such, even if petitioner's fundamental right would not have been affected his petition under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution would lie inasmuch as the alternative remedy provided became non-existent in the meantime and that the disputed property did not answer description of the abandoned property for which he could not have availed of any remedy other than by way of a writ petition. We, therefore, hold that the petitioner's application challenging the inclusion of the disputed property in the impugned Gazette notification and Memorandum Annexure "A" & "(1)" respectively is maintainable under Article 102(1) as well as Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution.</u>

11. In the result the Rule is made absolute and the inclusion of the petitioner's House No. 4 of Block No. SW(F) being holding No. 3 Road No. 6 of the Gulshan Model Town under PS Gulshan, Dhaka under serial 38 in the Gazette notification dated 23rd September 1986 (Annexure "A" to the petition) as well as Memo No. Shakha-9/AP/675 dated 12.5.88 (Annexure "A(1)" to the petition) are declared to have been made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect and the respondent No. 1 is directed to exclude the disputed property being serial No. 38 at page 9764(1) from the said Gazette notification dated 23rd September 1986.

As there is no appearance of the respondents there will be no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: From the judgment and order dated 9-6-81 passed by the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 5 of 1968.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed J:- In this appeal by special leave, the question is whether the High Court Division acted within its strictly limited jurisdiction under section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code, in reversing, in a second appeal, the lower Appellate Court's decision keeping in view the established principle that no second appeal lies on ground of erroneous finding of fact, however, gross the error may be.

2. Circumstances giving rise to this air peal may be described as follows: Respondent as plaintiff filed O.C. Suit No. 225 of 1960 in the Court of Munsif, Rajshahi, for recovery of khas possession of the suit land by ejecting the appellant defendant. He claimed the appellant to be his tenant from month to month in respect of the suit premises. The appellant denied the landlord-tenant relationship with the respondent and set up a claim of his independent title on the basis of purchase. The suit land consists of 3 Plots. Nos. 25, 26 and 27 recorded under three separate C.S. Khatians, Plot No. 24 belonged to Kalicharan; plot No. 27 belonged to Shashi Bhushan and Plot No. 25 belonged to Swarna Baishnabi. According to the respondent, Kali Charan purchased the other two plots, got his name mutated in the landlord's sherista, paid rent for those plots till his death, and after him his son, Pati Ram, defendant No. 2, inherited the property and possessed it in the same way. Defendant No. 2 executed a Power of Attorney dated 2-1-51. Ext. 1, in favour of one Sekandar giving him full power to transfer the suit land and Sekandar accordingly transferred the suit land consisting of all the three plots to the plaintiff by executing a registered sale-deed dated 9-4-51, Ext. 2. Plaintiff immediately took possession, constructed a few huts on the land and inducted thereon defendant No. 1 as a monthly tenant at a rental of Tk. 10/- from Chaitra 1358 B.S. The defendant after paying rent for a few months started defaulting and during "Rent-roll Operation" unsuccessfully tried to get his name recorded in the khatian as owner of the suit premises. The Revenue authorities after rejections recorded the plaintiff's name in the S.A. Khatian. Thereafter defendant No. 1 procured a sale-deed from Golap Sundari, Shashi, Bhusan's wife, and therewith tried to assert his title. The plaintiff served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon defendant No. 1 and thereby terminating the tenancy, filed the suit for ejectment. Contention of defendant No.1 was that he was never a tenant of the plaintiff, but that he had first entered into plot. No. 27 with permission of Golap Sundari in 1949 erected the huts thereon and entered into an agreement with her for sale of this plot on 26-11-56 and thereafter, by a registered sale-deed dated 3-8-59 purchased the plot. As to plot No. 26 which was inherited by Pati Ram from Kali Charan, defendant No. 1 claimed that by an agreement with Pati Ram, for sale he got possession of this plot from 1949, but Pati Ram subsequently proved faithless, sided with the plaintiff, and disowned the agreement. As to plot No. 25, his claim is that as it was lying vacant he took over its possession. He denied the plaintiff's title to the suit premises and particularly denied that he was inducted by plaintiff as a monthly tenant.

3. The trial Court on consideration of evidence found defendant No. 1 to be a mono they tenant of the plaintiff and that the tenancy was terminated by a valid notice and on these findings, decreed the suit. But on appeal the learned District Judge reversed the findings of the trial Court and arrived at his own finding to the effect that defendant No. 1 was not plaintiff's tenant but was in possession of the suit premises by his own right and on this finding allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. There was a second appeal by the plaintiff- S.A. No. 5 of 1968- in which Division Bench of the High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and decree dated 29 April 1982 reversed the lower Appellate Courts decision and restored that of the trial Court.

4. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed learned Counsel for the appellant. has seriously assailed the High Court Division's interference with the lower Appellate Court's decision and contended that the question involved is whether the appellant is respondent's tenant in the suit premises and that this is purely a question of fact. This question he has contended was conclusively determined by the lower Appellate Court Division which being final judge of fact, interference with its decision by the High Court is palpably illegal and beyond its jurisdiction given under section 100 C.P.C. The interference has been criticized on the ground that the High Court Division reconsidered and re-assessed the, entire evidence in second appeal, as if it were a first appeal whereas such re-assessment and reconsideration of evidence on a question on fact is strictly prohibited by law. The learned Counsel has argued that there was no illegality in the decision of the lower Appellate Court nor was there any error or defect in the procedure followed by lower Appellate Court in arriving at its findings, and as such, reversal thereof in second appeal is unwarranted. In support of these contentions the learned Counsel has referred to a number of cases decided by superior Tribunals including, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, all of which are in agreement on the established principle that a finding of fact, however erroneous and inexcusable it might be, stands immune from interference in second appeal.

5. Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed learned Advocate for the respondent, on the other hand has contended that the question involved in this appeal is not purely a question of fact, but it involves a substantial question-of law in that some important documents on the basis of which the respondent claims title have been misconstrued by the lower Appellate Court The learned Advocate has pointed out that though in a suit for ejectment the question of title is not directly an issue still in this case this question was incidentally gone into, and rightly so, but while considering the question of title the lower Appellate Court illegally and on erroneous view of law rejected the plaintiff's sale-deed, Ext. 2 based on the Power of Attorney, Ext. 1. The learned Counsel has further contended that a great number of Rent-receipts, Ext. 3 series, showing payment of rent by Kalicharan and thereafter, by his son, Pati Ram, both before and after the State Acquisition, and the record of rights, namely, S.A. Khatian in favour of the respondent, have been brushed aside by the learned District Judge on erroneous view of law and as such though the question involved, whether the landlord tenant relationship exists between the parties is a question of fact, yet the proper legal effect of the proved fact is essentially a question of law ; at best, the question involved in this case is a mixed question of law and fact. In deciding the question of fact, it has been further argued, the learned District Judge misdirected himself and as such his finding is not immune from interference in second appeal.

6. As it appears, the three plots, 25, 26 and 27 constituting the suit land, originally belonged to three persons, Kalicharan, Shashi Bhushan and Swarna Baishnabi. Of them Swarna Baishnabi was completely out of the picture from the very beginning. The appellant claims title on the basis of the sale-deed, Ext. 2, dated 9 April 1951 executed by Sekandar who got the Power-of-Attorney dated 2 January 1951, Ext. 1, from Kalicharan's son and heir Pati Ram, defendant No.2. The learned District Judge has observed that this transfer is not valid in that the Power-of-Attorney in his view does not contemplate power to execute any sale-deed but it contemplates power to get registered an "execute sale-deed". The High Court Division construed the Power-of-Attorney otherwise and found it to include and contemplate power of both execution and registration of a sale-deed for the purpose of transferring the land. Moreover, the principal namely, Pati Ram himself appeared in the suit and filed a written statement supporting the plaintiff's purchase by the sale deed, Ext. 2 executed on the basis of the Power-of-Attorney Ext.1. It is, therefore, found that the respondent's document of title has been rejected by the lower appellate Court on misconstruction, of the Power-of-Attorney.

7. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed learned Counsel contends that the question to be decided in this case is a question of fact and this does not involve an issue of law merely because some documents have been interpreted and construed. He has made a distinction between constructions of a document which is an instrument of title or is otherwise direct foundation of rights, and construction of a document which is not a document of title but is a document containing items of evidence or historical narration. On this point he seeks support from an observation of the Judicial Committee of Privy Council in the case of Midnapur Zimindary Company Vs. Uma Charan, AIR 1923 PC, 187. In that case, the date of an under-tenure was to be traced out and fixed from contents of some documents and oral evidence. No document creating the under-tenure came up for consideration, but some documents giving the historical narration of the under-tenure were construed and thereupon the High Court reversed the finding of fact arrived at by the lower Appellate Court. The Privy Council while reversing the High Court's judgment and restoring that of the lower appellate court observed:

"Where the question to be decided is one of fact, it does not involve an issue of law merely because documents, which were not instruments of title or contracts or statutes or otherwise the direct foundation of rights but were really historical materials have to be construed for the purpose.............There is no ground for a second appeal upon a question of fact unless it can be shown that the lower Appellate Court misdirected itself in point of law in dealing with this question upon the evidence."

Needless to say while there can be no question as to the soundness of this principle as laid down by the Privy Council; the facts of the case are different from that of the instant case wherein a document of title has been straightaway ignored on an erroneous interpretation of its basis, namely, the Power of Attorney. Misconstruction of this document, we find involves a question of law.

<u>8. The sale-deed, Ext. 2 includes three plots two of which namely Nos. 25 and 27 did not originally belong to Kalicharan; but evidence led by the plaintiff is that Kalicharan purchased those two plots, got his name mutated in the Landlord's sherista and paid rent accordingly. In support of this claim rent-receipt Ext. 3 to 3(h) have been produced. The learned District Judge, however, excluded these rent-receipts from consideration taking the view that the rent-receipts though purportedly issued by the ex-landlord, do not relate to the suit plots. The High Court Division disagreed with this view and observed, we think rightly, that unless a tenant's name is recorded in the Rent-Roll by mutation he cannot pay rent. The High Court Division further found that although the plot numbers were not mentioned in the receipts, other particulars including the exact amount of rent were specifically mentioned there and that this fact established connection between them and the plots in question. On the other hand, no rent was paid by Shashi Bhusan or his wife Golap Sundari or Swarna Baishnabi (owner of plot No. 25) at any time before the State Acquisition. Thereafter rent for all the three plots was paid to the government by Pati Ram defendant No. 2, son of Kalicharan, as per rent-receipts Exts.3(h)to 3 (p): and since plaintiff's purchase in 1951 he has been paying the rent The rent-receipts were excluded from consideration by the lower Appellate Court taking the view that these are provisional receipts and that they carry little weight in that “any person interested in a land may pay rent to the Government Acquired Estate". This view is erroneous for rent-receipts, though not documents of title are important items of evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows title. Again, plaintiff's name has also been recorded in the S.A. Khatian prepared in the period immediately following the whole-sale state-acquisition in 1956 and all objections raised by defendant No. 1 were overruled by the Revenue-officer and then by the appellate authority.</u>

9. As against the plaintiff's documents, as discussed above, defendant No. I produced his sale-deed, Ext. A, dated 3 August 1959 executed by Golap Sundari, whose husband Sashi Bhusan was the owner of plot No. 27. But from long before this transaction Sashi Bhusan himself was not in possession of the plot as appears from the payment of rent by Kalicharan in his own name, Plaintiff's contention is that Ext. A is a mere piece of paper without any consideration. Even if Ext. A is accepted as a genuine document of transfer of plot No. 27, it will give him title from its date, but as to his claim of possession from 1949, there is no basis. That he has been in possession of the premises from 1951 is an admitted fact but the question is in what capacity. If he had no title from 1951 to the date of the sale-deed 3-8-59 it will be quite reasonable to hold that its basis is the tenancy from the plaintiff, Of course the gap of 8 years was sought to have been filled by an unregistered agreement dated 26-11-56 Ext. B made between Golap Sundari and one Belaluddin, brother of defendant No.1 Hut evidence of Golap Sundari herself shows that she gave possession about ‘7 years ago', which goes back to 1957 at the earliest. Failure to pay rent on her part at any time belies the story of her own possession of the plot when her sale- deed was executed

10 As to the induction of defendant No. 1 as a tenant in the premises, there is no documentary evidence about the creation of the tenancy; and the explanation given by him is that after staying in the premises fc r 8 to 9 months he let it out to defendant No. 1, whose brother Belaluddin was his student. A big number of witnesses gave testimony' supporting the plaintiff's claim that the defendant No. 1 was inducted into the suit land by the plaintiff who himself raised the structures thereon. Defendant No. 1 on the other hand; examined two witnesses including himself the other being Golap Sundari, deposing that he possessed the suit land by his right and not as anybody's tenant. Had the matter as to existence of the tenancy been left to be decided by these two sets of oral evidence only the finding of the lower Appellate Court would have been final; but this is not the case here as the parties led documentary evidence as well in support of their respective claims.

<u>11. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed's main contention is that the fundamental question involved in this case is a question of fact and that in view of the established principle of law for deciding' a second appeal as formulated as far back as 1890 by the Privy Council in the case of Durga Chowdhurani V. Jewahir Singh. 18 ILR, Cal. 23, the High Court Division was not at libertyto re-assess the evidence to come to an independent finding of its own. At the outset, we have stated this 'principle' which is that no second appeal lies except on the grounds specified in section 100 C.P C. formerly, section 584 which was in force when the said case of Durga Chowdhurani went before the Privy Council. It has been held there:</u>

<u>"There is no jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal on the ground of an erroneous finding of fact however gross or inexcusable the error may seem to be. Where there is no error or defect in the procedure, the finding of the first Appellate Court upon a question of fact is final, if that Court had before it evidence proper for its consideration in support of the finding."</u>

<u>The question involved in that case was rather simple, whether an ejmali property had been partitioned between two brothers, upon the death of one whom his widow claimed to enjoy her husband's share exclusively. The finding of fact as decided by the lower Appellate Court was conclusive and the High Court's interference therewith in second appeal was held to be without jurisdiction. The principle of law as laid down in Durga Chowdhurani's case was followed in a great number of cases all through and Sayed Ishtiaq Ahmed has referred to three of them namely the cases of Abdul Mazid Vs. Khalil Ahmed, 12 DLR SC 132; Nadir Shah Vs. Lal Shah, PLD 1954 Lah, 447 and Deity Patta bhiramaswamy, Vs. S. Hanymayya, AIR 1959 SC 57. In those cases the Supreme Courts strongly deprecated the tendency in some of the High Courts to exercise the prohibited jurisdiction in second appeal purely on question of fact. Facts of those cases need no], be referred to here but on plain reading of those decisions it will tie clear that no question of law was involved in those decisions attracting the High Court's jurisdiction under section 100 C.P.C</u>

<u>12. Though a question of fact is different from a question of law but there are cases in which difficulty arises as to the distinction between them. In the case of Najar Chandra Pal V. Sukur Sk. AIR 1918 PC 92 the Privy Council took note of this difficulty and observed:</u>

<u>"Questions of law and fact are sometimes difficult to disentangle. The proper legal effect of a proved fact is essentially a question of law, so also is the question of admissibility of evidence and the question whether any evidence has been offered on one side or the other: but the question whether the fact has been proved, when evidence for and against has been properly admitted is essentially a question of fact.................High Court should not interfere with the finding of fact on the ground that upon the documents and evidence placed before the lower Court, the High Court would have come to a different conclusion.............The High Court's functions are completely circumscribed by the provision of the statute passed for the express purpose of securing some measure of finality in cases where the balance of evidence, verbal and documentary arose for decision."</u>

<u>But in a subsequent case, Dhanna Mal v Roy Bahadur Moti Sagar, AIR J972 PC 102, the Privy Council held that whether a tenancy is permanent is a question of law and observed the question whether a tenancy is permanent or precarious is one of .legal inference from fact and not itself a question of fact". It arose from a suit for recovery of rent and ejectment. Rent at enhanced rate was demanded by the landlord, but enhancement of rent was not permissible if the tenancy was permanent. The tenant did not plead in his written statement that the tenancy was permanent, and in a previous suit for rent he had submitted to the enhancement of rent. The lower Appellate Court found in favour of the tenant that the tenancy was permanent, but the High Court in second appeal reversed the finding and held the tenancy to be temporary taking the view that the question involved is an issue of law. High Court's decision was upheld "by the Privy Council which also approved of the High Court's describing the question as "a mixed question of law and fact", with warning that "insofar as dependsupon fact, the finding of the first appellate court must be accepted". In the case of Walt Mohammad v. Mohammad Baks, AIR 1930 PC. 91 the Privy Council reversed the decision of the High Court which had interfered, in second appeal, with the .lower Appellate Court's decision regarding a question of fact which was whether the land under a mortgage was sold away by the mortgagee. The Privy Council rejected the contention that "entries in the record-of-rights were foundations of title" but held them to be mere items of evidence to be produced by the vendee to prove the sale.</u>

<u>13. There are many cases in which determination of a question of law is dependent upon the determination of a question of fact and also cases in which a question of fact requires to be determined on construction of documents not exactly documents of title but documents having direct bearing on the question. In such cases fact and law intermixed giving rise to what is ordinarily called 'mixed question' of Jaw and fact, In those cases the High Court's interference with the decision of the lower appellate court may be warranted to prevent miscarriage of justice.</u>

<u>14. I n the well- known case of Sm. Bivabati Vs. Ramendra Narayan, AIR 1947 PC 20, the Privy Council reiterated "the established practice of the Board to decline to review the evidence for the third time where there are concurrent judgments of two courts on a pure question of fact" particularly when the circumstances justifying departure from the practice are not made out. One of those circumstance as set out in that judgment is "some miscarriage of justice or violation of some principle of law or practice...............violation being such a proposition of law that" if it is corrected the finding cannot stand". In every case the general principle to be followed is that a finding of face arrived at by the court of first appeal shall not be disturbed by the High Court, but a finding of fact to attain immunity from attack in second appeal must be based on evidence. If a finding is not based on evidence or if it is based on utter inadequacy of evidence on which no reasonable conclusion can be reached, then interference therewith in second appeal is certainly justified. Misreading of evidence is a ground for interference but mis-appreciation of evidence is not. A finding which is inconsistent with the evidence on record must call for interference in second, appeal. Again, if a decision of the lower Appellate Court consists of both 'oral and documentary evidence but a part of the documentary evidence is misunderstood it will not provide a ground for interference when the document does not form the preponderance of the evidence. High Court's power in second appeal does not include power to review the evidence to come to a finding of its own on a question of fact, but the High Court can give a finding which has not been given by the lower appellate court on the evidence on record; interference on that ground will be quite lawful. After all, every case must be decided on the facts and circumstances of that case keeping in view these broad principles.</u>

15. In the light of this discussion, it is to be seen whether in this case the High Court Division re-assessed or reviewed the entire evidence on a pure question of fact. Our answer will be in the negative. Finding of the lower Appellate Court cannot claim immunity in view of the fact that in arriving at the finding the lower appellate Court excluded for consideration the appellant's document of title on misconstruing its basis, namely the Power of Attorney and also a long series of rent- receipts on erroneous view of law, Even if the respondent had acquired any title in one of the three plots by his sale-deed of the year 1959 his prior possession for 7 to 8 years cannot be explained by anything except his possession as a tenant under the appellant. This is the inevitable interference from proved facts. In the circumstances, the High Court Division's interference is justified and within the jurisdiction prescribed by law.

16. The result therefore, is that the appeal is dismissed, but no order as to costs is made.

End.

full_judgment:
A. T. M. Afzal, J.: Contesting defendants No.1 and 3 in a suit for partition being Title Suit No. 17 of 1975 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, are appellants in this appeal by leave.

2. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 brought the suit claiming an area of .1100 ajutangsha out of .4264 ajutangsha of schedule "A" to the plaint which has been described as follows:

"Schedule "A"

Within Dacca Collectorate P. S. Ramna, Mouza Ramna S. A. Khatian No. 174 S. A. Plot No. 1162 Nature of land Pucca house, Area .4264 Ajutangsha."

3. The learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit fully in preliminary form subject to payment of advolorem Court Fee on the valuation of the suit by judgment and decree dated 23.6.79. On appeal by the defendant-appellants, the High Court Division, Dhaka by the impugned Judgment and decree dated 22 March 1984 modified the decree of the trial Court by holding that "the plaintiff do get a saham of .1062-1/2 acre of land out of "A" schedule property on partition by metes and bounds".

4. Now there is no controversy as to the issues and points raised and decided in the suit and the appeal. The plaintiffs share as declared by the High Court Division finally is also not in question.

<u>5. But leave has been obtained on a technical point alleging error and incompleteness in the order passed by the High Court Division. It is this "that the plaintiff having acquired no right, title and interest in the demarcated '0464 acre of C. S. Plot No. 16, '0875 acre of C. S. Plot NO.17 and .0800 acre of C. S. Plot No. 19 totally measuring '2134 acre which have been included in '4264 acre of S. A. Plot No. 1162 of S. A. Khatian No. 174, as has been described in Schedule "A" to the plaint, the learned Judges of the High Court Division have committed substantial error of law in failing to direct to identify and demarcate .2125 acre of C. S. Plot No. 17, as had been purchased by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by their deeds dated 4.1.54 and 5.1.54 out of land of Schedule 'A' to the plaint and to allot a saham of 1062-1/2 acre to the plaintiff only out of the said demarcated area of '2125 acre and dismiss the suit with regard to the rest of the disputed Plot No.1162."</u>

6. It may be stated at the outset that the objection as above was not raised in the First Appeal before the High Court Division. The appellants, therefore, cannot find fault with the impugned order passed by the High Court Division. Even then we shall examine if there is any substance in the contention raised.

7. The question is: Is any direction necessary to identify and demarcate beforehand .2125 acre of C.S. Plot No.17 in order to effect partition of the suit land? It is true that the Plaintiff has stated in his plaint that Defendant No.1 and his (plaintiffs) vendor defendant No.2 Abedulla obtained well- demarcated .2125 ajutangsha land from C. S. Plot No. 17 under two registered deeds dated 4.1.54 and 5.1.54 and started possession by erecting structures, etc. The Plaintiff has claimed his share on the basis of his purchase from defendant No. 2 Abedulla by two registered kabalas dated 5.2.74 and 15.2.74. Let us see, briefly, how the plaintiff has stated his case in the plaint with reference to the records of right C.S. and S.A and whether defendants have raised an objection at any stage with regard to the correctness of the S. A. record on the basis of which the suit has been instituted and contested.

8. Admittedly suit involves three original C.S. Plots no.16,17 and 19. One Sonabi Bewa had raiyati jote right in the first two plots and she possessed .08 decs of land of C.S.Plot No.19. Plaintiffs case is that the heirs of Sonabi Bewa transferred the said lands to Ram Charan Ramani by a registered deed of sale dated 20.12.46 who in turn made a transfer to Mvi. Mohammad Elahadad on 22.3.47 except a small portion of C. S. Plot No. 16 which he had transferred to one Nagar Bashi Gope. While the heirs of Mohamad Elahadad were in possession of the said lands, the plaint reads, they transferred aforesaid well demarcated .2125 ajutangsha land from C. S. Plot No. 17 to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by two registered deeds i. c. lease and rent sale deeds dated 4.1. 54 and 5.1. 54 and possession was delivered to the transferees. The aforesaid heirs then transferred .3100 ajutangsha from C.S. Plot no. 17 by two registered deeds dated 18. 2. 54 and 20. 2. 54 to defendant Nos. 1 and 3 and delivered possession to the purchasers.

9. It has been stated in the plaint that thus the defendant Nos. 1-3 acquired '3000 ajut land in plot No.17 and .3100 ajut in plot No.16 by different deeds and they also got possession in .0800 ajut land in C. S. plot No. 19 which their predecessors were in adverse possession from long before. Defendant Nos. 1 to 3 were new persons in the locality. They went into possession after purchase but on measurement it was found that they actually got .3000 ajut in plot No. 17, .0464 ajut in plot No .16 and .0800 ajut in plot No .19-in all .4264 ajut land in the three plots. The defendants remained satisfied with the said area and when S.A. operation began, the land been correctly recorded in the name of defendants 1-3 in S. A. Khatian No 174, Plot No. 1162 and the same record had been confirmed in all subsequent proceedings.

10. Plaintiffs further case is that defendant No. 2 while in ejmali possession of the said S. A. plot No. 1162 with his other co-purchasers, who are his full elder brother and brother's wife, defendants 1 and 3, by making some amicable arrangement without any measurement and partition by metes and bounds transferred '1100 ajutangsha out of '4264 ajutangsha of S. A. Plot No.1162 (schedule B to the plaint) by two registered sale deeds dated 5.2.74 and 15.2.74 to the plaintiff for a total consideration of Tk. 83,000/- and delivered possession thereof.

11. The defendant-appellants main contention was that the defendant No. 2 had no title and interest in S.A. Plot No.1162 as he was only a name-lender in the documents dated 4.1.54 and 5.1.54 by which '2125 ajut land out of C.S. Plot No.17 was obtained by defendant 1 and defendant 2, the latter being the younger brother of the former and allegedly minor at the relevant time. This contention has been negatived concurrently by the trial Court and the High Court Division. The defendant-appellants, however, never raised any objection as to the correctness of the S.A. Record or the amalgamation of the interests as under the C.S. records as described by the plaintiff in his plaint.

12. In the First Appeal the only objection was regarding identity of the suit land. It was sought to be contended that unless the specific portions of C:S. Plot Nos. 16, 17 and 19 are relayed by local investigation, it cannot be said which portion of those three plots comprises S.A. Plot No. 1162. The High Court Division observed in its judgment that the defendants raised no objection to the recording of this S.A. Khatian, rather they accepted the same as correct and paid rent on the basis of Ext. 5. After his purchase the plaintiff mutated his name in S.A. Khatian No. 174 to which the contesting defendants raised no objection. The High Court Division further observed that the defendants took no step to relay the C.S. Plots at the trial nor they challenged the framing of the suit on the basis of S.A. Khatian No. 174.

13. It will be seen that the plaintiff claims to have acquired title to the suit land on the basis of his purchase from defendant No. 2 following S.A. record. He instituted the suit on the basis of the same S.A. Plot No. 1162 of S.A. Khatian No. 174 to which the appellants never raised any objection at any time. In these circumstances it is difficult to agree with the submission of Mr. Pal that a direction is necessary to identify and demarcate 2125 acre of C.S. Plot No. 17 before allowing a saham of '1062- 1/2 acre to the plaintiff. In the context of the creation of the new Jama under the S.A. Khatian on the basis of which the plaintiff claims title and brought the suit for partition and regard being had to the fact that the appellants raised no objection as to the recording and consolidation of interests under the. S.A. Khatian No. 174 as asserted by the plaintiff, there is neither any reason nor necessity now for demarcating beforehand the area of land purchased by defendants 1 and 2 out of original C.S. Plot No. 17. The demarcation of the plaintiffs share out of S.A. Plot No. 1162 will be done by the Advocate Commissioner having regard to all the principles of partition and the defendants can take objection, if any, before the decree is made final.

14. In the result, therefore, the appeal must fail. It is dismissed without any cost.

End.
