case_source:
In the matter of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
And in the matter of an order dated 8.5.72, 22.4.72 and 16.2,72 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dacca in, Title Suit No.162 of 1968.
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J.-This Rule was issued at the instance of the plaintiffs calling upon the opposite parties to show cause why the orders dated 16th February, 22nd April and 8th May, 1972 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 5th Court Dacca in Title Suit No. 162 of 1968 should not be set aside.

Opposite party No. 2 only entered appearance in this Case and has shown cause by filing a counter-affidavit.

2. At the outset, we note that the two impugned orders, namely, order Nos. 208 dated 16th February, 1972 and 216 dated 8th May. 1972 have been impugned under misconception. So far as order No. 208 is concerned the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners concedes that the petitioner s are only aggrieved by certain observations made therein, but not by the actual order. So far as order No. 216 is concerned, the learned Advocate also concedes that the prayer for setting aside this order will become redundant, if the order No. 213 dated 22nd April, 1972 is set aside by this Court. Therefore, our consideration in this matter will be with regard to order No. 213 dated 22nd April, 1972 only, because, by this order the learned Subordinate Judge accepted the report of the Sheristadar with regard to the valuation of the suit, determining the valuation at Taka 1,52,000/- and that by this order the plaintiffs have been directed to put ad-valorem court fees on the basis of the said valuation.

3. The facts, in short, which are necessary for disposal of the Rule as indicated above, are as follows :-petitioner No. I as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 8 of 1963 on 16th April, 1963 in the Court of 3rd Subordinate Judge, Dacca which having teen transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dacca, was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 162 of 1968. The suit was for declaration that the plaintiffs are the owners of 1/4th share of .40 acre of land in respect of C.S. plot No. 59 under khatian No. 6947, Touzi No. 141 BI, P. S. Ramna, Segunbagicha, Topkhana Road, Dacca, and the proforma defendants are the owners of 3/4th share according to Mohammedan law of inheritance; and that an mutation be made to the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca regarding the filing of the suit as desired by him ordering him to withdraw the payment made to the defendant No. 2 and to withhold the payment yet to be made in respect of .20 acre of land of C. S. plot No. 59 is concerned in L. A. Case No. II of 1961-62 during the pendency of the suit. Proforma deferants were transposed to the category of plaintiff as plaintiff Nos. 2 to 6 on 27th June, 1963 subject to the question of limitation to be decided at the time of trial. Subsequently, the plaintiffs failed an application for amendment of the plant stating inter alia that the plaintiffs land measuring .76 acre is comprised of .36 acre out of plot No. 77 and .31 acre out of plot No. 59 and .09 acre out of plot No. 58 and the suit land measuring .20 acre is out of 31 acre of plot No. 59 but through mistake it was stated in the plaint that the plaintiff's .76 acre land is comprised of .36 acre of plot No. 77 and .40 acre of plot No. 59 and the suit land measuring .20 acre is out of .40 acre of plot No. 59. After hearing both the parties prayer for amendment was allowed by the order No. 27 dated 10th February, 1964. 'Thereafter, the plaintiffs filed another application for amendment of the prayer made in the plaint on 18th November, 1964 in the following manner:-

"A declaration that the plaintiff No. I is entitled to 1/4th share and the plaintiff Nos. 2 to 6 to 3/4th share in respect of the land acquired by Government on a declaration of their title to the entire .76 acre of land i.e. .36 acre from plot No. 77 and .31 acre from plot No. 59 and .9 acre from plot No. 58. This prayer for amendment was also allowed by order No. 48 dated 18th November, 1964.

4. In the plaint, it has been stated inter alia, that the plaintiff's predecessor Ali Mohammad purchased .76 acre of land with definite boundaries fully described in the registered kabala No. 1171 dated 13.7.26 from Karimon Shah and others who purchased the said .76 acre of land with similar boundaries described in the registered kabala dated 14.12.1921 from Dari Goala, owner of 3 plots i.e. plot No. 77 measuring .62 acre of land, plot No. 59 measuring .63 acre of land and plot No. 58 measuring 11 acre of land. Karimon Shah and his co-purchasers got possession of their purchased land as described in their kabala by boundaries. i.e. northern side of C. S. plot Nos. 77, 59 and 58 and possessed the said land peacefully and uninterruptedly. By purchase All Mohammad also got possession of the same land and peacefully and uninterruptedly possessed. After his death, the plaintiff's had been in peaceful and uninterrupted possession of the entire .76 acre of land out of C. S. plot Nos. 77, 59 and 58. The said land contained the boundaries :-North : Homestead of Asalat; South; land of Damrigoala sold to Moroni's mother; East Road and West: East bank of tank belonging to Karuna Balm. By mistake and inadvertance of the scribe, plot Nos. 58 and 59 were not mentioned in the documents of Karimon Shah and others but only plot No. 77 was mentioned. When Ali Mohammad, predecessor of the plaintiffs. purchased the said .76 acre of land from Karimon Shah and others the same mistake crept into his deed also. Plot No. 59 is adjacent west of plot No. 77 and plot No 58 is adjacent west of plot No. 59. plot No. 57 is Karuna Babu's Pukur is adjacent west of plot No. 58. This will be abundantly clear from the C S. map of the Mouza. In the revisional settlement plaintiffs possession in C. S. plot No. 77 has Len recorded as R.S. plot No. 557 with an area of .36 acre. Petitioner's possession in C. S. plot No. 59 has been recorded in two plots being R. S. plot No. 558 with an area of .21 acre and R. S. plot No. 627 with an acre of .10 acre of land. This .67 acre together with .09 acre of C: S. plot No. 58 constitute .76 decimals of plaintiffs land. It has been further alleged that through undue influence of Dr. A. Gafur, husband of Begum Rabeya Khatun, the said .009 acre of plot No. 58 was not recorded in the name of the plaintiffs but the entire land of dag ho. 58 including plaintiff's .09 acre of land has been wrongly recorded in the revisional settlement record in the name of Begum Rabeya Khatun who has no semblance of any right nor any scrap of paper in support of her alleged title and claim in respect of Plot No. 58 measuring .11 acre of land. Defendant No. 2 Begum Rabeya Khatun wife of Dr. Abdul Cafur purchased 4 kathas of land i.e. 71/2 acre of lard by kabala No. 3992 dated 12.8.1949 from Mehini Mohan Dry Bhowmic who purchased 10 kathas of land from Ali Ahmed who purchased 10 kathas cf land from plot No. 77 and 59 in two lots i.e. front plot No. 77 and 59 and from plot No. 58 and 59 from Muktakeshi Devi alias Moroni's mother who actually purchased .36 acre of land from Damri Goala from plot No. 77 and 59 and 58 though in the kabalas plot No.58 was mistakenly omitted tut in the boundaries given in the kabala covered the dug No. 58 as well. The boundaries of the 4 kathas of lard of kabala No. 3992 dated 12. 8. 1949 of Begun Rabeya Khatun defendant No. 2 from aforesaid Mohini Mohon Bhowmic are as under :-North Homestead of Ali Ahmed, South : P. W. Road, East : Kedar Nath Mukherjee now Felani Bibi and Khas tank. According to the plaintiffs by the said kabala No. 3992 dated 12. 8. 49 the above .1 kathas of and purchased by Begum Rabeya hatun Ire m the extreme south western Fortis n of dag Nos. 58 and 59 with a clear measurement of above 4 kathas. The measure tent of four boundaries which has been shown in the trap attached to thekabala deed are as under:- North boundary line 34'-6", South 28'-7", East boundary line 85'-3" and West boundary line 91'-4". Thereafter, the plaintiff; stated that with re-raid to requisition and acquisition of part of the suit land in L. A. Case No. 11 of 1961-62 and the quantity of land Was taken into possession by the Government, and the amount of compensation have been paid to the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs mentioned about the direction received from the Land Acquisition Collector to take recourse to the Civil Court for declaration of title to C. S. plot No. 59 but the same was cancelled subsequently. The plaintiffs obtained a direction from the Board of Revenue with regard to payment of compensation. Thereafter, the plaintiffs filed an application on 15th June, 1971 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Development) Dacca to acquire the strips of land originally requisitioned and acquired subsequently left from final acquisition, re-demarcate the land and pay compensation thereof according to the order of the Board of Revenue. According to the said direction of the Board of Revenue, the Additional Deputy Commissioner passed the necessary order directing the Special Land. Acquisition officer to re-demarcate the land in order to give effect to the direction but due to some unknown reason the matter is still pending. The plaintiffs assert that they are in peaceful possession of .09 acre of land of plot No. 58 for a period over 12 years but on 31.10.64 the defendant No. 2 with a malafide intention filed case No. 1310a'64 under section 144 Cr. P. C. through her husband Dr. M. A. Gafur in respect thereof and illegally obtained an exparte order of injunction restraining the plaintiffs from entering in to plot No. 58, with the ulterior motive of grabbing the dag No. 58 under the cover of the ex-parte order. On 9th January 1971 defendant No. 2 filed an application for hearing of the two preliminary issues which arc as under :-

(A) Is the suit barred by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act ?

(B) Has the plaint been properly valued and sufficiently stamped ?

5. On the same day defendant No. 2 filed another application for recalling the writ kismet to the pleader Commissioner till the disposal of the application, and accordingly the writ which was already issued was recalled. Thereafter on 8th July; 1971 the matter was fixed for hearing of the preliminary issues and after hearing the Advocates of both the parties, the learned Subordinate Judge noted the following order :-

"So issue writ for local investigation and put up for hearing of issue Nos. 1 and 2 after the report of the Commissioner.

6. On 17th August, 1971, defendant No. 2 filed an application under order 7 Rule II(a) (b) and (d) and under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of plaint and or for striking of the name of defendant No. 2 on the ground as under:-

"(i) cause of action of this suit no longer exist after cancellation of the award and of the notice dated 9. 4. 63.

(ii) on and Item 18. 11. 64, i.e., after the amendment of plaint by virtue of the which whole of 'A' schedule lard was covered in suit land was not valued according to present market value in the locality; that the plaintiffs are not in possession of 'A' schedule land.

(iii) Suit is barred by limitation.

7. Thereafter the application came up for hearing on 16th February, 1972. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties rejected the petition stating that he does not deem it necessary to consider the preliminary objection raised by the defendant which will be considered and disposed of at the lime of trial of the suit in accordance with law. In this order, however, the learned Subordinate Judge noted that in the facts and circumstances of the case the plaintiffs are to pay advalorom court fee and that the plaintiffs are to file the valuation statement by 28th Feb. 1972. The plaintiff filed the valuation statement showing Taka 49,200/- as the value of the entire suit land i.e. .76 acre of land. The plaintiffs also filed an application under section 151 of the Cede of Civil Procedure for reconsideration and review of the order No. 208 as regards the question of payment of advalorem court fee. Then the matter was fixed for hearing on 29th April, 1972. On 17th April, i.e. before the date fixed for hearing of the above application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court sent the valuation statement to the Sheristadar for checking and report. The Sheristadar also submitted his report regarding the valuation showing the valuation at Taka 1,52,000/- which was accepted by the Court on 22nd April, 1972 in the absence of the plaintiffs and the court directed the plaintiffs to pay advalorem court fee on the entire suit land less than the amount already paid, by 10th May, 1972. Subsequently, a petition under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by the plaintiffs and the same was rejected on 8th May, 1972. This is also one of the orders impugned before this Court. However, we have already indicated above that the order dated 22nd April, 1972 is the order which is actually under consideration of this Court.

7A. In the counter-affidavit filed by the opposite party (Defendant No. 2) it has been stated inter alia that the petitioner had never any title or possession in .20 acre of schedule 'B' land and the revisional khatian is wrong to that extent. Plot No. 58 has been correctly recorded in the name of this opposite party according to her title document dated 12. 8.49 and actual physical possession and the allegation of undue influence by her husband is false.

7B. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the learned Subordinate Judge acted illegally and with material irregularity in directing the plaintiffs to rut in the advalorem court fee on the total valuation of the statement as submitted by the Sheristadar, without considering the fact that possession of the plaintiffs in the entire suit lard of .76 acre of land is not disputed by the contesting defendant No. 2. In this context, the learned Advocate further submits that the impugned order directing the plaintiffs to pay advalorem court-fee without following the fundamental principle that the question of court-fee is to be determined on the basis of the scope of the suit as made out in the plaint and not on the basis of a statement made by the defendant.

<u>8. On perusal if the record, it appears that there is substance in the contentions made before us. From the order dated 22nd April, 1972 it does not appear that the learned Subordinate Judge applied his mind to the question of payment of advalorem court-fee wilt reference to the pleadings of the parties. While disposing of the preliminary objection raised by the defendant on 16th February, 1972 some observations were made to the c fleet that the plaintiff is required to pay advalorem court-fee on the valuation of the suit lard, so that a through investigation as regards plaintiff's alleged title to the suit lard can be made by relaying the plaintiff's title deed with the suit land as shown in the schedule, because such an comprehensive investigation cannot be made in the simple declaratory suit for which the plaintiff has paid fixed court of Rs. 20/- only and within the limited scope of the suit. Practically the above finding provided the basis for directing the plaintiffs to pay advalorem court-fee. The above view of the learned Subordinate Judge that in the absence of any payment of advalorem court-fee investigation of the suit by appointing Pleader Commissioner cannot be made is not correct and there is no legal bar in this regard. Even in a suit for simple declaration the Court is competent to issue commission, if necessary. Therefore, this cannot be a valid ground for recalling the writ and directing the plaintiffs to pay advalorem court fee. The question whether the plaintiffs are required to pay advalorem court-fee, is to be determined at the trial; before that it is not proper for the court to direct the plaintiffs to pay advalorem court-fee. The learned Advocate refers to a decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Md. Siddique Vs. Bhuperdra Narayan Roy Chowdhury and others in 13 D.L.R. 544. This decision supports the contention of the learned Advocate. It has been held that where the plaintiff in his plaint has not admitted the possession of the defendant in the property in the suit nor has admitted the defendants right to possess, the provisions of the section 42 of the Specific Relief Act regarding the seeking of further relief are not attracted.</u>

<u>9. The scope of the suit is to be determined with respect to the allegations in the plaint and not with reference to the allegation in the written statement. If after institution of the suit, some events take place and the plaintiff is dispossessed from a part of the suit land, this subsequent event will not effect the suit as framed. In the present case there are some allegations about the events subsequent to the institution of the suit. The husband of defendant No. 2 forcibly raised some structures on a portion of the lard claimed by defendant No. 2. If at the trial, on evidence, the Court is satisfied that the structures were raised after institution of the suit, the Court would be competent to pass appropriate order to give full relief to the plaintiffs without amending the plaint.</u>

<u>10. Rule 7, Order 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that every plaint shall slate specifically the relief which the plaintiff claims either simply or in the alternative, and it shall not be necessary to ask for general or other relief which may always be given as the Court may think just to the same rule shall apply to any relief claimed by the defendant in his written statement. Ordinary rule is that rights of the parties must be determined as it stands at the date of action and rot on the basis of the rights it occurred after the institution of the suit. In an appropriate case the Court can mould its decree in order to suit the event which has taken place after the institution of the suit. In such case the object of this rule is that the Court should not reject the plaint and try the case by taking notice of the subsequent event.</u>

11. Before concluding we would like to observe that the valuation statement submitted by the plaintiff along with the report submitted by the Sheristadar should have bun considered in presence of the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate rightly submits that in this case the. plaintiffs filed the valuation statement on the basis of the price fixed by the Government in the matter of payment of compensation for a part payment of the suit land acquired by the Government and that the suit which was instituted in 1963 when the valuation was given by the plaintiffs, was the appropriate valuation of the land. The learned Subordinate Judge altered the valuation without assigning any reason. In our opinion, the valuation should have been calculated on the basis of the rate per bigha as fixed by the Government for payment of compensation in respect of part of the suit land.

In view of what has been stated above, the Rule is made absolute. The order dated 22nd April, 1972 is hereby set aside. The petitioners are entitled to the costs of this Rule.

A.S.F. Islam Chowdhury, J.- I agree

End.

case_source: (From Judgment and order dated 19th June, 1986 passed by the High Court Division, Circuit Bench, Barisal in Civil Revision No.7 of 1982).
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: This appeal by leave at the instance of the defendant-Government is from judgment and order dated 19 June. 1986 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division, Circuit Bench, Barisal in Civil Revision No. 7 of 1982 making the Rule absolute.

2. Respondent No. 1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 153 of 1978 in the 6th Court of Assistant Judge, Barisal for declaration of title to the suit land on the averments; inter alia, that Babar Ali as original owner of 4.16 acres of land of CS Plot Nos. 179, 180, 811, 218, 1773 and 1853 of CS Khebat No. 54 of Mouza Char Akaria in Nim Howla right, that Babar Ali leased out the land of CS Plot Nos.1773 and 1853 and the land of the remaining 4 CS Plots measuring 3.77 acres was in his khas possession, that it was recorded as RS Plot Nos. 183. 202 and 205 of RS khatian No. 226 measuring an area of 3.78 acres which is the disputed land, that one Azim Sharip and others were the superior landlords of the CS khebats in Howla right, that the khas land of Babar Ali as stated above was diluviated by the river Lata in 1344-45 BS and reformed in situ within 7/8 years next, that Babar Ali died leaving a daughter Ulfatunnessa who possessed the disputed land by payment of rent that it transpires that the disputed land has been wrongly recorded in the names of the heirs and successive heirs of the superior landlords, defendant Nos. 1-51, 53, that the defendants have no title and possession in the disputed land, that Ulfatunnessa died leaving the plaintiff as her only heir, that he has been possessing the disputed land by payment of rent, that the plaintiff asked the defendants to rectify the ROR but they refused to do so in the last part of Magh 1384 BS which has clouded the title of the plaintiff and hence the suit.

3. Defendant No. 52 the Government--appellant contested the suit by filing a written statement raising several objections. The case of the appellant, briefly, is that 0.63 acre of land out of the suit land has been recorded as diluviated since 1344 BS by the river Lata in SA Khatian No. 1, that the same reformed in situ after long 20 years which is the khas land of the Government, that remaining 3.15 acres land has been recorded in SA Khatian No. 1074 in the name of the Mutwalli of the Waqf Estate and that the plaintiff has acquired no title on the basis of the illegal and collusive document from the superior landlords.

4. The learned Assistant Judge by hi judgment and decree dated 29.7.1980 dismissed the suit upon holding, among others, that the disputed land remained diluviated for more than 20 years and under the provisions of President's Order No. 135 of 1972 the right, title and interest of the original owner Babar Ali in the disputed land was extinguished and the same vested in the Government and, as such, the plaintiff has got no right, title and interest in the disputed land.

5. On appeal by the plaintiff from the said decree, Title Appeal No. 207 of 1980, the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Bakergonj dismissed the same by his judgment and decree dated 30.3.1982. In concurring with the judgment and decree of the trial Court the learned Additional District Judge, inter alia, found that the SA Khatian shows that the disputed land was lost to the river Lata since 1344 BS and as soon as it re-appeared, the Waqf Estate in view of the provision of President's Order No. 135 of 1972, cannot lay any claim to it and that the anxiety of the plaintiff to pay rent after the institution of the suit in the name of the Waqf Estate shows that the suit land re-appeared in the recent past.

6. The plaintiff then took a revision, Civil Revision No. 7 of 1982, from the appellate judgment and decree to the High Court Division in which the impugned judgment and order were passed. The impugned judgment shows that the concurrent judgment of the Courts below dismissing the suit was set aside without any further order.

7. In making the Rule absolute. the learned Judge of the High Court Division, inter alia, held that the lower appellate Court erred in giving retrospective effect to the provision of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950. briefly, the Act, by holding that the disputed property had vested in the Government by reason of the aforesaid provision as amended by President's Order No. 135 of 1972 inasmuch as the land in dispute had re-appeared prior to the date of coming into force of Part V of the Act wherein section 86 finds place.

8. Leave was granted to consider whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division rightly applied the provisions of section 86 of the Act as amended by President's Order No. 135 of 1972 in the Las of the present case and further, whether the learned Judge rightly interfered with the findings of fact made by the Courts below with regard to the re-appearance of the disputed land which was admittedly diluviated in 1344-45 BS and had vested in the Government, according to the defendant-appellant under section 86 of the Act.

9. In order to appreciate the point at issue it may be noted that section 86 of the Act is substituted by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 135 of 1972) which came into force on 4 November 1972. This section has undergone changes by subsequent amendments and substitutions. For the purpose of the present case, however, they are not material. What is material is sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 86 as were introduced by President's Order No. 135 of 1972. They are as follows:

86 (1) (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successor-in-interest shall be extinguished in such lands or portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972.

(3) All lands, so lost by diluvion under sub-section (2), which re-appeared before the date of commencement of the said Order, but in respect of which the right of the tenant, whose land was so lost, or his successors-in-interest, to re-possession was not finally recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court under any law for the time being in force and also all lands, so lost by diluvion under the said sub-section, which may re-appear on or after the said date, shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and shall be at its disposal.

4...........

5...........

10. In the case of A Mannan vs. Kulada Ranjan 31 DLR (AD) 195 it has been held that the provisions of the aforesaid two sub-sections of section 86 of the Act cannot be given any retrospective effect beyond the date of coming into force of Part V of the Act in the area in which the diluviated land is situated.

11. The land in dispute in the present case falls within PS Mehendiganj of District Bakergonj and it is not disputed that with regard to the aforesaid Thana Part V of the Act is applicable from 13.5.1958 (vide footnote to section 79 of the Act (1980) DLR Publication). It is, therefore, clear that sub-sections, (2) and (3) of section 86 will have no application by reason of our decision in the aforesaid case if a diluviated land in that locality reappeared before 13.5.1958.

12. In the present case plaintiff-respondent claimed that the disputed land had re-appeared within 7/8 years after diluvion in 1344-45 BS, that is to say, the land had re-appeared some time in 1944-45. On the other hand, the defendant-Government's case is that the land had reformed long after 20 years and it was under water even at the time of preparation of SA record.

13. The learned Assistant Judge disbelieved the plaintiff's case and observed that the disputed land remained diluviated for more than 20 years, that it was so till SA operation and thus under the provision of President's Order No. 135 of 1972 the right, title and interest of the original owner Babar Ali was extinguished and the disputed land had vested in the Government.

14. The learned Additional District Judge similarly, disbelieved the plaintiff's case and relying upon the RS record Ext. 1 which was finally published in the district of Bakergonj in 1952 and the RS Map which was also an Exhibit in the case which showed that the disputed land was lost to the Lata river, it was observed that the recorded entries and description as to the nature of the suit land as were there in the two public documents could not be outweighed by the oral testimony of the plaintiff and his two witnesses. The learned Judge also observed that in the SA record also the suit land was again described as lost by diluvion and the fact that the plaintiff had not paid any rent for a long time (Dakhilas for the years 1343 and 1360 BS were proved but those were disbelieved by both the Courts below) and failed to get the record of right corrected went to explain that the land was under water and it re-appeared after the SA operation. It was further observed that the anxiety of the plaintiff to pay rent after the institution of the suit in the name of the Waqf Estate shows that the suit land had re-appeared in the recent past.

15. Although the learned Judge of the High Court Division has rightly held that the aforesaid provisions of President's Order No. 135 of 1972 could not be given retrospective effect prior to the coming into force of Part V of the Act, the learned Judge has neither considered the concluded finding of fact made by the Courts below as to the re-appearance of the disputed land after the SA operation which falsified the plaintiff's claim nor made any definite finding upon consideration of evidence upholding the claim of the plaintiff that the disputed land had reappeared some time in 1944-45 or even before May 1958.

16. The learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the defendant-appellant having drawn our attention to the aforesaid facts submitted, and we think rightly, that the impugned judgment was not sustainable inasmuch there was no finding made contrary to that of the Courts below that the disputed land had re-appeared in 1944-45 as claimed by the plaintiff or, at any rate, before the coming into force of Part V of the Act in May 1958. He has pointed out that there is a finding in the penultimate paragraph of the impugned judgment to the effect that the disputed land had re-appeared prior to the date of coming into force of Part V of the Act but the said finding is not based upon consideration of any evidence at all nor it was noted as to when Part V of the Act came into force in the locality concerned.

<u>17. The learned Additional Attorney-General has argued that the learned Judge of the High Court Division has neither considered the concurrent finding of fact made by the Courts below based upon consideration of evidence as to the re-appearance of the disputed land nor gave any reason for interfering with the said finding of fact. The interference in revision, therefore, with the concurrent finding of fact and the resultant decree was in excess of the authority under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the learned Additional Attorney-General finally submits.</u>

<u>18. We find a good deal of force in his submission. None appeared on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent. It appears that the learned Judge of the High Court Division only considered the effect of the decision in Abdul Mannan's case 31 DLR (AD) 195 without applying his mind either to the facts of the present case and the finding made by the Courts below or to the application of the said decision in the facts of the present case. No doubt the disputed land could not vest in the Government if it had re-appeared prior to May 1958 but the whole question is whether the plaintiff was able to prove his case that the disputed land had re-appeared in 1944-45 or even before 1958. As already noticed the concurrent finding of the Courts below was that the disputed land was under water even during the SA operation and had re-appeared in the recent past. Both the Courts upon consideration of the plaintiff's evidence found that his case was not proved. In the face of such finding the High Court Division was not at all justified in interfering with the concurrent decree dismissing the suit without finding upon consideration of evidence that the plaintiffs case was proved and/or that the Courts below committed illegality in finding against the plaintiff resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Judge did neither, but merely found in one sentence without reference to the evidence on record that the disputed land had re-appeared prior to the date of coming into force of Part V of the Act. The learned Additional Attorney-General was fair enough to take us through the evidence of the plaintiff which, according to him and we also find, was not adequate and reliable for holding that the disputed land had re-appeared in 1944-45 as claimed by the plaintiff. The learned Judge has given no reason whatsoever to upset the finding of fact made by the Courts below in that behalf. Thus we feel no hesitation in accepting the submission made by the learned Additional Attorney-General.</u>

In view of the discussion above, the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment is set aside and the judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below are restored.

End.

None Appeared - For Respondent Nos. 2 -5.

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 5 March 1998 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1289 of 1996).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This appeal by leave has been preferred by respondent No. 5 of the writ petition No. 1289 of 1996 against the judgment and order dated 5th March, 1998 of a Division Bench of the High Court Division making the Rule absolute and thereupon declaring the Memorandum No. 448/Pro-Ka-Shi dated 15th August, 1994 issued by the Administrative Officer (respondent No. 5) Shahjalal Housing Estate, Sylhet intimating cancellation of the allotment letter No. 2639 dated 29-09-1983 in respect of the Plot No. 17, at Road No. 21 of Block-B and lease deed No. 3 dated 08-09-1985.

2. Facts, in short, are that writ petitioner-respondent No. 1 got allotment of residential plot No. 17 at Road No. 21, Block-B, of the Shahjalal Housing Estate, Sylhet on 29th September, 1983 for a consideration of Taka 65,071.80. As per stipulation of the allotment letter total amount of consideration money was to be paid in 4 installments. Respondent No. 1 on payment of 1st instalment amounting Taka 19,600.00 on 27th October 1983 got possession of the plot on 18th August 1985. The lease deed for 99 years was registered on 8th September, 1985. The respondent No. 1 paid two other instalments i.e. 2nd and 3rd instalments of the consideration money. On 1st June, 1995 the constituted Attorney of the respondent No. 1 went to deposit the amount of the 4th instalment, but the same was not accepted on the plea of non availability of relevant file and that later on he was informed by respondent No. 5 that allotment of the respondent No. 1 was cancelled on 11th August 1994 and that the said plot has been allotted to the appellant therein on 11th August, 1994 and that respondent No. 1 said to have been informed as regard the matter of cancellation of his allotment letter and lease deed by mailing the letter dated 15th August, 1994 addressed to his village home at Mohammadpur, P.S. Kulaura, Moulavi Bazar. Thereupon attorney of the respondent No. 1 who was living in New York, informed him about the cancellation of the plot for non-payment of 4th instalment and that for not constructing residential house as per Clauses 3 and 4 of the lease agreement. The respondent No. 1 faxed an application to the respondent No. 2 (herein) on 2nd June, 1995 requesting him to look into the matter and to accept the 4th instalment and that to allow him to make construction in the plot. In reply to the fax of the respondent No. 1 dated 2nd June, 1995 sent from New York respondent No. 5 informed the writ petitioner that matter of cancellation of his plot was intimated to him by the letter of 15th August 1994 mailed at his permanent address-village Mohammadpur, PS Kulaura, Moulvi Bazar.

3. Respondent No. 1 challenged the legality of the memo dated 15th August, 1994 contending, first, that he was not at all informed by issuing notice at the address which was communicated to the respondent Nos. 2-5 by the letter dated 10th July, 1989; that his allotment of the plot in question in Shahjalal Housing Estate would be cancelled for nonpayment of 4th instalment and that for not making construction as per terms of the lease deed, second, that letter dated 15 August, 1994 was sent to the address which was not the address for communicating any information regarding the plot since 1989 and that after return of the said letter with the remarks of the postal peon that addressee resides in a foreign country no attempt was made to communicate with the respondent No. 1 at the address which was available to the respondent Nos. 2-5 since 1989, and lastly, that the action of the respondent Nos. 2-5 cancelling allotment of the respondent No. 1 lacked bonafide since allotment was cancelled on 11th August, 1994 and that on that very day the plot was allotted to the appellant in the absence of any application from her side seeking allotment of a plot in Shahjalal Housing Estate, Sylhet. It was also contended by the respondent No. 1 that the allotment was made without making an advertisement in the newspaper inviting application from the intending seekers of allotment.

4. The Rule was opposed by the writ respondent No. 5 appellant (subsequent allottee) supporting the action of the respondent Nos. 2-5 therein. The respondent Nos. 2-5 did not enter appearance in the writ petition.

5. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute upon observing that in spite of knowing the last address of the petitioner the cancellation letter was addressed to his village home (writ petitioner-respondent No. 1 by the letter dated 10th July, 1989 informed the respondent Nos. 2-5 of his address for communication as regard the matter of his plot at Shahjalal Housing Estate and that he received communication from the respondent Nos. 2-5 up to 1991 at his address in USA) and that not only that decision as to cancellation though was taken on 11th August, 1994 and on the same date the plot was allotted in favour of the respondent No. 5 (appellant herein) and without making any attempt to circulate the order of cancellation in the newspaper and that the payment of 4th instalment was refused without justification and that possession that was delivered to the writ-petitioner was not at all taken from him and, as such, the same could not be redelivered unless the delivery was taken back from the writ petitioner and that resort to the provision of Clause 4 which gives right to terminate the lease in case of failing to complete construction of building within the stipulated time as in Clause 3 of lease deed "ought to be exercised according to law" and "thirdly, all actions could be set at naught if the same be malafide. In this case, we have noticed that the cancellation of the deed of lease and also the allotment in favour of the respondent No. 5 appears to have been done on the same day without application of respondent No. 5 would show that the action of the respondent No. 4 is tainted with malafide and such action is liable to be declared illegal and unlawful. And lastly, the notice has to be served upon the petitioner at the last known address as evidenced from Annexure-F and this has not at all been controverted and, as such, the impugned order of cancellation when the same has not been served upon the petitioner is wholly illegal and cannot be acted upon."

6. Being dissatisfied with the judgment and order of the High Court Division the writ-respondent No. 5, filed the petition for leave to appeal. Leave has been granted to consider the submissions that admittedly respondent No. 1 having not made any construction on the demised plot within the stipulated time and having not prayed for extension of time, the lease was liable to cancellation and the Housing Estate Authority having issued notice in the address of respondent No. 1 as mentioned in the agreement of lease, the High Court Division was wrong in holding the cancellation of lease to be without lawful authority,  that the Housing Estate Authority having power to cancel the lease on the happening of specified event and such event having happened, the High Court Division was wrong in holding the cancellation of the lease in question to be malafide merely because after passing the order of cancellation of lease the Housing Estate Authority allotted the plot in question to the appellant on the same day, that respondent No. 1 having left the country without making any arrangement for receiving notices in the address which he gave in the agreement of lease, respondent No. 1 cannot complain of non receipt of notices when those notices were sent by registered post in the address mentioned in the agreement of the lease and were returned unserved in the absence of respondent No. 1 and in such circumstance the High Court Division was wrong in finding the impugned order of cancellation as bad for non-service of notice.

7. It was asserted by the respondent No. 1 in his application dated 2nd June, 1995 addressed to the respondent No. 2 that he has been residing in USA since September, 1985 and used to receive letter from the office of the Administrative Officer, Shahjalal Housing Estate, Sylhet up to 1991 in his US address intimated by him by the letter dated 10th July, 1989 and since thereafter he did not receive any letter from the Shahjalal Housing Authority. It was further stated in the said letter that Shahjalal Housing Estate has the US address of the writ-petitioner in its record since he by his letter dated 10th July, 1989 intimated his address in US for communication with him as regard the matter relating to the plot allotted to him by the Shahjalal Housing Estate, Sylhet.

8. The notices of the Rule obtained by the writ petitioner-respondent No. 1 were served upon writ respondent Nos. 1-4 (personnel of the Shahjalal Housing Estate) but the said respondents did not enter appearance in the Rule and denied the fact of intimation of the address of respondent, No. 1 in USA in 1989 and of making communication with the respondent No.1 by the respondent Nos. 2-5 herein up to 1991 in connection with matter of plot allotted to respondent No.1 in the Shahjalal Housing Estate. It is seen from the Annexures K and K-1 to the writ petition that a letter was addressed on 13th May, 1993 to the village home of the writ-petitioner intimating him that time for payment of 4th instalment has expired and that he has also not started construction in the plot allotted to him and that by the said letter the writ-petitioner was asked to make the payment of the entire amount that has fallen due and also that in case of non-starting of construction allotment of the plot in question of the lease deed in respect Of the plot allotted would be cancelled without further communication. Thereafter, the writ respondent Nos. 1-4 (herein respondent Nos. 2-5) as seen from Annexure-L and L-1 to the writ petition cancelled the allotment of the respondent No. 1 on 11th August, 1994 and that sent a letter communicating cancellation of the plot and the lease deed to the village address of respondent No. 1.

9. The respondent Nos. 2-5 although made communication with the respondent No. 1 as regard the matters of plot No. 17 of Shahjalal Housing Estate till 1991 at the US address as per respondent No. 1's letter dated 10th July, 1989 but still then sent notice dated 13th May, 1993 asking the respondent No. 1 to pay the armor amount of 4th instalment and that to start construction as per terms of the lease to his village home.

<u>10. In July, 1989 respondent No. 1 made available to the Shahjalal Housing Estate authority his address to communicate with him in his US address in respect of the matter of the plot No. 17 and the Housing Estate Authority communicated with the respondent No. 1 up to 1991. In this background of the facts the contention of the appellant, who of course is not legally competent to contend so since respondent Nos. 2-5 have not denied the fact of communicating with respondent No. 1 in his US address as regard matters of the plot No. 17 of the Housing Estate, that the respondent No. 1 left Bangladesh without making arrangement for receiving communication in the address given in the lease agreement is not well founded one as because the respondent No. 1 informed the Shahjalal Housing Authority in July, 1989 his address for communication with him relating to the matters of his plot in the Housing Estate and that the Housing Estate Authority communicated with respondent No. 1 up to 1991 at the address in USA given by the respondent No. 1. Admittedly, neither the notice asking the petitioner to pay the arrears of the 4th installment and that to start construction within 30th June, 1993 was not addressed to the respondent No. 1 to his address for communication as regard the matters relating to the plot No. 17 of the Housing Estate. The same being the undisputed fact the contention of the respondent No. 1 that his allotment of Plot No. 17 of Shahjalal Housing Estate was cancelled without intimation to him is found to be correct and because of that the order cancelling the allotment and the lease agreement in respect of the Plot No. 17 of the Housing Estate have quite legally been declared illegal by the High Court Division. Although the respondent Nos. 2-5 did not enter appearance in the Rule that was issued in Writ Petition No. 1289 of 1996, yet the record as being maintained in the office of the respondent Nos. 2-5 in connection with the Plot No. 17 of the Shahjalal Housing Estate allotted to the petitioner was placed before the High Court Division and the learned Judges of the High Court Division on scrutiny of the papers maintained in the file noticed that there was no application by the respondent No. 5 appellant on 11th August, 1994 seeking allotment of plot in the Homing Estate. There is also another glaring fact that respondent No. is allotment of the plot was cancelled on 11th August, 1994 and that Shahjalal Housing Estate Authority allotted the said plot No. 17 to the respondent No. 5 appellant on that very day in the absence of any application from her side seeking allotment of plot in the Shahjalal Housing Society. It is an undisputed position that allotment was made without making any public notification calling for applications for allotment of the plot in question that was available to the Housing Estate upon cancellation of the allotment of the respondent No. 1. The High Court Division also noticed that notice calling upon the respondent No. 1 to pay the arrears amount that had fallen due because of non-payment of 4th instalment and that for starting construction by 30th June in default whereof the allotment would be cancelled without further communication was sent to the village address of the respondent No. 1 and that letter intimating cancellation of the plot and lease thereof was sent to the village address of the respondent No. 1 although the Housing Estate had in its record as back as from 10th July, 1989 address of the respondent No. 1 in USA for communication relating the matters of Plot No. 17 of the Shahjalal Housing Estate and that the Housing Estate authority communicated with the respondent No. 1 in his US address up to 1991 as regard the matters relating to the Plot No.17 of the Housing Estate.</u>

<u>11. In the background of the aforesaid facts the High Court Division held the action of the Housing Estate relating to the cancellation of Plot No. 17 that was allotted to the respondent No. 1 as malafide. In our view the High Court Division has committed no illegality in the background of the fact as stated herein before in arriving at the finding that action of the Shahjalal Housing Authority as regard cancellation of the allotment of Plot No. 17 which was allotted to the respondent No. 1 was malafide.</u>

<u>12. The learned Counsel appearing for the appellant in the face of the undisputed fact as was in Annexure-F to the writ petition relating to making available to the Housing Estate authority address of the respondent No. 1. for making communication relating to the matter of Plot No. 17 of Shahjalal Housing Estate and that the Housing Estate Authority having had communicated with respondent No.1 up to 1991 at his address in USA that was made available on 10th July, 1989 and that in spite of that the Housing Estate Authority sent the letter dated 13th May, 1993 asking the respondent No. 1 to clear the arrears had fallen due against 4th instalment and that to start construction by 30th June in case of failure whereof allotment of the respondent No. 1 would be cancelled was addressed to respondent No. 1's village home and that letter intimating cancellation of the Plot No. 17 that was allotted to the respondent No. 1 was sent to his village home address and that allotment to the respondent No. 5, appellant was made on the very day of cancellation of the allotment of the respondent No. 1 without having any application of the said respondent No. 5 finds it difficult to support the action of the respondent Nos. 2-5 as regard cancellation of allotment of respondent No. 1. The other contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the High Court Division was in error in, holding the cancellation of the allotment of the respondent No. 1 without lawful authority as because the said respondent did not start construction as per stipulation in the. lease deed and that he having had not also applied for extension of time is not sustainable in the background of the material on record since as seen from the action of the respondent Nos. 2-5 that merely because of non-starting of construction in the plot allotted within the stipulated time, the allotment is not liable to be cancelled straight away but authority may proceed for cancellation after giving notice to the allottee and in that regard the Housing Estate Authority sent a notice to the respondent No. 1 fixing date with which respondent No. 1 was directed to start construction and that in case of default without further communication allotment and lease agreement would be cancelled to the address which to the very knowledge of the respondent Nos. 2-5 was not the address for communication with the respondent No. 1 in connection with the matter relating to Plot No. 17 that was allotted by the said respondents to the respondent No. 1. In the background of the facts the High Court Division was quite correct in holding that cancellation of allotment and the lease deed of the respondent No. 1 in respect of Plot No. 17 of Shahjalal Housing Estate were without lawful authority since the same were done without giving any notice to the allottee, the respondent No. 1.</u>

<u>In view of the discussion made herein-above the appeal is dismissed with cost.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to a show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 28-1-1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 273 of 1993 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 21-7-1993 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 20 of 1992 dismissing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The added defendant No. 5 is the petitioner before this Court. Plaintiff is the opposite party No. 1. It is a suit for declaration that the cancellation of the allotment of the suit plot in favour of the petitioner is illegal and without jurisdiction and also for declaration for permanent injunction. The plaintiff''s case, in short, is that the plaintiff was the owner of 31.33 acres of land in CS Plot Nos. 3115, 3116, 3117, 3119, 3129, 3130, 3132 and 3454 in Mouza Bownia under Mirpur Police Station, Dhaka and the lands of the plaintiff of all the aforesaid plots were acquired by the Government in LA Case No.13/59-60. Since he was an affected person of such acquisition the Government allotted Plot No.212 in Road No.12 under Mirpur-11/E on 7-6-1979 under Memo No. 4900 for constructing the dwelling but of the plaintiff. But the Government failed to hand over possession of the said plot to the plaintiff. The plaintiff was residing in the suit plot with the verbal permission of the Government and there the plaintiff constructed house at a cost of Taka 2,00,000 and also established Gas Line, Water Line and electricity connection. Thereafter on the application of the plaintiff the suit plot was allotted to him on 27-1-1990 under Memo No. M-P-274/83-1823. The plaintiff deposited Taka 9,720.00 in four installments as the price of the suit plot. Then the Executive Engineer, defendant No.3 delivered formal possession of the suit plot to the plaintiff. But unfortunately the defendants in collusion with some greedy people illegally cancelled the allotment of the suit plot by a letter dated 28-12-1991 and also directed the plaintiff to hand over possession of the suit plot in favour of the defendant. So, the plaintiff was compelled to file the instant suit.

3. Defendants No. 1 and 4 and the defendant No.5 contested the suit by filing separate written statements. The case of the defendants No. 1 to 4 is that the suit is Not maintainable in its present form and the defendants did not at all allot the suit plot on 7-6-1979 in favour of the plaintiff. The plaintiff was not given any verbal permission to occupy the suit plot. So the plaintiff has no right title and interest in the suit plot. The added defendant No.5 submitted the separate written statement alleging inter alia, that since it was detected by the Executive Engineer while he went to deliver formal possession to the defendant No.5 that two allotment letters were issued in respect of the suit plot out of which the allotment letter in favour of defendant. No.5 was found correct whereas the allotment letter of the plaintiff was cancelled. The plaintiff manufactured a forged allotment letter which was detected in course of delivery of possession. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case the trial Court dismissed the suit of the plaintiff and the plaintiff preferred an appeal and the lower appellate Court after hearing the parties set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decised the suit in favour of the plaintiff.

4. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court the defendant No.5 preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr Roushan Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the suit in the present form is not maintainable and that the appellate Court judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal inasmuch as the evidence of the PWs as well as the documentary evidence were not properly considered by the learned Judge of the lower appellate Court. He further submits that through fraud and misrepresentation the plaintiff obtained the order of allotment and when it was detected that by practicing fraud the plaintiff obtained the order of allotment in his favour the allotment of the plot in favour of the plaintiff was cancelled by the appropriate authority and as such he submits that this appellate Court judgment is not maintainable in law.

<u>6. Mr Delwar Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 submits that the suit is maintainable in its present form inasmuch as this is a suit for permanent injunction. Both the Courts below held that the plaintiff is in possession and since the plaintiff is in possession he is entitled to file a suit for permanent injunction. In support of his submission he has referred to the cases of Manindra Nath Sen Sarma vs Bangladesh 1994 BLD (AD) 285 and Rafizuddin Ahmed vs Mongla Barman, 43 DLR (AD) 215. He further submits that the possession is the vital issue for a suit for permanent injunction. It appears that both the courts below found possession in favour of the plaintiff. Not only that the order of cancellation of allotment of the plot clearly shows that the plaintiff was in possession and as such, the plaintiff was directed to hand over possession to defendant No.5. The principle laid down in the aforesaid decisions is applicable in this case inasmuch as the plaintiff is in possession and that is why the suit for permanent injunction is maintainable.</u>

7. Mr Delwer Hossain further submits that the order of cancellation of the plot is illegal in view of the fact that the plaintiff did not violate any terms and conditions of the allotment letter and no reason was shown in the cancellation of the allotment letter and as such, it is absolutely illegal and arbitrary. He further submits that the suit plot was allotted in favour of the added defendant No. 5 on 5-6-1991 when the order of allotment of the plaintiff was in force. The plaintiff''s allotment was cancelled on 28-12-1991. He submits that when the order of allotment was still continuing the self same plot cannot be allotted to a third person and as such, the allotment letter in favour of the defendant No. 5 is illegal and malafide.

8. It appears from the material evidence on record that the lands of the plaintiff were acquired in LA Case No. 13/59-60. Since the plaintiff was an affected person he was allotted plot No. 212 at Road No. 12, Mirpur vide Memo No.4900. Since the Government could not deliver possession of that plot subsequently this allotment was cancelled. It is the case of the plaintiff that thereafter he started living on the suit plot and there he has constructed tin shed but and obtained Gas Line, electricity line and WASA line. Since he was the affected person he prayed for allotment of the suit plot in his favour. On his application the suit plot was allotted to the plaintiff by defendant No.4 on 27-1-1990 under Memo No. M-P-274 /83- 1824. The plaintiff on the direction of the defendants deposited the price money amounting to Taka 9,000.00 and the defendant No. 3 went there and handed over formal possession of the suit plot in favour of the plaintiff in accordance with the direction of the defendant No. 4 dated 18-7-1991 under Memo No. M-P-374 /83. But all on a sudden the defendant No.4 without showing any reason or giving any show cause cancelled the allotment of the suit plot by the letter dated 28-12-1991 under Memo No. 7038/1(6)(KA SHE). It further appears that while the allotment of the plaintiff was subsisting the suit plot was allotted in favour of the added defendant No. 5 namely, the present petitioner on 5-6-1991. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 that this added defendant No. 5 is not an affected person. He manipulated in the office of the defendants and fraudulently obtained the order of allotment while the allotment in favour of the plaintiff was subsisting. Even the cancellation letter does not show any reason or anything that the plaintiff has violated any terms and conditions for which the allotment of the plaintiff was cancelled. Mr Hossain further submits that admittedly the suit plot was allotted in favour of the plaintiff and formal possession was given by the defendants and the plaintiff also paid the consideration money of the suit plot. Further there is no allegation of violation of any terms and conditions of the allotment letter. In such a situation the plaintiff has acquired a vested right in the suit plot and as such, this allotment cannot be cancelled arbitrarily or without showing any reason. I find substance in the submission of Mr Hossain in view of the fact that there is no violation of volition of any terms of the allotment letter or no reason at all was shown for such cancellation. Further the defendant No.5 is not an affected person.

<u>9. Mr Roushan Ali submits that the allotment letter of the suit plot was obtained by fraud by the plaintiff and there was an enquiry on such allegation. But the record does not show any such enquiry report. Mr Roushan Ali further submits that the plaintiff failed to deposit the money according to the terms of the allotment letter and that is why the allotment was cancelled. But the cancellation order does not show any violation of any terms of the contract, rather it appears that the money paid by the plaintiff with respect to the suit plot was accepted by the defendants. After giving allotment and possession and after taking the money from the plaintiff and without showing any reason whatsoever the defendants are not entitled to cancel the allotment of the suit plot. As such I hold that the cancellation of the suit plot which was legally given to the plaitniff has been cancelled illegally and without jurisdiction and as such, the order of cancellation has no legal force.</u>

10. In have gone through the judgments of both the Courts below and it appears to me that the lower appellate Court has considered all the material evidence on record elaborately and after duly considering the same the lower appellate Court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff. So, I hold that the lower appellate Court has not committed any error of law occasioning failure of justice and as such, the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate Court do not require any interference by this Court.

11. In the result, this Rule is discharged and the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate Court are hereby affirmed.

12. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case I pass no order as to costs.

Send down the LC Records.

End.

Sazzad Hossain (Md) ----- Petitioner

full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J: This rovisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the defendant is directed against the judgment and order dated 19-5-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 271 vacating the order dated 4-2-2002 by allowing the plaintiff's application under section 151 of  the Code of Civil Procedure and rejecting the defendant's application under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for holding local investigation.

2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 183 of 1995 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, against the petitioner and proforma opposite party No. 2 as defendants for permanent injunction and thereafter the suit was transferred to the court of Joint District Judge and Additional Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka, and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 271 of 2001.

3. The case of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1, in brief, is that the suit property situated within District Dhaka, PS Gulshan appertaining to Mouza Mohakhali under CS khatian No. 107, Dag No. 355, measuring 1.44 acres belonged to CS recorded tenant Mir Mohammad Dorgi who died leaving behind his son Abdul Hamid Borgi; that Abdul Hamid Borgi thereafter died leaving behind three sons; Shamsuddin Ahammed, Noor Mohammad, Nurul Haque and a daughter Amena Khatoon and their names have been recorded in SA Khatian. It is further stated that SA recorded tenants sold the suit property measuring 41/2 kathas on 27-3-1990 under registered deed No. 3673 to the plaintiff and since then the plaintiff has been owning and possessing the same by demarcating the land with the mule bamboo fencing and raising moil bamboo house and appointing caretaker thereat. It is further stated that although the defendants have got no right and title on the property but they threatened the caretaker to enter forcibly into the property and demolish the bamboo house. It is also contended that the plaintiff claims the property to be situated at the northern portion of said CS plot No. 355 which is demarcated by the north plot No. 354, at the east Major Kashem, at the south DIT Road and at the west the wall of Zomiatul Modarashin.

4. The defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaintiff, inter alia, stating that at the north and west of suit plot No. 355, there situates CS plot No. 354 and from the west and south part of CS plot No. 354, 18 decimals have been acquired for Mohakhali-Gulshan link road and for commercial area; that the government also acquired 43 decimals from the south of suit plot No. 355 of the link road; that the land which is being claimed by the plaintiff is the part and parcel of RS Dag No. 2535 which has been acquired by RAJUK; that after such acquisition there remains no land of plot. No. 355 at its northern portion but the plaintiff is claiming the land thereat. The claimed land of the plaintiff is within Gulshan-Mohakhali Link Road. Under the shade of claiming land of CS plot No. 355, the plaintiff is trying to grab the property of the defendant in plot No. 354 which they are owning and possessing by purchase under deed No. 255596 dated 27-10-1976 and which is part and parcel of RS plot No. 2532. It is further stated that during tendency of the suit, the defendants filed an application under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for local investigation stating that the land claimed by the plaintiff actually situates mostly in plot No. 354 and partly in plot No. 355. The defendant prayed for ascertaining the land acquired in LA Case No. 63/5859 and LA Case No. 73 /5060. The defendant also prayed for ascertaining which part of CS plot Nos. 354 and 355 is attracted to the land RS plot No. 2535 as claimed by the plaintiff.

5. The learned Court after hearing the said application of the defendants under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure by his order No. 62 dated 4-2-2002 allowed the same and directed the defendants to deposit Taka 1500 as commission fee which the defendants deposited on 11-2-2002. The plaintiff on 4-2-2002 filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for vacating the order dated 4-2-2002 which allowed the application of the defendant for holding commission. The application was fixed for hearing on 11-2-2002 and which was again fixed or 3-3-2002 for hearing. On 3-3-2002, the plaintiff also filed written objection against the defendant's application under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Thereafter, on 27-4-2002, the plaintiff by filing an application under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the amendment of plaint stating that the claimed 41/2 Kathas of land of the plaintiff situates at the extreme north of SA plot No. 355 having its Municipal holding No. 28/8/1 Mohakhali, Dhaka.

6. Now the point for determination is, whether the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka, committed any error of law resulting in an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice.

7. Mr Garib Newaz, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the learned court by his order dated 4-2-2002 allowed the defendant's application under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, there was no scope to vacate the order by allowing the plaintiff's application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He further submits that the land claimed by the plaintiff at the north portion of plot No. 355 is already acquired by the Government and the defendant stated that the plaintiff in the name of claiming his land in the northern portion of CS plot No. 355 is actually trying to grab the property of the defendant situated at the southern part of CS plot No. 354 and, as such, the ascertainment of the claimed land by holding local investigation as prayed for was indispensably necessary.

8. No one appears on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party to oppose the Rule.

9. The pertinent question that calls for our determination is, whether the local investigation is necessary and proper for the purpose of elucidating the matter in dispute.

10. Now let us see the provision of law in this regard which is envisaged in Order XXVI rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs thus:

"Order XXVI, rule 9: In any suit in which the court deems a local investigation to be requisite or proper for the purpose of elucidating any matter in dispute or of ascertaining the market value of any property, or the amount or any manse profits or damages or annual net profits, the court may issue a commission to such person as it thinks fit directing him to make such investigation and to report thereon to the court within such time not exceeding three months as may be fixed by the court.

Provided that the court may, on the prayer of the commissioner and on sufficient cause being shown, extend the time."

11. Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for holding a local investigation on specified grounds when the court finds a local investigation necessary and proper for the purpose of elucidating any matter in dispute and an order of local investigation should not be passed where the court can decide the matter by taking evidence.

12. The plaintiff has filed this suit for a decree of permanent injunction restraining the defendants from entering into the suit property evicting their caretaker there from and demolishing his bamboo house. It appears from the plaint that the plaintiff has given a specific boundary. He claims only 4 kathas out of 1.44 acres of CS plot No. 355 under CS khatian No. 107.

13. But the contention of the defendants case is that at the north and west of suit plot No. 355, there situates CS plot No. 354 and from the west and south part of CS plot No. 354, 18 decimals have been acquired for Mohakhali-Gulshan link road and for commercial area; that government also acquired 43 decimals from the south of suit plot No. 355 of the link road; that the land which is being claimed by the plaintiff is the part and parcel of RS Plot No. 2535 which has been acquired by RAJUK; that after such acquisition there remains no land of plot No. 355 at its northern portion but the plaintiff is claiming the land thereat. Further claimed land of the plaintiff is within Gulshan-Mohakhali link road. The plaintiff in shade of claiming land of CS plot No. 355, is trying to grab the property of the defendants in plot No. 354 which they are owning and possessing by purchase under deed No. 25596 dated 27-10-1976 and which is part and parcel of RS plot No. 2532.

14. Mr Garib Newaz, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, also submits that the boundary shown by the plaintiff is not correct and that the land within that boundary does not fall under plot No. 355 but under plot No. 354.

<u>15. In this context, it is to be borne in mind that generally local investigation by an advocate commissioner is allowed to relay any land or property in order to determine the location of the suit property. It is the established principle of law that the court is required to dispose of the local investigation matter before posting the suit for preemptory hearing. In the case in hand, the defendants stated in their written statement that the property claimed by the plaintiff is the land of the defendants. In such a situation, local investigation is quite necessary. It is well settled that if the identity of the suit property is challenged by the other side, the question of holding local investigation for relaying the property in question is obligatory. From the language used in Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it is manifestly clear that a local investigation is imperative for the purpose of elucidating any matter in dispute. Particularly in a suit for permanent injunction, determination of the location of suit property is necessary before going into trial. Since the defendant stoutly claims that all the land of suit plot No. 355 has been acquired and now the plaintiff is trying to enter into the land of the defendants in no suited plot No. 354, in such situation, local investigation is necessary for the purpose of elucidating the matter in dispute by properly determining the location of the suit land which can only be properly ascertained by local investigation through survey knowing advocate commissioner.</u>

16. We receive support of the above view in the case Lakhmi Bazar Shahi Majid Committee and another vs St Francis Xavier Girls High School 51 DLR 557.

17. It is the recognized principle of law that if the identity of the suit land is challenged by the other side, the question of holding local investigation relaying the property is a must. It is very much needed in a suit for permanent injunction because injunction cannot be granted in an unspecified land.

18. In the facts and circumstance of the present case, we find necessity for local investigation for specifying the suit land otherwise the administration of justice will be jeopardized.

19. The order of learned Joint District Judge appears to have suffered from patent illegality and gross error of law. The learned court erred in law in passing the impugned order. We find sufficient substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. For the reasons stated above the Rule succeeds.

20. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order dated 19-5-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 271 of 2001 is set aside and the application for local investigation is allowed.

21. The order of stay granted earlier by this court stands vacated.

Communicate the order of this court to the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka, for his information and necessary action.

End.
