full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J: The Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why a direction should not be issued to dispose of the application dated 8-2-2011 (Annexure-J) to mutate the names of the petitioners by opening a separate khatian and also to receive rent from them according to law in respect of 4.69 acres of land under CS Khatian No. 11, SA Khatian No. 10, CS Plot No. 11, RS Plot No. 19; CS Plot No. 12, RS Plot No. 20; CS Plot No. 13, RS Plot No. 30; CS Plot No. 22, RS Plot No. 29 and 23; CS Plot No. 26, RS Plot No. 24; CS Plot No. 25, RS Plot No. 25; CS CS Plot No. 28, RS Plot No. 52; CS Plot No. 37, RS Plot No. 51 and under CS Khatian 24, 10 & SA Khatian No. 7, 14, RS Khatian No. 7, 14 & CS Plot No. 23, 9 & RS Plot No. 27, 34; which are homesteads, ponds and Nals situated at Mouza Giribordi, PS Sonargaon, District-Narayanganj.

2. Briefly, facts of the case as stated in the writ petition, are that the petitioners purchased 2.97 acres of land of CS Khatian No. 11 vide registered sale deed No. 8195 dated 14-12-1996 from Md. Shahabuddin, Md. Moslem Miah and Saidur Rahman, whose late father Bashiruddin, had purchased the properties from Mr. Bono Mali Haider and his brothers, who were the CS, SA and RS recorded owners of the said land. The petitioners also purchased 2.321/2 acres of land vide registered sale deed No. 3506 dated 27-5-1997 of C.S Khatian No. 9, 11, 13, 22 and 23 from the heirs of late Mrs. Jahanara Abedin, who had purchased the properties in 1970 from the brothers of the said Bono Mali Halder. Since the aforesaid sales of the suit land by the said two groups of vendors to the petitioners, the latter have been possessing the same.

3. It is stated that both the aforesaid vendors (Basiruddin and Jahnara Begum), prior to selling the aforesaid land to the petitioners, acquired the same by way of the verdicts of the civil courts. In 2001, when the petitioners came to know that the said property is a vested property, they filed Title Suit No. 189 of 2001 for a declaration that the property is not vested property and the suit was decreed on 12-10-2002. Although appeal against the said judgment and decree was preferred by the government before the High Court Division, but it was dismissed on the ground of being out of time by 1388 days. Again, the government's CPLA before the Appellate Division was dismissed for being out of time by 395 days. It is further stated that on 8-2-2011 the petitioners filed an application before respondent No. 5 to release the suit land from the list of the vested and non-resident property and, thereby, mutate their names in separate Jote Joma, but the respondents refrained from dealing with the petitioners' matter and, finally, having failed to mutate on payment of rent and taxes for the suit land, the petitioners issued a notice demanding justice to respondents on 30-3-2011 allowing the latter 7 days time to comply with the request without any result. Under the circumstances, the petitioners moved this Court for redress and obtained the present Rule.

4. No affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of any of the respondents.

5. Mr. Mainuddin, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that a decree of a competent civil court is binding upon all the authorities of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and, therefore, the respondents are legally bound to mutate the names of the petitioners in the suit land but they are not performing their legal duties and, as such, inaction of respondents is illegal. It is also submitted that in view of the fact that the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 189 of 2001 has, subsequently, been upheld by the High Court Division and, finally, by the Appellate Division, the respondents must take necessary steps to implement the same but the inaction and disregard of the respondents in executing the same clearly demonstrates their disobedience to the Constitution and law of the land. Therefore, respondents are required to be directed to mutate the names of the petitioners by opening separate khatian and also to receive rent from the petitioners.

6. It appears from Annexure-A to the writ petition that the petitioners title stemmed from Title Suit No. 84 of 1969, which was filed by late Bashiruddin, who is the father of the vendors of 2.97 acres of land of property in question to the petitioners. It is the vendors contention that their father, Mr. Bashir Uddin, entered into an agreement with the CS, SA and RS recorded owners of the suit land, Mr. Bono Mali Halder and others, to purchase 5.20 acres of land from CS Khatian Nos. 11, 24 and 10, but when the vendors failed to execute the sale deed in favour of Bashiruddin and his son, the latter filed Title Suit No. 84 of 1969 before Munsif, 4th Court, Narayanganj for specific performance of contract. It appears that though it has been contended that the said suit was decreed on contest but, from Annexure-A to the writ petition it appears that it was an ex-parte decree. It further appears that Annexure-A to the writ petition is a judgment and order, being No. 79, and the same was passed on 22-11-1976 when the civil trial court of first instance nomenclatured as "Munsif Court", but it transpires from Annexure-A to the writ petition that the name of the court is shown as "Court of Assistant Judge". It is not out of place to mention here that "Munsif Court" was re-named as Assistant Judge Court in the recent past. Therefore, it raises a serious doubt in the mind of this Court as to the genuineness of this document, which is a vital instrument for ascertaining the title of the suit land inasmuch as, the subsequent litigations are the offspring of the judgment and decree of the said Title Suit No. 84 of 1969. Based on the judgment and decree of the said suit, the vendors of the suit land claimed their title and ownership and sold the same to the petitioners. It transpires from Annexure-B to the writ petition that by filing Title Suit No. 61/83 in the Assistant Judge Court, Sonargaon, one Jahanara Abedin eventually came up with a claim of ownership and title to the suit land on the basis of 3 Sale Deeds dated 3-7-1970, executed by the brothers of Mr. Bono Mali Haider, but the court dismissed the said suit of Mrs. Jahanara Abed in on the findings that since the suit land in question were agreed to be sold by Mr. Bono Mali Halder and his brothers to Md. Bashiruddin and others and the said contract was executed by filing Title Suit No. 84 of 1969 on 14-5-1969 and, in view of the fact that the said three registered sale deeds are dated 3-7-70, those were found to be forged by the Court of Assistant Judge, Sonargaon by its judgment and decree dated 30-6-1988. However, when Mrs. Jahanara Abedin preferred an appeal against the said judgment and decree, the appeal was allowed on the compromise that Mrs. Abedin will get 2.32½ acres of land of CS Plot Nos. 9, 11, 13, 22 and 23 and Md. Bashiruddin and others would get 2.97 acres of land. At this juncture, when there has been a compromise between the said two parties by taking almost half of the properties for each of the parties, it raises a serious doubt in the mind of this Court inasmuch as, these two groups of people namely (1) Md. Bashiruddin and others and (2) Mrs. Jahanara Abedin and her heirs successfully managed to acquire the entire share of the suit land allocating 2.32½ acres of land for the family of Mrs. Jahanari Abedin and 2.97 acres of land for Md. Basiruddin and his heirs. When this was the position of the suit land, both the groups of people sold their respective shares to the petitioners. Md. Shahabuddin, Md. Moslem Miah and Md. Saidur Rahma, who are the heirs of their late father of Md. Bashiruddin, sold 2.97 acres of lands to the petitioners vide registered Sale Deed No. 895 dated 14-124996 while the heirs of Mrs. Jahanara Abedin sold 2.32½ acres of land vide registered Sale Deed No. 3506 dated 27-5-1997 of CS Khatian Nos. 9, 11, 13, 22 and 23. In this way, the petitioners became owners and possessors of the suit land of nearly 5 acres (in the prayer of the instant writ petition, the suit land is shown to be 4.69 acres, while from the statements of the writ petition the suit land appears to be 2.97+ 2.32½= 5.29½ acres). It is the claim of the petitioners that in the year 2001, when they came to know about the fact that the suit property is a VP listed property, they had to file Title Suit No. 189 of 2001 before the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj for a declaration that enlisting of the case land in the vested property list is wrong and illegal. The said suit was decreed on 12-10-2002 though it appears from Annexure-B to the writ petition that the fact of leasing the suit land vide VP Case No. 15/1968 was brought to the notice of the court by defendant Nos. 21 and 22 of Title Suit No. 189 of 2001.

7. Against the said judgment and decree dated 12-10-2002, the Government did not bother to prefer an appeal in time and, after 1388 days, when an appeal was preferred before the High Court Division, it was dismissed on the ground of limitation. The Government then filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal in the Appellate Division after out of time of 395 days and the same was dismissed as being time barred.

<u>8. It appears that the very basis of the claim of the petitioners as to the title to the suit land is the judgment and decree dated 12-11-1976 passed in Title Suit No. 84 of 1969 in favour of Md. Bashiruddin and others and the judgment and decree dated 27-7-1993 passed in Title Appeal No. 46 of 1988 in favour of Mrs. Jahanara Abedin. In view of the fact, that the likeliness of practicing fraud upon the court/s in obtaining both the judgment and decrees cannot be brushed aside, this Court opines that a judicial inquiry should be held with a view to investigate into worries of this Court as to the genuineness of Annexure-A to the writ petition, which is the judgment and order dated 22-11-1976 passed in Title Suit No. 84 of 1969, as this Court finds that there was no existence of any court with the nomenclature of "Assistant Judge Court" in the year 1976 but surprisingly the said document contains "মোকাম সোনারগাঁও সহকারী জজ আদালত” (after deleting the word সোনাগাঁও, the words নারায়নগঞ্জ ৪র্থ has been inserted). Question may be raised by the petitioners as to whether at this stage this Court is competent to look into the fact of committing forgery or practicing fraud upon court/s inasmuch as, the judgment and decrees in question have been passed by competent civil courts. On this point, our view is that in order to ensure social justice as enshrined in Article 10 of our Constitution, this Constitutional Court is empowered to grant and pass any necessary order/s as it deems fit and proper as equitable relief in addition to doing usual "fair and just" adjudication of any matter under ordinary law. Furthermore, it is the settled principle of law that fraud vitiates any rights, whether a legal right or vested right.</u>

9. Given the circumstances, the learned District Judge, Narayanganj is hereby directed to investigate into the proceedings of Title Suit No. 84 of 1969 and Title Appeal No. 46 of 1988 with the aim of revealing the true picture regarding the issues raised by this Court hereinabove and, then, provide a report to the Secretary, Ministry of Land within 2 (two) months from the date of receipt of this order.

10. The office is directed to send a copy of this judgment and order and a copy of the instant writ petition along with the annexures to the learned District Judge, Narayanganj at once without fail.

11. Respondent No 1. is directed to dispose of the application of the petitioner submitted to the Deputy Commissioner, Narayanganj, dated 8-2-2011 (Axmexure-I to the writ petition), taking into consideration the above observations of this Court as well as the aforesaid investigative report of the learned District Judge, Narayanganj within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of the report from the learned District Judge, Narayanganj.

Accordingly, the Rule is disposed of with the above observations and directions.

End.

parties:
Mirpur Mazar Co-Operative Market Society Ltd ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Capital Tower (Pvt) Ltd & Ors ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated August 18, 2003 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 50 of 2000)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: The plaintiff-petitioner has filed this petition seeking review of the judgment dated August 18, 2003 passed in Civil Appeal No. 50 of 2000. The appeal was filed by the defendant-respondent No. 6 against the judgment and decree of February 1, 1999 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Transfer Suit No. 1 of 1995 (the Title Suit No. 92 of 1993 was transferred from the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka) decreeing the same in part in the following manner:

It is declared that the deed of lease in respect of the suit land and in favour of the defendant No. 6, Capital Tower (Pvt) Ltd registered on 6-4-1993 is null and void."

2. The suit was filed seeking a decree for permanent injunction against the defendant Nos. 1-5 restraining them from leasing out the land described in the schedule to the plaint to the defendant No. 6 and from registering the lease deed in favour of the said respondent and also to restrain the defendant Nos. 1-5 from delivering possession to the said defendant. It was further prayed that in case the lease deed is executed and registered in favour of the defendant No. 6 in that case the said lease deed be declared as void. There was also a prayer for mandatory injunction against the defendant Nos. 1-5 for restoring the nature of the land in suit to its position as was prior to leasing out the land to the defendant No. 6.

3. Facts, in the background of which the suit was filed, in short, are that plaintiff-petitioner, Mirpur Mazar Co-operative Market Society Limited (the Market), owns three-storied Super Market building at 1, Darus Salam, Mirpur, Dhaka on the land measuring more or less three bighas leased out by the Government on April 24, 1981, that land measuring 1002 square yards situates to the east of the said market and the same, as asserted in the plaint, was described in the Master Plan as car park and the shop owners of the market are using the said land as car park for the last 20/25 years, that in 1978, the Market approached the Government seeking lease of the said land and thereafter again in July, 1981 and the Chief Engineer turned down the prayer of the Market stating that the said land cannot be allotted for extension of the Market, since the same has been shown as car park in the Master Plan of the Mirpur area, that 741.49 square yards from 1002 square yards have been allotted to the defendant No. 6 (appellant) at low price upon describing as institutional plot.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1-5 (respondent Nos. 1-5 herein) and also by the defendant No. 6 (respondent No. 6 herein).

5. It was the case of the defendant Nos. 1- 5 that the layout plan of the area was modified and the land leased out to the defendant No. 6 has been classified as institutional plot, that the allotment of the land was made to the defendant No. 6, since he applied for allotment of the same to establish a hospital; that there was an enquiry on the application of the defendant No. 6 and in the light of the enquiry report the Allotment Committee considered the application of the defendant No. 6 and took decision to lease out the land in suit as institutional plot to him. It was the definite case of the defendant Nos. 1-5 that the allotment was made upon due compliance of law and the allotment so made was neither improper nor illegal. It was also the case of the defendant Nos. 1-5 that there is only a layout plan of the area and that there was no Master Plan of the area.

6. It is the case of the defendant No. 6 that it got itself incorporated in 1992, that amongst the objects, one is to carry on business of clinic and hospital, that the Company applied to the authority seeking lease of the land in question or, in the alternative, another specified plot for the purpose of construction of a hospital building and after due enquiry the competent authority allotted 741.49 square yards on March 21, 1993 and delivered possession thereof on April 3, 1993, that the deed of lease was registered on April 6, 1993, that after leasing out of the aforesaid land still on the north of the land so allotted there remains land for use as car park.

7.  On the application of the plaintiff-petitioner before the High Court Division the suit, Title Suit No. 92 of 1993, was transferred from the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka to the High Court Division and the same was tried in the High Court Division. As mentioned hereinabove a Division Bench of the High Court Division on the materials on record decreed the suit in the manner as stated hereinbefore. The defendant No. 6 appealed, Civil Appeal No. 50 of 2000, as against the judgment and order of the High Court Division. This Division by the judgment as mentioned hereinbefore allowed the appeal and thereupon dismissed the suit.

8. It has been submitted on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioner that in paragraph 3 of the leased deed it has been specifically stated that the plot so allotted to the defendant No. 6-appellant is to be used for commercial purpose and the DW 2, deposing for the defendant No. 6, has stated that it has a plan to construct a building for running a hospital with the expectation of earning profit but in the schedule to the leased deed the plot so allotted to the defendant No. 6 has been described as institutional plot which is in contradiction to the purpose for which land so allotted is to be used as stated in paragraph 3 of the lease deed and, as such, the allotment so made to the defendant No. 6 was not transparent and the said defendant was unjustly favoured and consequently, the allotment so made and the lease deed registered pursuant thereto is tainted with unfairness and the authority in making the allotment violated the provisions of Articles 27 and 144 of the Constitution. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that the land in question was allotted at a too low price to the defendant No. 6 upon ignoring the offer of the plaintiff to purchase the same at a fair market price for maintaining its original purpose, that there was no basis for treating the plot allotment whereof was sought for the construction of the hospital that would be run on commercial basis as anything other than a commercial plot and there was no evidence on record that the project was non-profit making or charitable to justify the plot allotted of being described as any other kind of plot than a commercial plot or to justify allotting the plot at an abnormally low price by resorting to the device of naming it as 'institutional' plot so as to confer an undue advantage and unjustly enriching a favoured party, that the lands situate in the locality have been allotted to the others at a price much higher than the price at which land in question has been allotted to the defendant No. 6 and there was no material on record in support of the contrary position that land similar to the land in question at similar location in Mirpur or anywhere near and during the material period was sold at a price as low as the price at which the land was sold to the defendant No. 6, that as in the written statement of the defendant Nos. 1- 5 it was stated that leaving certain portion of land for car park the Master Plan of the area was modified and, as such, evidence of DW 1, that there was only modification of the layout plan of the area ought not to have been taken into consideration, that while the Chief Engineer in his letter dated 29-7-1981 rejected the prayer of the plaintiff for leasing out the land in suit to them for using as the car park mentioning that the land has been marked in the Master Plan as car park and, as such, the DW 1, who deposed for the defendant Nos. 1-5, was not competent to depose that there was a layout plan in respect of the suit land prepared in 1967, that the modification of the plan, as deposed by the DW 1, being for the benefit of the favoured party is an abuse of the authority under Article 144 of the Constitution and violative of Article 27, as well as being an arbitrary act to confer undue advantage to unjustifiably enrich a favoured party is contrary to the public interest, that no material was placed on record to show that 'institutional' plot/plots was sold at such a low price as the plot in question was sold and there was no yardstick for carving out 'institutional' plot out of the plots which are commercial plots and by no yardstick the plot so allotted to the defendant No. 6 can be said to be 'institutional' plot.

<u>9. The learned Counsel for the defendant-respondent No. 6 has submitted the contentions of the plaintiff-petitioner that Ext. 5A, letter of the Chief Engineer dated 29-7-1981, wherein it was mentioned that the land in question has been earmarked for car park has been disregarded by this Court and the contents of the said Ext. 5A as was not denied by the DW 1 and the said DW 1 as was not a competent witness to controvert the contents of the Ext. 5A wherein it was mentioned by the Chief Engineer that the land in question and some other land was earmarked as car park in the Master Plan of Mirpur area, his evidence that there was only layout plan of the Mirpur area and the same was modified ought to have been left out of consideration and the modification of the said Master Plan having been made to benefit favoured party is an arbitrary act to confer undue advantage to enrich a 'favoured party', contrary to the public interest and the contention that an important document (written statement) containing admission of the defendant Nos. 1-5 with regard to a material fact, namely, change of the Master Plan, was not included in the paper book, nor placed or considered by this Division while made the judgment sought to be reviewed and had the material statement of the defendant Nos. 1-5 in the written statement to the effect that the land in question was a vacant land and keeping of the land as necessary for use as car park the Master Plan of Mirpur has been modified in the public interest being considered along with other documents, in that case this Court would have taken a different view with regard to the change of Master Plan and, as such, the judgment of this Court warrants review and the review of the judgment is warranted as certain conclusions are based on errors apparent of the face of the record, eg, the evidence on record shows that the plot was a commercial plot and the price at which the land was sold abnormally low in fact 10% of the market price and there is no evidence to support the propositions to the contrary and there being uncontroverted evidence on record that the prevailing price of the similar land was over Taka 2 crore per bigha and the documents incorporated in the Concise Statement of the defendant No. 6 showed that the price of similar plot was over Taka 2 crore and, as such, selling the land in question to the defendant No. 6 (respondent No. 6) at the rate of Taka 20 lac per bigha amounted to a gross abuse of executive authority, have been dealt with and decided by this Court in its judgment sought to be reviewed. The learned Counsel for the defendant-respondent No. 6, upon referring from the judgment sought to be reviewed, has submitted that the question as to whether the plot allotted to the respondent No. 6 is commercial or institutional plot and the question relating to fixation of price of the land so allotted to the respondent No. 6 have elaborately been considered by this Court and, as such, it is not correct to say that this Court while disposing of the appeal did not consider the nature and character of the land and the price which was fixed for the land so allotted to the respondent No. 6. The learned Counsel lastly, submitted that the question pertaining to the mode in which the land has been allotted to the respondent No. 6 has also been considered by this Court and that the considerations made and thereupon findings arrived at being based on materials on record and no contrary material having been placed to contradict the materials brought on record by the respondent No. 6, the judgment of this Division warrants no review.</u>

<u>10. The submissions of the learned Counsel for the petitioner that in spite of describing the land in the schedule as 'institutional plot' but in view of the recital in the leased deed, particularly in view of the recital in paragraph 3 of the leased deed, the land allotted to the respondent No. 6 being a commercial plot and further it being in the evidence of the DW 2, who deposed for the respondent No. 6, that the said respondent would establish a hospital which will be run at a profitable rate and consequent thereupon the plot in question being commercial plot though described as 'institutional plot,' as such, the price of the plot as has been fixed as 'institutional plot' is much below the price fixed for the commercial plot appears to be not well founded since materials were placed on record by the respondent No. 6 to show the price of the plots described as 'institutional plots' at which were sold earlier and at the relevant time and therefrom it was noticed by this Court that the plot in question allotted to the respondent No. 6 was priced at an amount as was fixed for the 'institutional plot'. Since this question has been elaborately dealt with by this Division and no material having been placed at the time of hearing of the review petition to show that at the material time 'institutional plots' were allotted to others at a price higher than the price that was fixed for the similar kind of plot so allotted to the respondent No. 6, the contention as to selling the plot in question to respondent No. 6 at low price is of no merit. The other contention of the learned Counsel for the petitioner is that the price of the land of the similar kind, ie, the price of the land allotted to the Respondent No. 6, was much lower the prevailing market price of the similar situated land in the similar location, i.e. in Mirpur, is not correct, since the said contention has been made on the premise that the land so allotted to the respondent No. 6 is a commercial plot but, in fact, the plot so allotted to the respondent No. 6 is 'institutional plot' and material was brought on record from the side of the respondent No. 6 to show that at the relevant time the 'institutional plots' were sold at the price at which the price of the land allotted to him was fixed. This contention of the respondent No. 6 was not dislodged by placing any material either at the time of hearing of the appeal or at the time of hearing of the review petition. This being the position, the contention that the land was allotted to the respondent No. 6 at a price much lower than the market price prevailing at the relevant time is of no merit. The other contention of the petitioner was that Master Plan of the Mirpur area was revised and thereby the respondent No. 6 has been unjustly favoured. This contention of the learned Counsel for the petitioner in view of the evidence of DW 1 is not well founded. It is correct in the letter Exhibit 5A it was mentioned by the Chief Engineer, that the land allotment whereof was sought for by the petitioner was earmarked in the Master Plan as car park and also in the written statement. It is in the evidence of DW 1, that, in fact, there was no Master Plan for Mirpur area and there was layout plan of the area in question prepared in 1967 and later on the same was revised. From the petitioner's side no material was placed to show that, in fact, there was a Master Plan for Mirpur area. Suffice it to say that there can hardly be any Master Plan for any specified area within the town and there be a Master Plan generally of the town i.e. Dhaka City or Dhaka Town. In our judgment we have considered the contention of the learned Counsel for the petitioner as regard change of Master Plan. Since no new material has been placed to show that our decision that there was no Master Plan of the locality but there was a layout plan which was revised by the competent authority was erroneous, as such, we find no reason to take the view different from the view already taken as regard the contention that there was change of Master Plan to unjustly favour the respondent No. 6. The other contention of the learned Counsel for the petitioner that the important document, i.e. written statement containing the averment that the land in question was a vacant land and upon specifying an area for use as car park, the Master Plan of Mirpur area was revised in public interest, was not placed in the paper book and the same was not placed at the time of hearing of the appeal and was not considered by us appears to be not well founded as at the time of hearing of the appeal the learned Counsel for the petitioner argued that plot in question was allotted to the respondent No. 6 upon revising the Master Plan and the revision of the Master Plan has caused vanishing of the car park and the Court considered the said contention in the background of the evidence of DW 1 who deposed on behalf of the defendant Nos. 1-5, the government functionaries.</u>

<u>11. It may be mentioned that no material was brought on record from the side of the petitioner, who was respondent in the appeal, to dislodge the evidence of DW 1 that there was no Master Plan of Mirpur area but there was a layout plan of the said area and that has been revised by the competent authority. The other contention is that there was no yardstick for carving out certain plot as 'institutional plot' and that by no yardstick the land so allotted to the respondent No. 6 can be considered 'institutional plot.' The matter of classification of plots by the authority upon objective basis is a policy matter which is not new or first of its kind as regard the plot so allotted to the defendant-respondent No. 6 and, as such, it is not for the Court to make pronouncement that particular plot should have been classified as one other than the one already classified by the competent authority. In our view, what the Court is required to do is to examine whether the classified plot has been allotted upon due compliance of law or, in other words, in making allotment procedure followed previously was followed. It is seen from the materials on record that the plot so allotted to the respondent No. 6 is not the lone 'institutional plot' but prior to making allotment to the respondent No. 6 there have been allotments of 'institutional plot' to different persons or bodies and there has also been allotment of 'institutional plot' subsequent to the allotment to the respondent No. 6. This being the position it can hardly be said that by making the allotment in question to the respondent No. 6, he has been favoured. The other exception that has been taken by the learned Counsel for the petitioner relates to the mode in which plot in question has been allotted to the respondent No. 6 has also been considered by us in our judgment sought to be reviewed and no material has been placed before us to take the view different from the view already taken by us in the judgment sought to be reviewed as to the mode of allotment of the plot in question.</u>

12. In view of the discussions made hereinover we find no substance in the petition.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
Anwarul Hoque Chowdhury, J:—This Rule arises out of an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge, Khulna affirming those passed by the learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 324 of 1976.

1. Facts in short are that one G.M. Ali Baksha, Headmaster of Agarghata High School P.S Paikgachha District Khulna as sole plaintiff filed a suit, being Title Suit No. 324 of 1976 in the Court of Munsif for a declaration that the resolutions adopted by the Managing Committee of the Agarghata High in removing him is illegal, ultra vires and that the plaintiff is still in service. The plaintiff's case is that he is the founder Head-master of that school who have been serving since its birth as Head master and was also the Member Secretary of the School Managing committee. With regard to the discharge of a teacher and appointment of a new teacher controversy arose in a meeting of the Managing Committee and out of that grudge defendant no. 1 namely Sarder Ahmed Ali Mondal of the said Managing Committee of the School along with other members of the said Managing Committee made a design to remove the plaintiff and with that view defendant no. 1 and other members of the said Managing Committee convened a meeting of the said Committee on 11.6.76 stating that the same is being convened at the requisition of 6 members but the names of requisitions were not mentioned. The notice was served upon the plain-tiff on 21.6.76 at 10-15 A.M. in the morning though 7 days prior notice is required for such a meeting and the meeting was held on that date where only 5 members were present and a resolution was adopted in the meeting removing the plaintiff from his service as Head master. On 30.7.76 another meeting was held which adopted the resolution of the previous meeting and was confirmed. The plaintiff was not allowed to speak anything and only after removal of the plaintiff from the service he was directed to show cause within 7 days. The plaintiff gave his reply to the show cause notice on 3.7.76 and thereafter defendant no. 1 convened a meeting on 8.7.76 but in that meeting the cause shown was not accepted and a copy of the resolution was sent to defendant no. 10 namely, D.D.P.I., Khulna Division, Barisal for approval who on receipt of the same appointed an inquiry commission on 19.7.76 but before that on 11.7.76 the plaintiff got a notice signed by defendant No. 1 directing the plaintiff not to attend the school alleging that the plaintiff have been removed from his service. All these meetings were illegal, ultra vires of the committee and it had militated against the principle of natural justice. It was also alleged that the meeting was neither legally convened, not properly notified nor conducted in the manner as provided in the Recognised non-Government Secondary Schools Regulations 1973 hereinafter referred to as the Regulations that the Board had not given any approval to the removal of the plaintiff and by such illegal removal the plaintiff had sustained injury. Hence, the suit.

2. The suit was contested by defendant No. 1. The defence case inter alia is that there were charges against the plaintiff for misappropriation of huge amount of school fund, tempering and interpolation with the Books of Accounts but despite repeated requests he did not convene any meeting of the Managing Committee and a requisition meeting was convened on 21.6.76 where from the plaintiff was absent willfully and the meeting was adjourned till to 30.6.76 When on 30.6.76 the plaintiff attended the meeting and his verbal statements were heard but these were not found satisfactory. A charge sheet was issued against him. Thereafter, the plaintiff submitted his written statement and his statement was considered but found unsatisfactory and accordingly, he was served notice on 11.7.76 as to his termination and since then the plaintiff is not in service and the matter has been placed for approval of the Board and the decision is in process, that the plaintiff has been legally discharged and he has no legal right to institute any such suit as the relationship between the plaintiff and defendant is nothing but that of a master and servant for which a suit for damage only if any, would lie for breach of a contract.

3. The learned Munsif after hearing the parties and on consideration of the relevant law decreed the suit on contest. The removal was declared to be illegal and ultravires and it was declared that the plaintiff is still in service as Headmaster in that school.

4. On appeal, they said was affirmed by the learned District Judge, Khulna. As against that this Revisional application was moved before this Court and a Rule was obtained which is being disposed of by this judgment.

5. Mr. Shaikh Razzaque Ali, the learned Advocate appeared in support of the rule and having taken me through the judgments of the courts below and the evidence on record has contended that the courts below erred in law in not finding that the relationship between the Managing Committee and the plaintiff was that of a master and servant, there being no statutory provision or law guiding the service conditions of the plaintiff. The instant suit being a suit to enforce a contract would not be maintainable in which case, only damages would be competent. That had not been considered by any of the courts below, causing prejudice to the petitioner. He has further urged that the finding of the courts below that the resolutions were not only illegal and without jurisdiction but also a malafide one is wrong in view of the fact that the course of action followed by the Managing Committee was fair and equitable and the plaintiff was heard in person and he was afforded enough opportunity to ex-plain his position and as such the action of the Managing Committee cannot be said to be malafide. This inference of malafide was drawn illegally and it had caused prejudice to the petitioner as the said had prompted the courts below in coming to the finding of fact from a wrong inference. He has lastly argued that the courts below had failed to appreciate that no decree could have been passed in the suit like this because the Suit was hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, it being only a declaration suit without any consequential relief. This was the initial illegality caused by the courts in violation of statutory provision of law making the proceeding coram non-judice and thus revisable by this Court in its Revisional jurisdiction.

6. Mr. Md. Latifur Rahman the learned Counsel appeared for the opposite party no. 19, who is the present Head Master of the School in place of the plaintiff and he has adopted the arguments of Mr. Sk. Razzaque Ali, in full.

7. Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing in opposition to the Rule has contended that the courts below neither acted illegality in the exercise of its jurisdiction nor it had exercised the jurisdiction illegally with material irregularity for this Court to exercise its jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He has next urged that the concurrent finding of fact of the courts below to the effect that the plaintiff Head Master had not been given any opportunity of being heard is based on evidence on record. That being essentially a finding of fact this Court would not interfere with that finding in its Revisional jurisdiction. He has further agreed that it is on record that 7 days clear notice was not given while convening the meeting of the said Managing Committee as required under the law and the finding of the court that there was no agenda of the meeting which was done in violation of the law is also a finding of fact gathered from the evidence on record and that need not be interfered with by this Court in its Revisional Jurisdiction Further the learned Lawyer submitted that the illegality would be manifest as sub-section 3 of Section 15 of the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Jessore (recognised non-Government Secondary School) Regulations 1973 provided that "The date and time of each meeting shall be fixed by the Member-Secretary in consultation with the Chairman, but the meeting may also be held on the requisition of two-thirds of the members, but seven days notice shall be given for such a meeting". Sub-section (4) of Section 15 provides that" The notice for a meeting of the Committee shall set forth the business to be transacted at the meeting in the form of agenda and no business other than those included in the agenda shall be transacted except with the consent of two-thirds of the members present. The said sub-section further provided that no matter involving the appointment or dismissal of teacher or expulsion or rustication of a student shall be taken up unless the matter has been placed on the agenda issued with the notice of the meeting". According to the learned Advocate, these facts clearly show that the holding of the meeting without prior 7 days notice and without the agenda, was incompetent and everything that was resolved in that meeting was also illegal and of no legal basis. He has further urged that in a proceeding for removal, a teacher, cannot be removed without being heard and in the facts and circumstances of the case it is evident that a show cause notice was served upon the plaintiff only after he had already been removed from his post. This is a violation of the principles of natural justice which will be read in to the law in its absence and then for the courts below having found that no show cause notice were issued and the plaintiff having not been heard, it caused a violation of the principles of natural justice and therefore, the action taken was illegal and all those were found legally by the court's below, calling for no interference by this Court.

8. This is an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and I am very much conscious of the limitations as under section of 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This Court must exercise the power on revision within the tenor of the law and not hearing the matter as a Second Appeal. It is thus a question of any irregularity or illegality committed by the court that need be cured in the exercise of the power under section 115 of the code of Civil Procedure. When asked to point out the illegality committed by the Courts below it was contended by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the courts below came to an illegal finding as to the relationship between the petitioner and the Managing Committee which was that of a Master and servant.

9. The question whether the relationship between any two persons is that of a Master and servant is more or less a question of fact and not a question of law. But if this finding as to the factum of the relationship between Master and the servant is arrived at by any misreading of any document creating the relationship or by a misreading of any contract of service, the said would be a question of law. In the instant case that is not the matter be-cause it is not the case of the petitioner before this Court that in view of any contract of service or letter of appointment, as issued by the Managing Committee to the Head Master, the said letter of appointment would be constituted as spelling out the relationship of a Master and servant, denying a right of hearing when removed as a servant, serving during the pleasure of the Master. This however, is not the matter here. What was argued by Mr. Sk. Razzaque Ali is that the plaintiff opposite party being only the Head Master of a school and the Managing Committee of the said school having been empowered by Board's Regulations 1973 to appoint, suspend, dismiss and remove a teacher the Headmaster would be deemed to be an employee under the Managing Committee to be removed at will of the Managing Committee, if that is considered necessary for the school and thus the relationship between the Managing Committee and the Head Master would be the relationship of two private individuals, the relationship of an employer and an employee and that of a Master and a servant. That being the position, a suit of restitution as in the instant case also would not lie because an unwilling master cannot be forced to accept the service of a servant and hence if there was any dismissal by causing a breach of the terms of the contract it would cause a breach of a contract for which damage would lie and not reinstatement as was done in the instant case.

10. In the instant case the pertinent question is whether the finding of the courts below with regard to the relationship of the Headmaster and the Managing Committee of the school was a finding which can be called illegal. This question is to condition which constitutes the relationship between a master and a servant is now well settled. In the case of Short v. Henderson Ltd. a case of the House of Lords under the Workmen's Compensation Act, Lord Thankerton reiterates the four indicia of contract of service. These are : (a) the master's power of selection of his servant ; (b) the payment of wages or other remuneration : (c) the master's right to control the method of doing the work ; and (d) the master's right of suspension or dismissal. His lordship then goes on to say that the particular requirement of a contract of service is the right of the master in some reasonable sense to "control the method of doing the work," and this factor of superintendence and control has frequently been treated as critical and decisive of the legal quality of the relationship of master and servant. In the case of Gould v. Minister of National Insurance reported in All England Report" 1951 (Vol. 1) the case of a Music Hall artist at page 368 the court had to consider whether a contract between the management and the Artist was to be regarded as a contract of service or it need to be regarded as "contract for services". It was held there that the contract gave the management the right to prohibit any part of the performance or the right to ask a new song but performing the very act of singing deserved the personality of the artist which the manages can neither control nor interfere. Their lordships thus held that in that case it was a, contract for services only and not a contract of service and hence there was no question of any master and servant relation. It was also held there that this question of the relation of master and servant would be a simple question of fact and not a question of law unless it is contained in a written document spelling out the relationship. It would be question of law when the relationship would be derived from any construction of a written agreement. In the instant case the Head Master is required to do a skilled job that is to teach, over which the management Committee would have no control, no control as to the method of teaching or doing the job of teaching and hence for his services he cannot be called a servant under the management committee for the managing committee would have no control in the method of doing the Head Master's job as a teacher because that would be a personal quality. That being the position the relationship between the Head Master and Managing Committee would not be a relationship between a Master and a servant specially when the Head Master having a public representative character doing a skilled job. This finding having not been based upon any construction of a document or letter of appointment the said finding as to the relationship, based as the evidence on record, would again be entirely a finding of fact which need not be interfered with by this Court in its Revisional Jurisdiction. It need be further observed that this relationship of master and servant contemplated a relationship between two individuals standing in two different capacities as such as between the owner and the servant. Or the worker representing only the Master and the servant and none else and affecting none else in the society at large. But the moment the matter would have a public character or the employee would be working in a public capacity the relationship of pure master and servant would vanish and he would not be dismissed at pleasure. A similar matter came up before the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the case of Bangladesh Small Industries Corporation. Vs. Mahabub Hossain reported in 29 D.L.R. (SC) 39. Their Lordships of the Supreme Court in the relevant portion of the Judgment held that:-

"The law of Master and servant as applicable for determining the right of an employee dismissed from service is based upon the view that such a right is exclusively founded upon. a contract of service between an employer and an employee and that inasmuch as such a contract is incapable of being specifically enforced under the provision of the Specific Relief Act, an action for restoration of the dismissed employee to its former office is not maintainable in law. It conceives a private individual serving another private benefits and the relationship does not involve any element other than the contractual one. In such a case, the employee is interested only in his remuneration, which can be measured only in monetary value. in the same way, the employer employs the particular individual for his own private purpose which is exclusively his own concern and in which nobody else is interested and if in case of a breach of any contractual obligation arising out of the contract of employment, the employer is prepared to forgo the service of his employee and at the same time pay the dismissed employee adequate monetary compensation, it is nobody else's business to be concerned about it. But if the office of employment has got a public character, the relationship transcends the confines of a contractual character and ceases to be the concern of the individuals, namely; the person who dismisses and the person who is dismissed. In such a case, the person who exercises the power of dismissal does so on behalf of a public corporation in which the general public or a substantial section of the general public is interested and such power is exercised under some authority of law. He cannot rest cynically contented by saying that it is the personal affair of an individual or some individuals whose representative he is and he is prepared to pay the dismissed employee, the necessary compensation if the order of dismissal is ultimately found to be illegal and this is nobody else's business to be bothered about. These are the considerations which naturally lifts the cases of public employment out of the strict category of the master and the servant rule. In such a case, the terms and condition of service may also be regulated by some statutory provisions and the termination of service may be made in violation of such provisions. In that event as well, the master and servant rule cannot be invoked in order to deny the relief of reinstatement to the discharged employee."

11. I am in respectful agreement with the observations of their Lordships of Supreme Court which is in complete accord with the view I have taken and which is binding upon this Court and I find in the instant case that the relationship between the Head Master and the School Managing Committee was not that of a master and servant. It was not the relationship between two individuals only character and not between master and servant. Next, the Managing Committee, representing the public interest and a section of the public had a duty to work in accordance with the Rules under which the Managing Committee was created. The Rules provided, as already been referred to hereinbefore, that a meeting cannot be held without 7 days clear notice and the agenda in case of removal of a teacher must be issued along with notice to the members sitting in the meeting and a removal need to be referred to, out of necessity, to the form of a removal proceeding as known to law. All these were not done in the instant case and that was found by both the courts below legally, causing no error, calling for interference by this Court.

12. Mr. Sk. Razzaque Ali, next submits that the law relating to the service of a Head master contemplated no such proceeding as Regulation 23(b) of Regulations 1973 gave power to the Managing Committee to remove teachers. That being the position it cannot be concluded that there would be the necessity of a proceeding and a detail hearing given to a dismissed employee.

13. There is no substance in this contention as this is not the position under the law. On a reference to Section 30 of the East Pakistan Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 it is seen that sub-Section (1) of Section 30 of it provided that an employee of a recognised Intermediate College or Secondary School shall be bound by the general conditions of service namely : (a) He shall not take part in, or subscribe in aid of or assist in anyway any political movement or any activates (b) He shall not canvass (2) Any person who contravenes any of the conditions of service as stated in sub-section (1) shall be liable to disciplinary action including removal from his post by any order of the authority which appointed such person" on a proceeding initiated against him", Section 30 is captioned as "general conditions of service of the teacher of the Inter-Mediate College and Secondary School". This clearly shows that under the general conditions of service the teacher of the Secondary school cannot be removed without a proceeding initiated against him. Law therefore, contemplated a proceeding for the removal. If there be a proceeding it need be included and conducted in accordance with the provision known to law namely that in the proceeding drawn against him he must .be given a reasonable opportunity of controverting the allegation made against him and be allowed to lead evidence in support of his case and if that was not done, the proceeding in removing the accused would be coram non-judice and all that would be done by any authority in pursuance of that decision arrived at in such a proceeding in violation of the rules of natural Justice, would be a nullity. This is the legal position and it had rightly been held so by both the courts and I find no illegality committed by the Courts in this regard to be corrected under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

14. It was next argued by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the court below was oblivion of the fact that the suit as framed was not maintainable at all being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Because according to the learned Advocate for the petitioner this suit was a mere declaratory suit without any consequential relief which the petitioner was competent to ask at the time of filing the suit and a suit like this nature would not be maintainable. In support of this the learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to a decision of the Rangpur Bench of the High Court Division reported in 35 D.L.R. 224 where it was observed by his lordship of the single Bench that the suit of a Bank employee for a mere declaration .without a prayer for damages for illegal dismissal would be hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, The case cited before this Court of the Rangpur Division is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, because in the instant case it appears from the plaint that it was not a suit for mere declaration but that it was a suit with a consequential relief namely for a declaration that the plaintiff be declared to be still in service which means consequential reinstatement. There was also a prayer for injunction restraining the Managing Committee from interfering with the work of the plaintiff as Headmaster of that school. It thus, cannot be said that it was a suit for a mere declaration only without any consequential relief. Further, it is seen that even in the written statement of the defendant’s appellants before the trial court no such objection as to the maintainability of the suit had been taken. No such issue was framed. The parties never fought out the case on that basis except an issue to the effect as to "whether the suit is maintainable in the present form", where it was not argued that the suit is not maintainable being hit by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, whether this objection can be taken at this stage before this Court on Revision would be explained at the appropriate stage. Going back to the scheme of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act it is seen that the object of the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is only to avoid multiplicity of suits. It was thus provided that in a suit for declaration the plaintiff must come with all the reliefs which he was capable of asking at the time of filing the suit because the law would not allow the plaintiff to file indefinite number of suits for indefinite number of declarations one after the other, and part by part. On a reference to the proviso to Section 42 it is seen that no declaration of title be made by a court where the plaintiff being capable of asking for further relief then a mere declaration of title omits to do so. Whether a suit is to be hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act would depend upon the facts of each particular case. No hard and first rule can be spelt out which would be applicable to all cases. All would depend on the fact whether the plaintiff in a given case had asked for all the relief he would be capable of asking at that moment. A court will not throw out a suit unless it is satisfied beyond all doubts that the plaintiff ought to seek further relief and yet has claimed nothing beyond mere declaration. Honestly speaking, a suit to have a declaration as to the true construction of a law or to have a declaration that an act done was done illegally and in violation of statutory law which need to be declared void and of no effect, is not the sort of declaratory suit that are prohibited by the proviso to section 42 of the Act as they might be cases where no further relief could be asked or where no further relief need be asked and a decree passed in such a suit cannot be said to be non-executable for a declaration as to the illegal and void character of the act done would automatically mean the restoration of the position previous to the illegal act.

15. Hence, it must be a relief appropriate to and necessarily consequent upon the right or title asserted and should be such as the plaintiff would be in a position to claim by virtue of the title he seeks to establish or be declared and that must be asked from the defendants immediately in consequence of the declaration for the declaration to be complete as to the dispute in its totality. Therefore, if a plaintiff would be entitled in some remote way to some other relief in consequence of the declaration but which are not immediately related to the cause of action the said cannot be called further relief within the meaning of the Proviso to the Act and hence the plaintiff in such a case cannot be compelled by the Court to ask for relief, whether he wants it or not and if the plaintiff in a given case is not in need of any other consequential relief the suit will not sin against the proviso to section 42 of the Act. All thus would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case and this ought to be decided at the outset and to allow an amendment of the plaint if so required after an objective examination of the further relief that need be claimed as it is seen that Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act does not authorise an out right dismissal of a suit for sinning against the proviso. The court is to allow amendment of the plaint and that being the position there are authorities to show that when a person being the defendant did not take the plea in his written statement that the plaintiff's case should be dismissed, being hit by the proviso to Section 42 of the Act, the defendant cannot on appeal or on revision be allowed to set out a new case which he did not make out in his written statement as to maintainability of the suit which need to have been agitated at the earliest possible opportunity, which was not done in the instant case and further I find that the suit was not hit by section 42 of the proviso as it was not mere declaration but there were consequential relief to the extent it was capable of being asked at the time of the institution of the suit by the plaintiff. Further in a matter like this the finding whether a suit is hit by section 42 is a finding of fact to be decided by the court initially and if the court proceed j with the suit finding no objection under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, higher courts on Revision would be very reluctant to interfere, if the court at the first instance had not exercised the discretion arbitrarily which, however, is not the case here.

16. In the case of Mir Gholam Sarwar reported in 13 D.L.R at page 341 a Police Officer was removed from service. It was challenged. That suit was framed to the effect that the order of dismissal of the plaintiff was illegal and that the plaintiff still holds his office as Sub-Inspector. In that case an objection was taken at the initial stage of the suit as to maintainability 'which was however overruled by both the courts. The said objection was taken again on appeal and their Lordships held that in a suit for declaration that the order of dismissal is illegal and that he is still in service and without any further relief for arrears of rent would not be hit by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

17. In the case of Vithoba Rhanji v. Vithal Sakroo reported in A.I.R. 1958 (Bombay) at page 279, it was held that in order to decide whether the plaintiffs' suit was one which was exclusively a suit for a bare declaration or whether in essence it was a suit for any further relief, it will be necessary for the court to scan the allegations as in the plaint with some care and analyze the substance of the plaintiffs' claim it is not enough for a Court to consider the mere allegations that the plaintiff has chosen to make but the Court must go behind the mere form and verbiage of the plaint and ascertain what indeed is the true relief which the plaintiff is asking for.

<u>18. The case of Abdur Rashid vs. Hari Pada Sarker, reported in 22 D.L.R. at page 668, is the case of a Headmaster of a Secondary School removed from his post. The Headmaster as plaintiff filed a suit for a declaration that the said removal was bad and for a further declaration that he is still in service. In that suit it was further prayed that the defendant be restrained from interfering with the plaintiff's duties and function as Head Master of the said School until he is dismissed in due course of law. On appeal before the High Court his Lordships held that a notice for holding a meeting of the Managing Committee of the Secondary School under the Ordinance, the provision of 7 days notice is mandatory in nature and not mere directory and that under the said Regulation the time for holding a meeting of the managing committee need be fixed by the Secretary in consultation with the Chairman. It was further held that prior approval of the Board is essential for removal of a Head Master and in the absence of any prior approval by the Board, a resolution passed by the managing committee removing the Head Master is without jurisdiction and thus illegal. In that case no one pleaded that the suit was not maintainable.</u>

<u>19. That decision under report is relevant to the facts of this case and being in respectful agreement with the observations of his Lord-ship in the case I find that the courts believe rightly found that there was a violation of the Regulation made by the Board of Secondary Education, Jessore as to the meeting of the Managing Committee which removed the Head Master and the non-service of the agenda with the notice and the failure to give a reasonable opportunity to the plaintiff Head Master, violated the mandatory provisions of law as under the Regulation and also the provisions of natural justice, there being the existence Of no feaster and servant relationship and thus the said removal is bad in law and it was rightly declared that the plaintiff is still in service.</u>

20. I do not find any illegality done by the courts below in arriving at the findings of facts to the effect that the removal was bad in law I, therefore, find no substance in this Rule which is accordingly, discharged. In the facts and circumstances of the case, there will however be no order as to costs.

Send down the records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C.J:- This appeal arises from Civil Revision No. 909 of 1975 decided by a Single Judge of the High Court Division, Comilla Bench on 3rd January, 1983.

2. An application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was filed by the predecessor-in-interest of the respondent Nos. 1-12 along with respondent No. 13 in the 1st court of Munsif, Sylhet for pre-emption of .33 acre of land of case plot No. 5209 out of total 3.36 acres of land of 16 plots purchased by the appellant by a single kabala dated 3-4-72. Their case is that they are co-sharers by purchase and owners of contiguous land and as such they are entitled to partial pre-emption on proportionate consideration of Tk. 1,035/- out of total consideration of Tk. 10,000/-. The pre-emptee-appellant and respondent Nos. 14 and 15 who arc vendors contested the case by filing a joint written objection. Their case is that the pre-emptors are not entitled to any relief without making deposit of Tk. 10,000/-, they are not co-sharers of the holding and have no land contiguous to the lands sold, they have no land to the contiguous north and east of the plot and that the proportionate value of the case land will be at least Tk. 2,000/- being the best land of the entire lot sold under the kabala. Also the case was bad for non joinder of necessary parties. Pre-emptee-appellant did not, however, contest the case at the time of trial.

3. The trial court, on finding that though the pre-emptors are not co-sharers they have plot Nos. 5211 and 5242 to the contiguous north and cast and that there was no mention of defect of parties in the written objection allowed the pre-emption. It also held that the pre-emptors were not legally bound to deposit the entire consideration money of Tk. 10,000/- with compensation. Appellant preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 275 of 1973 before the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet, but with no effect. Appellant filed the aforesaid civil revision case before the High Court Division which, by its judgment dated 3-1-83, upheld and affirmed the judgment and order of the first appellate court.

4. Being aggrieved pre-emptee-appellant moved this Court and obtained leave to consider whether the partial pre-emption of a portion of one of the plots transferred by a kabala on the basis of principle of ownership of contiguous land was wrong as being contrary to law and the decision of this Court in Ahmed Hossain vs. Basharat Ali, (1980) 32 DLR 54 AI) corresponding to 1977 BSCR 397.

5. Mr. Maksumul Hakim, Counsel for the appellant, submitted that since the pre-emptors' land, namely, plot No. 5211 is not contiguous to the entire land of the transferred plot No. 5209, not to speak of contiguity to the entire land transferred by the kabala concerned, the order of pre-emption as affirmed by the first appellate court and the High Court Division finds no support in law or the decisions pronounced by this Court. He referred to the following cases, namely, Akhtarun Nessa vs. Habibullah, (1979) 31 DLR 88 AD, Ahmed Hossain vs. Basharat Ali, (1980) 32 DLR 54 AD, Haji Tajamal Ali being dead his heirs: Kamarunnessa vs. Abdus Sattar, (1982) 34 DLR 217 AD which contained the principles regarding partial pre-emption.

6. In the case of Akhtarun Nessa and another, the pre-emptor who was found to be a tenant holding land contiguous to only two plots out of three plots transferred, was held to be entitled to pre-empt only the land to which his land was contiguous. It was, however, held that "a pre-emptor was not entitled to pre-emption in respect of the land transferred to which he had no contiguity". Further, "where land transferred consists of more than one plot, a tenant or tenants having land contiguous to the plot or plots may apply for pre-emption but in such a case, a tenant having land contiguous only to one of the plots, cannot claim pre-emption of other lands".

7. In the case of Ahmed Hossain and others which was relied upon by the learned Counsel for the appellant, it has been observed that "it is very often noticed that pre-emption under section 96 is allowed to a tenant having land contiguous to one of several-plots transferred, and pre-emption is allowed even in cases where the lands are not in a compact block, which is contrary to the provision of law itself". As to why in case of transfer of more than one plots by a sale deed it should not entitle a tenant having land contiguous to one of such plots to pre-empt also other plots the Court observed as follows:

"Every C.S. Plot or R.S. plot or S.A. plot under the land laws, as depicted in the survey maps represent a separate entity, clearly identifiable in a holding recorded in a khatian. If more than one plot of land arc transferred by a sale deed a tenant having land contiguous to one of the plots, cannot lay his claim of pre-emption beyond that plot, because, the contiguity cannot be stretched to other plots. This proposition would not only be in full agreement with the different provisions of section 96, but also in conformity with the very object of the legislation."

8. The decision appears to lay down the proposition that pre-emption can be allowed when the plot of land transferred is contiguous to the land of the pre-emptor.

<u>9. The case of Haji Tajamal Ali referred to in the cases just mentioned and in approving the rule against partial-pre-emption enunciated in them held that "where a contiguous land holder seeks pre-emption and 'contiguity' being the only basis for his claim, he may pre-empt only that part of the land transferred to which his land is contiguous unless the land transferred is a compact block of area".</u>

10. On the basis of the aforesaid decisions the learned Counsel for the appellant assailed the following observations of the learned Judges of the High Court Division:

"Be that as it may, the plot No. 5211 at the north of the land transferred by the kabala in question is contiguous to the land transferred and as such the pre-emptors are entitled to pre-empt the Kabala land. In this respect the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee petitioner has submitted that since plot No. 5211 owned by the pre-emptors touches only half of the Kabala land, the pre-emptors would be entitled to proportion hate pre-emption to the extent of half of the land transferred. The provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act gives rights to a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred to pre-empt the land. There is nothing in the provision of section 96 that the contiguity must be in full and if there is partial contiguity the pre-emption would be allowed to the extent of contiguity. In this view I do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee petitioner that the pre-emptors would be entitled to partial pre-emption on the ground that the contiguity covers only half of the land transferred."

<u>11. He took particular exception to the sentence underlined by me in the aforesaid observations. It appears that there is no evidence regarding the extent of contiguity of the pre-emptor's land to the land sought to be pre-empted, namely, plot No. 5209, or as to which of the pre-emptor's land is contiguous to the said land and whether it is a compact block or divided into well demarcated separate plots. Mr. Hakim also mentioned that inasmuch as 16 plots measuring an area of 3.36 acres were sold at Tk. 10,000/- without plot wise value of each of these plots, the partial pre-emption allowed on the basis of valuation of the case plot made by the pre-emptor without ascertaining its actual value cannot be sustained in law. It is true that there is no evidence regarding the actual value of the case plot. In view of the legal position and the facts and circumstances of the case, it would seem that for determining the extent of contiguity between the lands concerned and the actual value of the lands sought to be pre-empted the case should be sent back on remand.</u>

12. The appeal is, therefore, allowed and remanded to the first appellate court to decide the extent of contiguity and valuation of the land, if necessary on taking fresh evidence. There will be no order as to costs.

End.
